a10a_1381024.text: Boy, that's absolutely incredible targeting down there. Congratulations.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Engle
a10a_1381024.text: You can almost begin to start smiling, can't you?

a10a_1381024.speaker: Young
a10a_1381024.text: To the boys in the back room. Yeah.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1381024.text: Ill bet Phil Shaffer has a smile across his face if he's around. Over.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Engle
a10a_1381024.text: Yes. He's in a room down the hall. But I'm sure he's grinning.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Young
a10a_1381024.text: Tell him to have one on me.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Engle
a10a_1381024.text: Roger. Will do.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1381024.text: How come all you people are up? How come all you people are up this early in the morning?

a10a_1381024.speaker: Engle
a10a_1381024.text: That's normal working hours, Gene-o.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1381024.text: I will try to pick you out a couple more interesting characteristics. Again, you can see that one sprayed crater up to the side. Actually, here's a better view, I can see the landing site coming in now, and we'll go down and take a look at Messier, Messier B, the Taruntius twins; we can see it from here. We'll put the zoom to them.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1381024.text: You can walk right up the landing site just like we did when we were down there. You can see Secchi; you can see the Apollo Ridge; you can see all those little ridges reflected very well in sunlight. You can't quite see our Sidewinder or Diamondback Ridge at this time, however.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Engle
a10a_1381024.text: OK. We understand. Yeah, that little crater that you're bringing into focus, bringing in the zoom now, with the rays, that's a real interesting little feature in it.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1381024.text: Yeah. Would you ask Jack Schmitt, please ask him what the name of that crater is, just for identification? I think we may nave seen that before. Over. And it's Censorinus A.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Engle
a10a_1381024.text: I think, I think you got a "got you" on Jack Schmitt. He's grimacing and his head is furrowing now, but he'll have a name for you here in a minute.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1381024.text: OK.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1381024.text: Jack, since we didn't get any pictures of Censorinus, we thought we'd zoom in on it from here.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Engle
a10a_1381024.text: Roger, Jack says the name of that one is temporarily Tom's Crater.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1381024.text: That sounds good. OK. And right ahead from the bright crater as you walk on across there, you can see Moltke. There's Moltke, and right up in there, if anybody from Oklahoma's listening, that's what we've termed the Oklahoma Hills. It's on the right. Over.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Engle
a10a_1381024.text: Roger. We got those, Tom.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1381024.text: In fact, this camera's got such good resolution I think I can even zoom on Moltke from here.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Engle
a10a_1381024.text: OK. We'll stand by.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1381024.text: Can you see the bright crater in the center of the screen there?

a10a_1381024.speaker: Engle
a10a_1381024.text: Roger. We got it.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1381024.text: That is Moltke. The Landing Site 1 is right to your left there. At least, it's in my monitor. So here we can see Landing Site 1. In fact, we can even see crater 130 in this tube. And all the white area which would probably be the tan area. It's white in my black and white - It's white in my black and white tube, but it's brown and tan out there as you look there. That's what we call the Oklahoma Hills. Over.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Engle
a10a_1381024.text: Roger, Tom. We've got it. It looks great. That's too bad that you all don't have color TV up there. This is a great view.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1381024.text: Yes. OK. I brought the zoom back again. That maria material is really looking a deeper brown, now.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Engle
a10a_1381024.text: Roger. OK.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1381024.text: Hey, Joe, we're starting to see the terminator come in, I believe. We're starting to see the terminator come in on the far side which is really getting to be interesting. And we might say we're real thankful for it too.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Engle
a10a_1381024.text: Rog. Understand.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1381024.text: We're going to show you a picture of the far side of the terminator in just a few minutes. One thing I'd like to point out if I could back on Messier. Those two sprayed craters, and I've made some drawings of them to bring back as to what it does - Leave it here, I'm going to zoom on them.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Engle
a10a_1381024.text: OK.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Young
a10a_1381024.text: Well, we've got a lot of pictures to bring back and I'm sure they'll be very interesting to you, but I'm afraid they're going to ask as many questions as they answer.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1381024.text: OK. If you look in the center of your screen you see two vertical craters. You got them? And you have the sprayed rays that come out down this way. Do you see those? Over.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Engle
a10a_1381024.text: Roger. We got it, Tom.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1381024.text: OK. That's the Messier Craters and from here again you can see the maria material. It is a brown and the inside of the crater is a light tan and the rays that are sprayed out of them. As you can see, there are just two rays pronged out of it. Out over the highland area it goes up to Censorinus, and those are tan rays that come out over the darker material. Now we're getting to see some of the back side, some rilles, some of the rugged side. We'll go down in this area.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Engle
a10a_1381024.text: Roger.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1381024.text: OK. I guess it can be, if you're upside down, it could be front side or back side.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Engle
a10a_1381024.text: OK.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1381024.text: The shadows are really lengthening and - The shadows are really lengthening in the terminator area and you can definitely see the terminator approaching.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Engle
a10a_1381024.text: Rog. We can see it on our screen here, Gene-o.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Young
a10a_1381024.text: I think what it is, is we're approaching it.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Engle
a10a_1381024.text: Good call, John.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1381024.text: One thing that we were real happy to see around - Rog. One thing that we're all happy to see around the Moon was some nighttime, because from the time we made TLI until we arrived at the Moon it was strictly out there in daytime all the time. It's really a pleasant change to get back for a little nighttime. Over.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Engle
a10a_1381024.text: Rog. Understand.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1381024.text: Joe, it's still incredible. It almost doesn't look real. This Moon is set against a blackest black, incredibly black, that you can ever imagine.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Engle
a10a_1381024.text: Rog, Understand.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1381024.text: The black has about the texture that you see often times that comes out of an oil smoke fire. It's really a - It's a jet black.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Engle
a10a_1381024.text: Roger. Copy. And you're about 2,000 miles [3,700 km] out now, 10.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1381024.text: Rog. Understand 2,000 miles [3,700 km] out.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1381024.text: I never thought anything could be as enjoyable as this, even with the fuel cell light on.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Engle
a10a_1381024.text: Rog.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1381024.text: Okay. Again, here's a real good size crater with patterns. I'll zoom in on it.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Engle
a10a_1381024.text: Roger.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Engle
a10a_1381024.text: Roger. We can pick it up now and we're picking up the rays, Tom.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1381024.text: OK. As you look at that crater, again, the bottom floor of it is tan. You can see some slumping on the walls; the sites are chalky white; the rays going out are light tan; the area surrounding it is a darker tan, and then you move over to the maria area which is a darker brown than up here. But the crater is really a beautiful crater. It stands out with all those rays on it.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1381024.text: And down below, you can see the remains of an old crater still in the maria material. Try to put it right in the center of your screen and it is right at the edge where the mare starts. Can you see it? Over.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Engle
a10a_1381024.text: Roger. We got it. And it looks like there's another one on over to the left and down a little bit, another old crater with some maria in the middle. It may be shadows.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1381024.text: Sure is. Right there.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Slayton
a10a_1381024.text: What color did you say that was, Tom?

a10a_1381024.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1381024.text: Say again. Over.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Slayton
a10a_1381024.text: What color did you say that was?

a10a_1381024.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1381024.text: Oh, is that our Guidance Officer? Roger. If that was Phil Shaffer talking, just tell him that he's got a bottle of champagne due him for that vector. Over.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Engle
a10a_1381024.text: That was Deke. He was wondering - verify the color of that maria.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1381024.text: OK. I know what he's talking about but I'll - We'll talk about that later.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1381024.text: He's got one coming for not passing up any PADs while were gone from John.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1381024.text: Hey, I bet we fooled old Snoopy.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Engle
a10a_1381024.text: Rog.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1381024.text: OK, Houston. I've got an interesting sight like we've never seen. Houston, take a look at this. We've never seen this before. The varied colors. You see the two mare areas on the left.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Engle
a10a_1381024.text: Roger. Got them.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1381024.text: Well, the one right - They're different shades. The one right in the center is a darker brown than the one over to the left. You can see where they've flowed together there. It is a lighter brown, tending to a tan. I'll put the zoom on and hope you can get it. Here it is. We've never seen this before ourselves.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Engle
a10a_1381024.text: OK. It's showing up pretty good right now, the way you're describing it. There you go. It looks great.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Young
a10a_1381024.text: Looks like a couple of different flows there.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1381024.text: Right in the center of your screen you should see the discontinuity between the two maria areas. The one on the right is a darker brown, nearly a chocolate brown now, and the one on the left is a tan. Over.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Engle
a10a_1381024.text: Roger. That's just how they're coming in down here, Tom.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1381024.text: Rog. Great. Hey, if you look over in the distance, you can see the nighttime coming on the Moon up near the terminator and you do get some outstanding features there.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Engle
a10a_1381024.text: Roger. We've got that.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1381024.text: That's the first time we've been able to look at this distance and see a real discernible difference in the maria materials. But this is really kind of a classic, I think the - You can see the flows, and also if you take a look, I'll try to zoom some more - the maria on the left, you can see some of the darker material near the upper edge of that where it's flowing in there.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Engle
a10a_1381024.text: Roger.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1381024.text: OK. That's the picture we have now. You can see we probably are well on our way out close to 3,000 miles [5,550 km] now. It's still a beautiful view. In fact, just looking at it, you recollect that we've come a long ways in a few years, so just imagine where were going to go in a few more years. Over.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Engle
a10a_1381024.text: Roger that, Tom.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1381024.text: Again, I just want to check the resolution of this camera and zoom in on Censorinus, and the landing site where Apollo 11 will land, and Ill go back and zoom in on that again. Over.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Engle
a10a_1381024.text: Roger.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1381024.text: OK. There is Censorinus. Over here is the crater Moltke, above Maskelyne, Maskelyne B. We come down here to Little Bright Crater there. It's right near the dip of the Oklahoma foothills there. It's called Moltke, and to the left, right in this area, is the landing site where Apollo 11 should land. Over.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Engle
a10a_1381024.text: OK. We got them all, Tom. They are coming through real good.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Young
a10a_1381024.text: Boy, right now, it's like watching it through a telescope. It's fantastic.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1381024.text: Right in the center of your screen is the landing site. Again you can see the hills on the other side down in this area. But the approach is very well marked by Censorinus there on one side and the lead in there from the two Maskelyne craters. Over.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Engle
a10a_1381024.text: Roger. We're getting real good resolution down here, Tom.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1381024.text: OK.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1381024.text: I guess we've been up nearly 24 hours now, but it feels so great, I don't think we will go to sleep for a few more hours. Over.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Engle
a10a_1381024.text: OK. Understand, Tom.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1381024.text: Just looking at this is about the best go pill you could ever stand. Over.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Engle
a10a_1381024.text: Roger.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1381024.text: Tom's going to try and zoom in on Langrenus for you. It's a pretty interesting crater; it's in the sunlight at the moment.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1381024.text: OK. What you have there is the crater Langrenus, and again, that is somewhat on the path that leads up to the Apollo Landing Site number 2. It comes right down this way. There you have the other craters, and, there is Messier, comes on down across In fact, there is the crater Weatherford and Mount Marilyn, down to Censorinus and comes right on over into Moltke and the landing site.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Engle
a10a_1381024.text: Rog. Very good tour.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1381024.text: Yeah. John sort of explained it here a second ago for us all. He said he can't believe what he is seeing, and we really can't. We just can't believe what we're seeing. I tell you, Joe, this satellite of ours, this Moon of ours, had a rough beginning somewhere back there. Over.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Engle
a10a_1381024.text: Rog. Understand, Gene.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1381024.text: It's really a privilege to sit - it's really a great privilege to just sit here and, as the spacecraft moves radially outward and look at it, to feel - just to share some of our views here with you. Over.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Engle
a10a_1381024.text: Copy that. Thank you.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1381024.text: The important thing about that camera, Joe, is what you're seeing is happening and what you haven't seen ain't happened yet.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Engle
a10a_1381024.text: Roger.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1381024.text: OK. There you are. I hope the colors come out the same to you, the same as we see them here. You can see the discontinuity there By those two craters. Over.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Engle
a10a_1381024.text: Roger. It looks great, Tom: just like you're describing it.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1381024.text: OK. Thank you.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1381024.text: OK, Houston. This is Apollo 10. All three of us are commenting again about this fantastic view out here and how it's probably just as well that we approached this thing in night side where you can't see it, because if we approached at this angle coming in, you would really have to shut your eyes. Over.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Engle
a10a_1381024.text: Rog. Understand.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1381024.text: Hey now, I wasn't skeptical when we were coming in. I just said I'd believe all that targeting when I saw 60 miles [111 km], and I'm a believer, and you've got one on me. But boy, I tell you if we were going forward now it would be a different story.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Engle
a10a_1381024.text: Roger.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Young
a10a_1381024.text: Along that line, I want to congratulate you on that 5-degree window mark. It was perfect.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Engle
a10a_1381024.text: OK. We copy.

a10a_1381024.speaker: Mission Control
a10a_1381024.text: 138:32:45 Apollo 10 now 2,700 [nautical] miles [5,000 km] from the Moon.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1383222.text: Houston, Apollo 10. You know you've often heard of the nursery rhyme about the man in the Moon. We didn't see one there, there were three men around the Moon and pretty soon we hope that there are three men - pardon me, two men on the Moon and one circling. But as far as seeing a man in the Moon directly, we just didn't see it this time. Over.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Engle
a10a_1383222.text: OK, Tom. Thank you.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1383222.text: And we were looking, too.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Engle
a10a_1383222.text: Roger.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Young
a10a_1383222.text: If there were any people down there, they had a lot of rocks to play with.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1383222.text: It won't be long now until Snoopy's descent stage will be there with a big red, white, and blue American flag on it, though.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Engle
a10a_1383222.text: Roger that.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1383222.text: Houston, for just a quick break here we want to be able to show you that we're slowing down now as we leave the Moon. You've seen a fantastic sight. We want to just take you inside the cockpit and say hello for a minute, and then when we come back out you should be able to see the - to really get a better view of the Moon there with respect to having a whole sphere. Over.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Engle
a10a_1383222.text: OK. Mighty fine. We're standing by, Tom.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Engle
a10a_1383222.text: OK. Your picture is coming in real good, real clear.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Young
a10a_1383222.text: Hello, everybody.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1383222.text: While the view outside is fantastic, inside here, we look like about three scroungy characters, but we really feel great, and it's been a fantastic trip. Over.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Engle
a10a_1383222.text: Roger, Tom.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Engle
a10a_1383222.text: You guys looking mighty good in there.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1383222.text: Roger. You getting any color on us in here?

a10a_1383222.speaker: Engle
a10a_1383222.text: Roger. The color is real good inside.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1383222.text: Well, we feel great, and we've felt great ever since lift-off, and it's been a fantastic voyage. In just a minute we'll turn the camera around and show you John. Over

a10a_1383222.speaker: Engle
a10a_1383222.text: Roger. Who is winning the beard-growing contest in there?

a10a_1383222.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1383222.text: Well, I don't know. John's got the mustache won. I don't knew about the beard.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1383222.text: I'm the baby of the group, Joe.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Engle
a10a_1383222.text: OK.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1383222.text: OK. We'll show you John.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1383222.text: John's got a little blue ink on his fingers.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Young
a10a_1383222.text: I was writing a letter and I broke my pen. Does it show up in living color?

a10a_1383222.speaker: Engle
a10a_1383222.text: Open your hand up again.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Engle
a10a_1383222.text: Yes. It sure does.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Young
a10a_1383222.text: How about that.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Young
a10a_1383222.text: You can see we're pretty happy about this whole business.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Engle
a10a_1383222.text: Roger that. It sure looks good to see you again.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1383222.text: What are you doing?

a10a_1383222.speaker: Engle
a10a_1383222.text: We got your message on the blue dye, John.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1383222.text: Roger. You've got to watch when you write a lot with blue pens, and we're going to take you back outside and show you the Moon as we see it. Over.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Mission Control
a10a_1383222.text: 138:39:37 And we have a view from 3,000 [nautical] miles [5,550 km].

a10a_1383222.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1383222.text: All three of us are commenting again that for the scientific interest, about the difference in color on that one maria area I pointed out to you there as soon as I saw it, and it's really becoming pronounced now. The basic maria area - I'm going to zoom in again is like a chocolate brown, and from this Sun angle and over to the left is like a tannish brown. And again Ill zoom in and just see how it looks to you. Over.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1383222.text: Joe, the Moon is starting to lose its spherical shape. It's becoming oblong now with the terminator, with us going around into the area of the terminator.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Engle
a10a_1383222.text: Roger. We are showing that on our screens down here.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1383222.text: You know, looking at the Earth terminator and the Moon terminator is the only way we can figure out which is up and which is down, and sometimes they don't agree.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Engle
a10a_1383222.text: Roger.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Young
a10a_1383222.text: For you people who aren't in the space flight business, I say it sure is fantastic and you really ought to try it.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Engle
a10a_1383222.text: Thank you, John. I hope to someday.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1383222.text: This is Apollo 10. It appears that the tube - Roger, Joe. Houston, it appears that the tube is starting to saturate when I go to full zoom and then it's gathering in too much light and it's coming back normal from the Sun's rays. Are you getting that on your screen? Over.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Engle
a10a_1383222.text: No. We're still getting a real good picture down here. Tom.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1383222.text: OK. I'll go back to the full zoom and just hold it there for a little bit.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1383222.text: Joe, I've always believed that nothing is impossible, and now I'm convinced of it, and I hope that what we are doing here and what's going to go on in the future is going to be something that's going to be a betterment to all mankind. I'm convinced of that.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Engle
a10a_1383222.text: Roger that.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1383222.text: Houston, how does your picture look now, and are you saturated at all? Over.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Engle
a10a_1383222.text: Roger. We're starting to get saturated now, Tom.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1383222.text: OK. It appears that probably when I go to the wide angle enough to zoom it, it starts to saturate a little bit, so I'll keep it down to lower at this time.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Engle
a10a_1383222.text: Roger. It's a whole lot better now.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1383222.text: Also you notice - How you can really start to notice near the horizons how rugged it is, and do you see the little peaks sticking up on it?

a10a_1383222.speaker: Engle
a10a_1383222.text: Roger. We picked, those out.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1383222.text: Say, Houston. The Moon, as we move away and our velocity slows down, the Moon is starting to grow less in diameter relative - as far as our visual view, so what we'll do is terminate the TV now and we'll bring it back on in a little while after we squared away here and show you a little bit better distant view. Over.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Engle
a10a_1383222.text: OK. Mighty fine, Tom.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1383222.text: OK. And this is Apollo 10 signing off for a while, and we'll be back in about 30 or 40 minutes and see how it looks then. Over.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Engle
a10a_1383222.text: OK, 10. This is Houston. We'd like to dump the tape now, and we'd like to keep the High Gain Antenna while we do that.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Young
a10a_1383222.text: Yes sir.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1383222.text: Will this attitude be ok, Joe?

a10a_1383222.speaker: Mission Control
a10a_1383222.text: 138:44:18 At the conclusion of the television transmission, Apollo 10 was about 3,390 nautical miles [6,280 km] from the Moon. The Trans-Earth Injection maneuver, which started the spacecraft back to Earth, as you heard early in the television transmission, was very close to nominal. The maneuver is targeted to bring Apollo 10 back to Earth at a Ground Elapsed Time of 192 hours, 4 minutes, or just 4 minutes - 8 days and 4 minutes after lift-off from Cape Kennedy. At the present time the spacecraft is traveling at a speed of 6,046 feet per second [1,842 m/s], and we show 3,436 nautical miles [6

a10a_1383222.speaker: Engle
a10a_1383222.text: Roger. That will be fine.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Young
a10a_1383222.text: Houston. You want to delay - We're going to get the Realign and going to PTC REFSMMAT? That's what you are saying, isn't it? Is that correct?

a10a_1383222.speaker: Engle
a10a_1383222.text: That's correct.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1383222.text: Roger, Houston. This is 10. We would like to stay in this attitude for a while, if it's ok. If we don't violate any thermal constraints. Over.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Engle
a10a_1383222.text: OK. Let me check on that, Tom. I think that will be ok.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1383222.text: All right.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Engle
a10a_1383222.text: 10, this is Houston. Roger, Tom. You can stay in that attitude. There is no restraint on the thermal world.

a10a_1383222.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1383222.text: OK. Real fine. Thank you, Joe. Over.

a10a_1384719.speaker: Engle
a10a_1384719.text: OK, 10. This is Houston. You can have the computer back now. And your REFSMMAT is in.

a10a_1384719.speaker: Young
a10a_1384719.text: We've had the computer for quite a while.

a10a_1384719.speaker: Engle
a10a_1384719.text: OK. I'm sorry.

a10a_1384719.speaker: Young
a10a_1384719.text: I hope. Because we've been playing with it.

a10a_1384719.speaker: Engle
a10a_1384719.text: You're right.

a10a_1384719.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1384719.text: Hello, Houston. This is 10.

a10a_1384719.speaker: Engle
a10a_1384719.text: Go ahead, 10.

a10a_1384719.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1384719.text: This is - We're circling 26 to 26½ volts up here pretty regularly right at the moment.

a10a_1384719.speaker: Engle
a10a_1384719.text: Roger. We copy.

a10a_1384719.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1384719.text: We're going to see if we can bring it up a little bit. We're going to see if we can bring it up a little bit. We've got the DDC power off - DEDA power, rather, and a couple of other things, and we'll watch it, but I just wanted to let you know we're looking at a low 26½.

a10a_1384719.speaker: Engle
a10a_1384719.text: Roger. We copy. We'll look at it.

a10a_1384719.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1384719.text: And I guess we're up to about 27 now, so we're probably in pretty good shape.

a10a_1384719.speaker: Engle
a10a_1384719.text: OK, 10. I'm going to turn you over to the Marines now. I'll see you a little later.

a10a_1384719.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1384719.text: Roger, Joe. Thanks a lot for all the help there on CapCom and the whole mission is real great. We'll see you back in Houston probably, next Tuesday. Over.

a10a_1384719.speaker: Engle
a10a_1384719.text: Roger that. You're right in the groove.

a10a_1384719.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1384719.text: Thank you, Joseph.

a10a_1384719.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1384719.text: Houston, Charlie Brown. Do you want me to put my High Bit Rate to Low?

a10a_1384719.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1384719.text: Stand by one. [Pause.]

a10a_1384719.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1384719.text: Affirmative, Apollo 10. Put your High Bit Rate to Low.

a10a_1384719.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1384719.text: OK. [Long pause.]

a10a_1384719.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1384719.text: Apollo 10, Houston. We're going to keep the configuration weve got until we get P52 finished and the dump finished. Over.

a10a_1384719.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1384719.text: Rog. [Long pause.]

a10a_1384719.speaker: Young
a10a_1384719.text: Houston, on these P52s REFSMMAT Realigns, can you give us attitudes to go to so that we can avoid the gimbal lock alarm?

a10a_1384719.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1384719.text: Roger. I think we can do that. Stand by. [Long pause.]

a10a_1384719.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1384719.text: Hello, Houston. I've got some onboard readouts for you.

a10a_1384719.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1384719.text: Roger. Go ahead, 10.

a10a_1384719.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1384719.text: OK. Batt C is 37, Pyro A is 37, Pyro B is 37.

a10a_1384719.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1384719.text: Roger. Understand Batt B...

a10a_1384719.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1384719.text: ...RCS A is 55, B is 7...

a10a_1384719.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1384719.text: Apollo 10...

a10a_1384719.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1384719.text: ...RCS A is 55 percent - Okay. I'm ready now. RCS A is 55, B is 71; C, 66; D is 63 per cent. [Pause.] Over.

a10a_1384719.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1384719.text: Roger, Apollo 10. We copy, 37, 37, 37, 55, 71, 66, 63, and you can do your P52 in the present attitude and go right from there to PTC. Over.

a10a_1384719.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1384719.text: OK. P52 in present attitude and right from there to PTC. As it says on page 94 of our Flight Plan, we can tell we're returning because we're facing the other way. A phrase by that one famous dog. [Long pause.]

a10a_1384719.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1384719.text: Houston, our condenser exhaust temperature is cycling again between the limits, and I think it just triggered a quick Master Alarm on fuel cell 2, but it's cycling again just like it was in lunar orbit.

a10a_1384719.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1384719.text: Roger, 10. We copy. [Long pause.]

a10a_1384719.speaker: Mission Control
a10a_1384719.text: 138:59:35 This is Apollo - This is Apollo Control. We're estimating about 15 minutes for the change of shift press briefing as the Maroon team of Flight Controllers goes off shift. Participants will be - stand by.

a10a_1384719.speaker: Young
a10a_1384719.text: Houston, Apollo 10. You said it's okay to realign the PTC right now?

a10a_1384719.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1384719.text: Stand by one. [Long pause.]

a10a_1384719.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1384719.text: Apollo 10, Houston. Go ahead with your PTC alignment.

a10a_1384719.speaker: Young
a10a_1384719.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a10a_1384719.speaker: Mission Control
a10a_1384719.text: 139:00:28 This is Apollo Control. To pick up again on the press conference; participants will be Maroon team Flight Director Milton Windler, Spacecraft Communicator Joe Engle, Astronaut geologist Jack Schmitt. They are estimating about 15 minutes arrival at the main auditorium here at the Manned Spacecraft Center. We rejoin the air to ground communications between Apollo 10 and Mission Control.

a10a_1384719.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1384719.text: Apollo 10, Houston. We'd like you to turn on your fuel cell 2 H 2 purge line heater. Over.

a10a_1384719.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1384719.text: Yeah. I've had the H 2 purge line heater on about 5 minutes now, Jack.

a10a_1384719.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1384719.text: Roger, Gene.

a10a_1384719.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1384719.text: And I'm planning a H 2 - and an O 2 purge at 140. Is that correct, 139:30?

a10a_1384719.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1384719.text: Stand by. [Pause.]

a10a_1384719.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1384719.text: That is affirmative, Gene. 139:30, purge fuel cells.

a10a_1384719.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1384719.text: OK. Thank you, Jack. I assume not fuel cell 1, though. Is that correct? Just 2 and 3? [Long pause.]

a10a_1384719.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1384719.text: Gene, just purge 2 and 3, not 1. Over.

a10a_1384719.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1384719.text: Thank you, Jack.

a10a_1390259.speaker: Young
a10a_1390259.text: Houston, Apollo 10. Confirm that this is an option 1 platform Realign.

a10a_1390259.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1390259.text: Houston, Apollo 10. Say again.

a10a_1390259.speaker: Young
a10a_1390259.text: Roger. Confirm that this is an option 1 platform Realign.

a10a_1390259.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1390259.text: Stand by one.

a10a_1390259.speaker: Young
a10a_1390259.text: Im sure it is. I just wanted you to make sure.

a10a_1390259.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1390259.text: OK, John. That's an option 1 confirmed.

a10a_1390259.speaker: Young
a10a_1390259.text: Roger.

a10a_1390259.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1390259.text: Hello, Jack. I've got some Rad readings.

a10a_1390259.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1390259.text: Go ahead with the Rad.

a10a_1390259.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1390259.text: Commander is 26042, Chimp [CMP] is 05311, and I'm 15043.

a10a_1390259.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1390259.text: Roger. Copy 26042, 05311, 15043. Thank you.

a10a_1390259.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1390259.text: And negative on the - on the pills today.

a10a_1390259.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1390259.text: Roger. Copy.

a10a_1390259.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1390259.text: And the fans have been cycled.

a10a_1390259.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1390259.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a10a_1390259.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1390259.text: Apollo 10, Houston...

a10a_1390259.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1390259.text: Houston, we're going through a regulator check at this time.

a10a_1390259.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1390259.text: Roger. We copy.

a10a_1390259.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1390259.text: Go ahead.

a10a_1390259.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1390259.text: Yes. We'd like to know - Did you turn the GDC off by going to ECA? Over.

a10a_1390259.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1390259.text: Roger. We turned it off and then turned it back on here since we're going to do this IMU Realign. Over.

a10a_1390259.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1390259.text: Roger. Understand off and then on. Thank you.

a10a_1390259.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1390259.text: Yep. We want to check again how much it increased our voltage and after we get the IMU completely torqued around, then I'm going to turn the GDC/ECA bar to ECA. Over.

a10a_1390259.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1390259.text: OK, Tom.

a10a_1390259.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1390259.text: Houston, this is 10. When I start up the secondary glycol pump I get a Main Bus A undervolt. Probably is a transient, but I turned it off at this time.

a10a_1390259.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1390259.text: Roger. We copy.

a10a_1390259.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1390259.text: I'm sure it's a start-up transient, but I haven't start - I haven't tried it again, so recommend we just delete it. It did start up and [garble] the secondary evaporator has been working well. Do you - shall we delete that test or shall we give it a try?

a10a_1390259.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1390259.text: Stand by one. We'll check. [Pause.]

a10a_1390259.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1390259.text: Apollo 10, Houston. Delete the secondary loop check. Over.

a10a_1390259.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1390259.text: Very good. Thank you, Jack.

a10a_1390259.speaker: Mission Control
a10a_1390259.text: This is Apollo Control. Something in the nature of a 'gee-wizz' number: At the time of the Trans-Earth Injection burn, Apollo 10 was some 211,373 miles [391,463 km] away from Earth on the back side of the Moon. Change of shift briefing is scheduled to begin momentarily in the main auditorium. Air to ground Apollo 10 transmissions will be picked up at the conclusion of the press conference; and at 139 hours, 13 minutes Ground Elapsed Time; this is Apollo Control.

a10a_1393016.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1393016.text: OK. We got it now. Looks good.

a10a_1393016.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1393016.text: When you see the terminator coming on there, it looks like the Moon is lopsided. John is holding the camera, panning, and Gene is opening focus on it. And it's a beautiful view there. Over.

a10a_1393016.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1393016.text: Yes. Really looks good from here, Tom.

a10a_1393016.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1393016.text: OK. How's your color look on it now? Over.

a10a_1393016.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1393016.text: In the MOCR here, we're seeing a green and white Moon.

a10a_1393016.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1393016.text: Well. Green and white?

a10a_1393016.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1393016.text: Yeah. It's green up near the terminator and white up near the - near the other limb.

a10a_1393016.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1393016.text: You must be talking about the cheesy part of it, huh?

a10a_1393016.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1393016.text: Yeah. I guess you guys must have done that to it.

a10a_1393016.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1393016.text: Yes. You might say something like that. OK. Again, just for correlation on the colors that we have - about the best area of that mare that I can describe, looks like a chocolate milkshake. That's about the best of color of brown that I can describe. Over.

a10a_1393016.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1393016.text: Roger, Tom. We copy. Move that camera a little bit to the right.

a10a_1393016.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1393016.text: We'll get it in with our monitor. Stand by one. [Long pause.]

a10a_1393016.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1393016.text: OK, 10. That's real good.

a10a_1393016.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1393016.text: How's it look from here, Jack?

a10a_1393016.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1393016.text: That's real good now, Gene.

a10a_1393016.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1393016.text: And, Houston, 10. How does your color look? Over.

a10a_1393016.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1393016.text: Stand by one, Tom. I don't know if we're getting true color in here.

a10a_1393016.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1393016.text: OK. [Pause.]

a10a_1393016.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1393016.text: Our color is looking real good now, Tom.

a10a_1393016.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1393016.text: OK. [Long pause.]

a10a_1393016.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1393016.text: You're looking at the window. The mode now - We backed off so you can see the shade or the shadow of the hatch window, so you got an idea what size it might be if you could see any of the window frame at all. John's backed off to the point where the Moon is out through the hatch window.

a10a_1393016.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1393016.text: Roger. I can just make out the edge of the hatch window.

a10a_1393016.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1393016.text: It gives you an idea of relative size as to what we're seeing compared to the window itself. [Long pause.]

a10a_1393016.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1393016.text: OK, Houston. We just wanted to give you one last show to show how it started - the lighted parts started to look oblong as we can move out and see the terminator start to continue to move out further and slow down. And it's been real great to - being able to show you this so you can share the same view that we have. Over.

a10a_1393016.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1393016.text: Roger, Tom. And it looks real good and I know the folks here at home are really enjoying the show. I bet you feel like you're really moving out.

a10a_1393016.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1393016.text: That initial climb out was just fantastic, Jack. Like we were telling Joe earlier that it's a good thing we approached the Moon from the other way because if we approached it from this way straight going like that, you wouldn't - you'd have to shut your eyes. Over. [Long pause.]

a10a_1393016.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1393016.text: And, Tom...

a10a_1393016.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1393016.text: It's going to be real interesting for us to look at is - Oh. Pardon me. I was just going to say it's going to be real interesting for us to look at the TV films after we get back. Over.

a10a_1393016.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1393016.text: Yeah, Tom. I know you'll enjoy that. The TV experts wanted me to tell you that your adjustment of the color camera for both exterior and interior is just perfect. Over.

a10a_1393016.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1393016.text: OK. Real fine. Thank you. [Long pause.]

a10a_1393016.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1393016.text: OK, Houston. This is Apollo 10. We've been up about 21 hours, nearly 22 hours, and we think we'll go ahead and start setup for the sleep cycle and just go ahead and start with the PTC attitude. And at this time, we'll go ahead and turn the TV off, and this is Apollo 10 signing off for the TV.

a10a_1393016.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1393016.text: Roger, Tom. Thanks a lot for the TV show. It's a little early around here for some of the folks, but I know some of them will get it later in the day. It's a real good show.

a10a_1393016.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1393016.text: OK.

a10a_1393721.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1393721.text: OK.

a10a_1393721.speaker: Young
a10a_1393721.text: Houston, on this PTC, do you want to establish 20-degree deadband at one-tenth of a degree per second, or you want to try this other thing?

a10a_1393721.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1393721.text: John, this is Houston. We want the 30-degree deadband with a three-tenths degree per second. Over. Correction, three-tenths degree per second.

a10a_1393721.speaker: Young
a10a_1393721.text: OK. It's set up just the way you did - set up just the way we did coming here. Right?

a10a_1393721.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1393721.text: That's affirmative, John. And when you get down to disabling jets, we want you to disable all jets in quads C and D and we're standing here looking at the procedure, if you want us to help you out on it.

a10a_1393721.speaker: Young
a10a_1393721.text: Roger. Understand. Charlie and Dog?

a10a_1393721.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1393721.text: That's affirmative.

a10a_1393721.speaker: Young
a10a_1393721.text: OK. [Pause.]

a10a_1393721.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1393721.text: Hello, Houston. Apollo 10. Over.

a10a_1393721.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1393721.text: Go ahead, 10.

a10a_1393721.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1393721.text: OK, Jack. Looking ahead in the Flight Plan, what we'd like to do is make this a pretty long sleep period. I understand that the first midcourse occurs in 15 hours and was initially looked at about 1 foot per second, which shows we're right in the slot. And what we'd like to do is sleep in a little bit longer than what was outlined here, see, since we've been up for about 22 hours. Over.

a10a_1393721.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1393721.text: OK. Let's get these people to arrange that. Stand by. please.

a10a_1393721.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1393721.text: OK. [Long pause.]

a10a_1393721.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1393721.text: Tom, looks like we're planned to let you sleep in already and the only thing that would possibly change that Flight-Pan-wise is some P23 activity, which we can postpone. Over.

a10a_1393721.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1393721.text: OK. We're all of us kind of bushed out now, just a little bit tired from doing all this today, and John particularly. He's really worked hard on that landmark tracking and his eyeballs are a little sore, so if we can postpone that for a little while and just sleep in, we'd sure appreciate it. Over.

a10a_1393721.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1393721.text: Sure. We'll work that out. And we want to ask you if you've been getting any caution and warning on fuel cell 2 recently.

a10a_1393721.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1393721.text: No. The cycling is still there, but it hasn't cycled into the caution and warning region.

a10a_1393721.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1393721.text: Roger. It turns out that the purge fuel cell 2 didn't change anything, and we're trying to work something out, so this won't be bothering you during the time you're trying to sleep. Over.

a10a_1393721.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1393721.text: OK, Apparently the package or the pump, or whatever is cycling, doesn't bother you down there. Huh?

a10a_1393721.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1393721.text: Well, the exhaust temperature's getting down near the caution and warning limits. It hasn't gone over them yet. But we thought, if they started doing it, why, it was going to bother you and we're trying to figure out something else.

a10a_1393721.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1393721.text: Yeah. I know. But my question is, your analysis of what's causing the cycle, maybe the pump is going on and off, or there's a temperature sensor that's out of balance or something. Whatever you think it might be, it isn't bothering you, huh? [Long pause.]

a10a_1393721.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1393721.text: Gene, we're just taking a look at fuel cell 2, and we're analyzing what it's doing, but at the moment, it is of no excessive concern. Over.

a10a_1454715.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1454715.text: No. We haven't fired a thruster. The attitude's looking real good. And we got a little traveling music, if you'd like to listen.

a10a_1454715.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1454715.text: Go ahead. Over.

a10a_1454715.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1454715.text: OK. Stand by. [Long pause.]

a10a_1454715.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1454715.text: OK, 10. Houston. How'd the traveling music come through?

a10a_1454715.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1454715.text: That was really great, Jack. You people have come up with some [laughter] some real great [laughter] numbers there for us. We sure appreciate it. Over.

a10a_1454715.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1454715.text: Well, thank you, Tom. Since the other day you made a special request for the Marine Corps Hymn, why, everybody around here has been trying to get us to play that. But I can't allow them to do that since you'd have to stand up, and you guys have said you don't know which way is up so we can't play that one.

a10a_1454715.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1454715.text: [Laughter.] OK. Understand. Over.

a10a_1454715.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1454715.text: Hey, Jack, how come it takes so much longer to train you to be a CapCom than Charlie and Bruce and Joe? [Long pause.]

a10a_1454715.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1454715.text: What Gene's trying to say is that good Marine Corps training must have come through, there. Over. [Pause.]

a10a_1454715.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1454715.text: I hear you. Keep talking. [Pause.]

a10a_1454715.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1454715.text: Just kidding, there. Over.

a10a_1454715.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1454715.text: Well. You may notice that your exhaust temperature in fuel cell 2 is stabilized out, and sure enough, it's been that way for the last few hours. So it looks like that's no sweat. Your trajectory, by the way, is right on. You're laying right in the middle of the fairway there - it - taking us - It's going to take us about 15 hours to predict the uncertainties in your trajectory, as a matter of fact, so we're going to skip midcourse 5. And we have a choice of making either midcourse 6 or 7. And we're going to make midcourse 6, I believe, and it'll only be 1½ feet per second [0.46 m/s]. Ov

a10a_1454715.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1454715.text: Roger. That just sounds beautiful. It looks like that burn back of the Moon - the guidance and the trajectory, and everything put us right in the - just right down the alleyway of the fairway. Over.

a10a_1454715.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1454715.text: Righto. You're going to pass through the lunar sphere of influence at 148:39. And during the time you were sleeping, you got to the point where you stopped decelerating, and you are now accelerating, and you're 187,300 [nautical] miles [346k,880 km] out, and you're about 4,800 feet per second [1,460 m/s].

a10a_1454715.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1454715.text: Roger. 4,800 feet per second [1,460 m/s]. We've got a beautiful view out here of both the Earth and the Moon in our hatches and say every half a rev, we can see both of them for quite a while. And when you get High Gain lock through Goldstone, we'll show them to you for just a couple of minutes. Over.

a10a_1454715.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1454715.text: Sure would like to take a look at that. Let's see if we can crank that up.

a10a_1454715.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1454715.text: Roger. I don't know if Goldstone has contact yet. I'll leave that up to you. Over.

a10a_1454715.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1454715.text: Hey, Jack, I just put battery A [on] charge. Started about 2 minutes ago.

a10a_1454715.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1454715.text: OK. That was one of the items in the Flight Plan update, and I understand you've got Batt A charge on the line. Got a little bit of advance weather in the landing area. The forecast for your landing time is 1,800 [feet, 550 metres] scattered, 10,000 [feet, 3,000 metres] broken, high broken, winds 120 [degrees] at 15 [knots, 7.8 m/s]. Seas will be 5 feet [1.5 metres], and there are scattered showers in that area, which means less than 10 percent of the area has showers. Right now, there's a stationary front sitting over that area, but it's quite weak. And the recovery forces this morning conduc

a10a_1454715.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1454715.text: And, 10, we've got some morning news here, if you want to listen to it sometime. [Long pause.]

a10a_1455716.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1455716.text: Hello, Houston. Apollo 10. Over.

a10a_1455716.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1455716.text: Apollo 10, Houston. How do you read me now?

a10a_1455716.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1455716.text: Roger, Jack. Reading you loud and clear. I guess we switched antennas, and we lost comm just about the time you said 1,800 scattered. Over.

a10a_1455716.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1455716.text: Oh, all right. We'll go through that again. Your forecast weather for the landing area is 1,800 [feet, 550 metres] scattered, 10,000 [feet, 3,048 metres] broken, and high broken. The winds will be 120 [degrees] at 15 [knots, 7.8 m/s], 5-foot [1.5 metres] seas, and there are scattered showers in the area, which means, however, there's less than ten per cent getting showers, and the recovery people were conducting a simulation in your landing area this morning. There's a stationary front in the landing area. However, it's relatively weak, as you can tell from the weather. And we'll continue upda

a10a_1455716.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1455716.text: Roger. Go ahead.

a10a_1455716.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1455716.text: OK. Apollo 10 morning newscast from the Manned Spacecraft Center Public Affairs Office. Everybody's really raving about your latest television pictures. They say, the television pictures of the Moon beamed to Earth from Apollo 10 shortly after TEI are being described as the most spectacular of the mission. Because of the early morning schedule for much of the U.S., the transmission is being replayed at various hours throughout the day. However, the consensus of opinion here is the same as yours, utterly fantastic. Aside from the Apollo 10 news, here is a summary of other news highlights and a

a10a_1455716.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1455716.text: [Laughter.] Roger. Houston. That's quite a bit of news. And tell the governor down in Pago Pago we appreciate it but he doesn't have to go to any special effort. Over.

a10a_1455716.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1455716.text: Yes. Well. I didn't read the last sentence here. It said. "Maybe there will be dancing girls there"; But now you know. And by the way, the unemployed local philosopher now says that...

a10a_1455716.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1455716.text: Oh, well. If he wants to go to the special effort.

a10a_1455716.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1455716.text: Yes, I thought you might change your mind. By the way, the unemployed local philosopher...

a10a_1455716.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1455716.text: [Garble].

a10a_1455716.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1455716.text: ...now says that due to your efforts, color television is now on its way back.

a10a_1455716.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1455716.text: Roger. Give our best to the unemployed philosopher there. And that total situation down in Samoa sounds like it's - Is that going to be a top hat or topless type of affair? Over.

a10a_1455716.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1455716.text: Just come as you are, Tom.

a10a_1455716.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1455716.text: OK.

a10a_1455716.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1455716.text: OK. Hey. Jack. You got our astrocast today?

a10a_1455716.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1455716.text: Stand by. We'll see if we can get them. [Long pause.]

a10a_1455716.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1455716.text: And. Apollo 10. Houston. Looks like your TV lines will be ready from Goldstone at 146:47, 40 more minutes.

a10a_1455716.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1455716.text: Roger. 146:47. [Pause.]

a10a_1455716.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1455716.text: Hey. Jack, when we get back if we have time. I'd sure like to hear [garble].

a10a_1455716.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1455716.text: Sorry. You'll have to speak into the microphone. I didn't catch that.

a10a_1460934.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1460934.text: Apollo 10. Houston. How do you read?

a10a_1460934.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1460934.text: Roger. Houston. Reading you loud and clear. Over.

a10a_1460934.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1460934.text: OK. I hear you the same. The afternoon television program has slipped to 147 hours, and if you want some TV attitudes and High Gain angles for subsequent television programs, why, I've got them here.

a10a_1460934.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1460934.text: Roger, Jack. Actually, this PTC attitude we're in now, just as we can pan it when we slowly rotate. We can - in a period of time, we can get both the Earth and the Moon in right this attitude while we're still in PTC. But I don't know whether you can get High Gain lock. Over.

a10a_1460934.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1460934.text: OK, 10. Houston. Looks like you could probably give us TV in the PTC mode with your High Gain at pitch, plus 30; and yaw, 270. Over.

a10a_1460934.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1460934.text: Roger. Pitch, plus 30; and yaw, plus 270. Roger. In fact, why don't we go ahead and just - We'll make a try early and see if we can maintain High Gain lock. Over.

a10a_1460934.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1460934.text: Roger.

a10a_1460934.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1460934.text: And we'll do that later on. We're watching our voltages now. Houston, is Deke around there? Over.

a10a_1460934.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1460934.text: Negative, Tom. He was in here earlier, and he'll be back.

a10a_1460934.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1460934.text: OK. There's one thing that we wanted to put down as a flight change in procedure after we land. All three of us are still itching rather badly from all the fiberglass that we had in here from that insulation. I've got a little bit of rash on my hands. So, say, after the normal ceremonies on the carrier. I'm saying the first thing we're going to do is to take a shower and get rid of this fiberglass. Over.

a10a_1460934.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1460934.text: Roger. We copy.

a10a_1460934.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1460934.text: Hello, Houston. This is 10.

a10a_1460934.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1460934.text: Go ahead, 10.

a10a_1460934.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1460934.text: OK. Looking back over my records, the last two readings I gave you for the Chimp [CMP] are wrong on the Rad readings. Wait a second. I'll be right back with you.

a10a_1460934.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1460934.text: Jack, the up-to-date readings as of right now - If you want them, I'll give them to you.

a10a_1460934.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1460934.text: Go ahead.

a10a_1460934.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1460934.text: Okay, commander is 26043, the Chimp is 05043, and the Limp [LMP] is 15044. And the last two or three readings on the Chimp; it's my fault, it may have been wrong. I just copied them wrong. But the incremental increase that you've seen on my Rad meter is typical of the increase in the other two right along.

a10a_1460934.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1460934.text: Roger. Copy. Thank you. [Long pause.]

a10a_1460934.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1460934.text: And, Apollo 10, Houston. We'd like you to verify a switch. Please verify Glycol Evap Temp In switch in the Auto position. Over.

a10a_1460934.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1460934.text: No. Jack. It's in Manual. Glycol Evap Temp In is in Manual. [Long pause.]

a10a_1460934.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1460934.text: OK, Gene. Let's put the Glycol Evap Temp In in Man - correction - in Auto. Over.

a10a_1460934.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1460934.text: OK. It's in Auto. I'm not sure when it went to Manual, though.

a10a_1460934.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1460934.text: Roger. Our data shows that it was probably in Manual, and you didn't verify it. It should be in Auto unless you've got a reason otherwise. Let us know.

a10a_1460934.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1460934.text: No sir, Jack. It should have been in Auto. I guess maybe I hit it accidently or something, I don't know.

a10a_1460934.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1460934.text: Apollo 10. Houston. When you have window number 5 looking at the Moon, then your High Gain Antenna angles will be pitch, minus 62; yaw, 266. Over. [Long pause.]

a10a_1460934.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1460934.text: OK. When we've got window 5, it'll be pitch, minus 62; and yaw, 266. Roger. Thank you. Jack. [Long pause.]

a10a_1460934.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1460934.text: And, by the way. Gene, your astrocast from your friendly communicator here says "Discussion fills much of the morning, and you'll learn a great deal that would never have come to your attention. That is, if you listen well."

a10a_1460934.speaker: Young
a10a_1460934.text: That's right. I was going to have a briefing for him on the stars and planets today.

a10a_1460934.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1460934.text: Yeah. And by the way. John, yours is "Keep your attention focused on your own affairs this Saturday. The necessary chores are quite enough for the time being, and leave all the frills for another time and place." Over.

a10a_1460934.speaker: Young
a10a_1460934.text: I promise.

a10a_1460934.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1460934.text: Hey, Jack, if you're wondering about me, babe, I can't come back [garble] with that one. [Long pause.]

a10a_1460934.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1460934.text: What have you got for the [garble] commander? [Long pause.]

a10a_1460934.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1460934.text: Oh, his isn't anything very exciting. This says here "Problems tend to get out of hand, and logic is not quite enough. There is nothing to do but ride it out with a certain amount of leniency." Sounds like the boss. [Pause.]

a10a_1460934.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1460934.text: [Laughter.] Hey, you guys are too much down there today. Over. [Long pause.]

a10a_1460934.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1460934.text: Apollo 10, Houston. If you want to acquire on the High Gain a little early, you could go to pitch, plus 30; and yaw, 270 right now. Over.

a10a_1460934.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1460934.text: Pitch, plus 30; and yaw, 270. We'll wait a second, Jack. We're getting some chow here.

a10a_1460934.speaker: Young
a10a_1460934.text: Houston, I just want to give you an informal report on the star visibility up here in the PTC REFSMMAT.

a10a_1460934.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1460934.text: Roger. Go ahead

a10a_1460934.speaker: Young
a10a_1460934.text: With the Sun, the Moon, and the Earth light shafting, even with that, we're able to - And we're pointed up to the north constellations and so we're looking out at about an angle of 35 degrees to the ecliptic pointed up. Was able to recognize the Big Bear [Ursa Major] and the Big Lion [Leo] and, of course, Jupiter, Arcturus, Alphecca, and even old Rasalhague, and the Navigator's Triangle [formed by the stars, Deneb, Altair and Vega]. And from then on, due to the Sun, things sort of get washed out, and they get washed out right on around until you pick up the Big Dipper again. But I'll tell you,

a10a_1460934.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1460934.text: OK. We understand you're able to recognize the Big Bear [Ursa Major], the Big Lion [Leo], Arcturus. Rasalhague, and then you're washed out to the Big Dipper and your eyes are getting better. Over.

a10a_1460934.speaker: Young
a10a_1460934.text: No. Through - past Rasalhague, clean through the first part of the Great Square [of Pegasus], and then it blanks out due to the Sun shafting on the optics.

a10a_1460934.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1460934.text: Roger.

a10a_1460934.speaker: Young
a10a_1460934.text: If you got a star chart in front, of you, somebody can show you what I'm talking about. But I mean to tell you - There's a place in there, just about 180 [degrees] out from the Sun, where it is exactly like night time. Just great. Every star is visible.

a10a_1460934.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1460934.text: Roger. We copy , John.

a10a_1462920.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1462920.text: Roger. We copy , John.

a10a_1462920.speaker: Young
a10a_1462920.text: And the - another thing about that thing, Jack, is the shafting that keeps you from recognizing the star patterns isn't all from the Sun. The Earth is, of course, pretty close by the Sun. and when it comes out, it wipes out your night vision, too.

a10a_1462920.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1462920.text: Roger. [Pause.]

a10a_1462920.speaker: Young
a10a_1462920.text: But the Moon - just for a very limited region around it, - oh, it looks like about 30 degrees - is all it hurts - 15 to 30. Pretty hard to get a correct handle on that number because it fades in and fades out.

a10a_1462920.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1462920.text: Roger. How about around the Earth? How much does it wash out? [Long pause.]

a10a_1462920.speaker: Young
a10a_1462920.text: Well. like I say, from... [Long pause.]

a10a_1462920.speaker: Young
a10a_1462920.text: I was able to see Mars in the... [Long pause.]

a10a_1462920.speaker: Young
a10a_1462920.text: Actually, the Earth doesn't hurt you too bad. For example, I was able to see Altair. [Pause.]

a10a_1462920.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1462920.text: Roger, John.

a10a_1462920.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1462920.text: And. Apollo 10, Houston. I have a consumables update and a Flight Plan update when you're ready.

a10a_1462920.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1462920.text: Houston, this is 10. How do you read? Over.

a10a_1462920.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1462920.text: 10, reading you loud and clear.

a10a_1462920.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1462920.text: OK, Jack. Go ahead with your consumables update.

a10a_1462920.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1462920.text: OK. Consumables at 147 hours; RCS total, 56 percent, 46, 63, 56, 59. That's 18 percent above the Flight Plan. H 2 totals, 24.5; O 2 , 336. Over.

a10a_1462920.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1462920.text: I got it all, Jack, and go ahead with the Flight Plan update.

a10a_1462920.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1462920.text: OK. Flight Plan update at 151 plus 30, delete all reference to midcourse correction 5. And at 152 hours, we want a wat - a waste-water dump. Over. [Pause.]

a10a_1462920.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1462920.text: OK. There will be no MCC 5, and at 152, you want a waste-water dump.

a10a_1462920.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1462920.text: That's at 152 hours, waste-water dump. [Long pause.]

a10a_1462920.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1462920.text: OK. Got all that.

a10a_1462920.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1462920.text: And, Gene, I've got a lot more data on High Gain Antenna angles for lockup at different attitudes it - if and when you want them. Over.

a10a_1462920.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1462920.text: OK, Jack. Why don't you give them to me now?

a10a_1462920.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1462920.text: OK. When you're in the PTC mode at a roll angle of 335 degrees, your left-hand window will be pointing at the Earth, and at roll 065, your right-hand window will be pointing at the Moon. At a roll degree - an angle of 318 degrees, you should be able to get lock with a pitch of plus 44 and a yaw of 272.

a10a_1462920.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1462920.text: Hold it, Jack. OK. Hold it, Jack. Wait a minute. Wait a minute. Go. Hit me again with all of that, a little slower.

a10a_1462920.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1462920.text: OK. When your roll angle reaches 318 degrees, your High Gain Antenna pitch should be plus 44 and your yaw should be 272. [Pause.] Over. [Long pause.]

a10a_1462920.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1462920.text: OK. You say when our roll is 335 we ought to have the left-hand - the Earth out the left-hand window, and when it's 065, we ought to have the Moon out the right-hand window.

a10a_1462920.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1462920.text: That's affirmative.

a10a_1462920.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1462920.text: And when the roll is 318, the pitch for High Gain is plus 44 and yaw is 272. Do you want me to set this High Gain on a Reacq mode? [Long pause.]

a10a_1462920.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1462920.text: That's affirmative, Gene. Once you acquire lock, let's go Reacq.

a10a_1462920.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1462920.text: OK. Fine. I'll try to acquire it this next time around.

a10a_1462920.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1462920.text: Hey, Jack, what are my Reacq angles going to be? Or do you want me to just read them off the meter and set them up when we lose this lock?

a10a_1462920.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1462920.text: And. Apollo 10, Houston. On the High Gain angles, set them up at pitch, plus 30; and yaw, 270. And then she'll roll in and then lock in the Earth. Over. [Long pause.]

a10a_1462920.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1462920.text: Jack. I haven't been reading you at all but we got High Gain lock now. So my question was what's my Reacq angles? [Long pause.]

a10a_1462920.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1462920.text: OK, Gene-o. They're plus 30 and 270. Over.

a10a_1462920.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1462920.text: Plus 30 and 270. Thank you.

a10a_1462920.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1462920.text: And we've got High Gain lock.

a10a_1462920.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1462920.text: OK. Great, Jack.

a10a_1462920.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1462920.text: Apollo 10, Houston. We're ready with the P27 update when we can have the computer. Over. [Pause.]

a10a_1462920.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1462920.text: You've got Accept.

a10a_1462920.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1462920.text: Roger, thank you.

a10a_1464944.speaker: Lousma
a10a_1464944.text: Apollo 10, Houston. We're finished with your computer. You can Block.

a10a_1464944.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1464944.text: Roger.

a10a_1464944.speaker: Mission Control
a10a_1464944.text: This is Apollo Control at 146 hours, 50 minutes. Flight Director Glynn Lunney and the Black Team now in the Control Center relieving Flight Director Pete Frank and the Orange Team. Apollo 10 184,640 miles [341,953 km] from Earth; velocity, 4,820 feet per second [1,469 m/s].

a10a_1464944.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1464944.text: Apollo 10, this is Houston. Over.

a10a_1464944.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1464944.text: Good morning, Bruce. How are you this morning?

a10a_1464944.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1464944.text: Good morning. I'm fine. We would like to verify that you are in Manual at the present time on the High Gain Antenna. And then at 4 minutes after the hour GET, go to Automatic. Over.

a10a_1464944.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1464944.text: OK. I'm in Reacq now. You say you want me to go to Manual?

a10a_1464944.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1464944.text: Roger. Go to Manual now, and then in about a minute, or a minute and a half, go to Automatic and you should reacquire.

a10a_1464944.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1464944.text: OK.

a10a_1464944.speaker: Mission Control
a10a_1464944.text: 147:04:09 This is Apollo Control. Goldstone expects to have good lock-on with its 210-foot [64 metre] antenna at 147 hours, 10 minutes; about 6 minutes from now.

a10a_1464944.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1464944.text: 10, this is Houston, we've got a High Gain lock now.

a10a_1464944.speaker: Young
a10a_1464944.text: Roger, Bruce. How far away - How far are we out now?

a10a_1464944.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1464944.text: 184,000 nautical miles [340,750 km]. Over.

a10a_1464944.speaker: Young
a10a_1464944.text: Wow.

a10a_1464944.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1464944.text: And range is decreasing.

a10a_1464944.speaker: Young
a10a_1464944.text: The Earth and the Moon are about the same.

a10a_1464944.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1464944.text: Roger.

a10a_1464944.speaker: Young
a10a_1464944.text: There's an encouraging sign.

a10a_1464944.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1464944.text: 10. Houston. For your information, you will cross the equipotential point between the Earth and the Moon at GET 148:39, and that point is 179,525 miles [332,480 km] out from the Earth. Over.

a10a_1464944.speaker: Young
a10a_1464944.text: Roger. Is that about where the computer switches over?

a10a_1464944.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1464944.text: Roger. It's very close. Over. [Long pause.]

a10a_1464944.speaker: Young
a10a_1464944.text: You know, but it's of academic interest, isn't it?

a10a_1464944.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1464944.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a10a_1464944.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1464944.text: Bruce, how soon are you going to be ready for the TV? [Pause.]

a10a_1464944.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1464944.text: It's going to be about 5 minutes yet. 10. Over.

a10a_1464944.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1464944.text: OK. Fine. It'll take us that long to get it all set up.

a10a_1464944.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1464944.text: Roger. Out.

a10a_1464944.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1464944.text: And, Bruce, would you check and find out what our hydrogen potential is down there in terms of tank loss and also in terms of our purge capability for fuel cell 1?

a10a_1464944.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1464944.text: OK. Stand by and we'll get that for you. [Long pause.]

a10a_1464944.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1464944.text: Apollo 10, this is Houston. Over.

a10a_1464944.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1464944.text: Go ahead. Jack - or Bruce.

a10a_1464944.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1464944.text: Roger. With the hydrogen that you currently have available in both tanks, you have a 20 - that is, a 20-hour continuous hydrogen purge capability, which you can split up among the fuel cells any way you like. If you lose one tank and power down to 50 amps - 50 amps, you can get by until 225 hours GET or a little over 30 hours after anticipated splashdown. Over.

a10a_1464944.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1464944.text: That's great, Bruce. Thank you very much.

a10a_1464944.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1464944.text: Looks like you are in good shape. [Long pause.]

a10a_1470950.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1470950.text: Bruce. I am a little bit confused on how you want me to handle the High Gain now. I am in Auto. Do you want me to go to Reacq? And are you switching back to Omni D? How do you want us to handle this High Gain for TV?

a10a_1470950.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1470950.text: Stand by.

a10a_1470950.speaker: Mission Control
a10a_1470950.text: 147:12:01 Goldstone does have acquisition and is ready to receive television when the crew send.

a10a_1470950.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1470950.text: Apollo 10, this is Houston. I've got your antenna OPS plan here.

a10a_1470950.speaker: Young
a10a_1470950.text: Roger. Stand by.

a10a_1470950.speaker: Young
a10a_1470950.text: Are you ready for the TV?

a10a_1470950.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1470950.text: Roger. We're ready.

a10a_1470950.speaker: Young
a10a_1470950.text: Hello, Houston. This is Apollo 10. 184,000 miles [340,750 km] from Earth. You got a picture yet?

a10a_1470950.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1470950.text: Apollo 10, this is Houston. Roger. We are not receiving the picture yet. I'll give you a Mark when it starts coming in here.

a10a_1470950.speaker: Young
a10a_1470950.text: OK. We're sending.

a10a_1470950.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1470950.text: 10. this is Houston. It looks like we're going to lose your High Gain Antenna in about 30 seconds. Suggest you wait until we reacquire the next rotation on the High Gain. Over.

a10a_1470950.speaker: Young
a10a_1470950.text: Roger.

a10a_1470950.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1470950.text: OK. Will you give us a Mark when that will be and - Go ahead. Are those Reacq angles still good?

a10a_1470950.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1470950.text: Roger. What we would like you to do is, we'll command Omni Delta when we start losing signal strength there. And then you should go Manual on the High Gain Antenna. We'll give you a Mark when to go back to Automatic. And we'll switch you back in to High Gain. This will eliminate any LOS. If you stayed in automatic Reacq, we'd have LOS about 36 percent of the time. You're not in close enough yet, though. so that we can get TV on the Omni. Over.

a10a_1470950.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1470950.text: OK. Great. That sounds great. Bruce.

a10a_1470950.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1470950.text: And I will give you a call when to go back into Auto and try to give you a couple of minutes warning tor the TV. I think it's better this way than it you start out and run on TV for a minute or so then have to break it up and start again.

a10a_1470950.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1470950.text: Agree.

a10a_1470950.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1470950.text: Houston, do we have High Gain right now?

a10a_1470950.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1470950.text: Negative, 10.

a10a_1470950.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1470950.text: 10, this is Houston. You should be in Manual at the present time on High Gain Antenna.

a10a_1470950.speaker: Young
a10a_1470950.text: Roger. I am, Jack; I'm waiting for your Mark until we acquire High Gain again.

a10a_1470950.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1470950.text: Roger.

a10a_1470950.speaker: Mission Control
a10a_1470950.text: 147:20:32 We expect to re-acquire the High Gain Antenna in about 3 minutes.

a10a_1470950.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1470950.text: Apollo 10, this is Houston.

a10a_1470950.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1470950.text: Go, Bruce.

a10a_1470950.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1470950.text: Roger. At 147:23 GET, we would like you to go to Auto on the High Gain Antenna. We'll expect acquisition almost immediately. You will be in AOS with the High Gain for about 11 minutes. Over.

a10a_1470950.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1470950.text: Oh, that's great. Thank you.

a10a_1470950.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1470950.text: Bruce, what we ought to be able to do is pick up the Earth out of Tom's window [garble] this pass and pick up the Moon out of my right-hand window at the end of the pass.

a10a_1470950.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1470950.text: Roger. Understand. The Earth out or the left-hand window at the beginning, and the Moon out of the right-hand at the end.

a10a_1470950.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1470950.text: Let me know when you are going to relatch the High Gain switch.

a10a_1470950.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1470950.text: You're getting very noisy now. Say again?

a10a_1470950.speaker: Young
a10a_1470950.text: Roger. Do you have a picture?

a10a_1470950.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1470950.text: Not yet. We've got to get you on High Gain first.

a10a_1470950.speaker: Young
a10a_1470950.text: Roger.

a10a_1470950.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1470950.text: Hey, We got a picture.

a10a_1470950.speaker: Mission Control
a10a_1470950.text: 147:23:03 Black and white picture coming now.

a10a_1470950.speaker: Young
a10a_1470950.text: Roger.

a10a_1470950.speaker: Mission Control
a10a_1470950.text: 147:23:07 Color will come in any second.

a10a_1470950.speaker: Young
a10a_1470950.text: Houston, this is Apollo 10, 184,000 miles [34,750 km] out. This is the Earth, half-Earth. It's about - the Moon right now. We have practically a full Moon. The Earth, as you can see it right now, is - The terminator is going right across the middle or the Atlantic. You see that big circular weather belt that goes up across the United - up across the east coast of the United States, covers up Florida, and it appears that some sort or point is in the Gulf of Mexico between Florida and Texas. It's difficult to make out any land masses and I doubt that you could see any, but with the monocular, I

a10a_1472500.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1472500.text: OK, 10. We've got the Moon now. It's coming in nicely. [Pause.]

a10a_1472500.speaker: Young
a10a_1472500.text: Roger. That's the same zoom that you had when you were looking at the Earth, and you can see the apparent size relationship of the two bodies right now.

a10a_1472500.speaker: Young
a10a_1472500.text: Well, we have a three-quarter Moon. I take it all back. [Pause.]

a10a_1472500.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1472500.text: Actually, on the monitor down here, 10, the Moon appears to be a little larger in diameter yet than the Earth.

a10a_1472500.speaker: Young
a10a_1472500.text: That's, what I said. It's about twice the apparent diameter to me. And it sort of looks tan still to us. [Pause.] You can see the Sea of Crises very plainly, all the great seas, Serenity. And you notice the crater structure very clearly with those rough craters down in the southern - southern lunar hemisphere.

a10a_1472500.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1472500.text: Roger. We can pick them out on our monitor.

a10a_1472500.speaker: Young
a10a_1472500.text: How does your color look down there?

a10a_1472500.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1472500.text: The black and white is very clear, 10. The color looks like it's saturating a little bit on the Moon.

a10a_1472500.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1472500.text: It's ok up here. Roger.

a10a_1472500.speaker: Young
a10a_1472500.text: The Moon is a - The Moon is a very bright body from here. When looking at the Moon through the optical system in our spacecraft, within about 15 degrees or so of the Moon, the stars are blanked out so that you can't tell what constellations right now - if you were looking this way in the optics. We're behind the Moon. Our window system on the vehicle right now is in excellent condition. We can see just as clearly as anyone could ask for, on all five windows. [Long pause.]

a10a_1472500.speaker: Mission Control
a10a_1472500.text: 147:28:18 John Young is the narrator.

a10a_1472500.speaker: Young
a10a_1472500.text: OK. In about an hour and 10 minutes, we'll be passing from the gravitational potential field of the Moon into the gravitational potential field of the Earth. So you can see, even though the Moon's apparent diameter is larger, the gravitational attraction of the Earth right now is gonna - is just about to take command. [Long pause.]

a10a_1472500.speaker: Young
a10a_1472500.text: We've noticed in the TV monitor that the Moon has several, egg-shaped bumps, and if you're seeing those on your screen, they're not real.

a10a_1472500.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1472500.text: There's a few.

a10a_1472500.speaker: Young
a10a_1472500.text: Around the edges.

a10a_1472500.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1472500.text: This is Houston. Roger. We noticed some, I guess they're characteristic of this particular TV camera you're flying - this unit. [Pause.]

a10a_1472500.speaker: Young
a10a_1472500.text: OK. Houston. You can watch the Moon pass behind the right hand window of the spacecraft. It's rotating around, and then it will be - You'll probably be able to pick it up through the hatch window. See. It's going behind the window frame right now.

a10a_1472500.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1472500.text: Roger. Amazing.

a10a_1472500.speaker: Young
a10a_1472500.text: That shows what our rotation rate is, basically. [Pause.]

a10a_1472500.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1472500.text: Roger, 10. We've been timing you down here. It looks like about three revolutions per hour. [Pause.]

a10a_1472500.speaker: Young
a10a_1472500.text: OK. Now we're looking at the Moon out through the center hatch window.
