This mode of operation for finding out where you are with relationship to the rest of the world, for aligning your platform, for knowing your relationship with your velocity vector, and having a very essential psychological feel for what's going on is excellent. With this kind of an operation, we always know where we are and where we're going; and even more important, we know where to go to look for the stars which we use to align our platform. And that's necessary for us to perform all our navigational maneuvers and correc

a10a_1472500.speaker: Young
a10a_1472500.text: I'm afraid that we're probably going to be seeing more of the Moon, as we come back, than the Earth, because we don't really have, right now, the ability to maintain High Gain lock when the Earth is in the right - is in the right and center hatch windows. So, we are probably going to be showing you the Earth only out of the left-hand window.

a10a_1472500.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1472500.text: This is Houston. Roger. Out. [Long pause.]

a10a_1472500.speaker: Young
a10a_1472500.text: Going behind the center hatch window now.

a10a_1472500.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1472500.text: 10. this is Houston. We've got about 1 more minute until we lose you on the High Gain.

a10a_1472500.speaker: Young
a10a_1472500.text: Roger. [Pause.] Well, I think that shows what we mean by where we are and what the relationship of the Moon/Earth system is right now and where we are in respect to it.

a10a_1472500.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1472500.text: Stand by a minute. The...

a10a_1472500.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1472500.text: 10, this is Houston. We...

a10a_1472500.speaker: Young
a10a_1472500.text: How did the color resolution look, Bruce?

a10a_1472500.speaker: Young
a10a_1472500.text: Roger.

a10a_1472500.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1472500.text: The large screen here was saturating, but we've got another monitor in the back, and the comments were that it was excellent.

a10a_1472500.speaker: Young
a10a_1472500.text: Roger. There's a great big - a great big swirl right over the - light over the point south of Florida, goes up through the eastern states. That was clearly visible on the - at least through the - in the monitor up here. So, you'll probably be able to see it down there, and, also, another swirl; it looked like it was up north, somewhere, possibly as far north as the Canadian border there, coming down to sort of join them together. Couple of very interesting weather pattern.

a10a_1472500.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1472500.text: Roger. We were able to see the cloud patterns, very clearly here, on the black and white monitor; and I understand, from people who were watching the smaller color monitors, that the color was excellent. Over.

a10a_1472500.speaker: Young
a10a_1472500.text: Roger. Well, or course. I didn't expect you were seeing any more than we were on our monitor; and you couldn't - couldn't recognize any land masses to speak of or any - possibly you could see South America, down there in the south, under that big bank of cloud cover, because that's the only thing that I could really pick out with my naked eye.

a10a_1472500.speaker: Young
a10a_1472500.text: Yes. The Earth today is just a white and blue planet.

a10a_1472500.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1472500.text: Roger. 10. We couldn't make out any of the land masses down here, either. Even on the color monitor. But that circular area or clouds did stand out very clearly. We were able to locate the areas you were describing.

a10a_1472500.speaker: Young
a10a_1472500.text: OK. Houston. I guess we will terminate. We just wanted to give you a feel for this spectacular picture. As we get a little closer to the Earth. I think it will be worth trying again. Probably we could maintain better look - have better Earth-viewing if we stopped the PTC or rotated in the other direction, probably.

a10a_1472500.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1472500.text: Roger. We appreciate all the viewing we can get, though.

a10a_1472500.speaker: Young
a10a_1472500.text: OK. I guess I feel if we rotate the PTC in the other direction, we can pick up the Earth and maintain High Gain lock, and that's going to be the plan of interest from now on, as far as we're concerned.

a10a_1472500.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1472500.text: OK. Let us kick that around down here, and we'll be back with you.

a10a_1472500.speaker: Mission Control
a10a_1472500.text: This is Apollo Control at 147 hours, 39 minutes. That TV transmission was 11 minutes, 25 seconds in duration. We still expect the TV pass, that is scheduled for 152 hours, 35 minutes.

a10a_1472500.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1472500.text: Apollo 10, this is Houston. We'd like you to go to Manual now on the High Gain Antenna, until it slews into position, and then to Reacq. Over.

a10a_1472500.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1472500.text: OK.

a10a_1472500.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1472500.text: Houston. Roger. Out.

a10a_1474457.speaker: Young
a10a_1474457.text: Houston, this is Apollo 10. Over.

a10a_1474457.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1474457.text: Apollo 10, this is Houston. Go ahead.

a10a_1474457.speaker: Young
a10a_1474457.text: Roger. What we're doing now is in a temporary hold here for stowage and securing. I think we are ending up bringing back more than we took.

a10a_1474457.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1474457.text: Roger. We'll be asking you some questions about your stowage in a few minutes. We were getting organized to run through the LCL here with you. Over.

a10a_1474457.speaker: Young
a10a_1474457.text: Roger. Furthermore, it is quite clear to me that it you pack up a food bag, when you open it up and eat the food out of it, you've still got more stuff to dispose of than you started with.

a10a_1474457.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1474457.text: Roger. The surgeons are...

a10a_1474457.speaker: Young
a10a_1474457.text: I guess what I'm saying is right now...

a10a_1474457.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1474457.text: The surgeons are wondering if you have negative intake, or something.

a10a_1474457.speaker: Young
a10a_1474457.text: No. We're eating. What I - what I wonder is how we're going to get 15 pounds in a 10-pound sack?

a10a_1474457.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1474457.text: In scientific terms, Bruce, that is known as a "blivet" [World War II term for ten pounds of manure in a five pound bag]. Over.

a10a_1474457.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1474457.text: [Laughing.] Houston. Roger. Out.

a10a_1474457.speaker: Mission Control
a10a_1474457.text: 147:49:55 Apollo 10 is 181,779 nautical miles [336,655 km] from the Earth. Velocity, 4,846 feet per second [1,477 m/s].

a10a_1474457.speaker: Duke
a10a_1474457.text: Hello, Apollo 10. Houston. Over.

a10a_1474457.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1474457.text: Hello, Charlie. How are you?

a10a_1474457.speaker: Duke
a10a_1474457.text: Pretty good, Gene. How are you guys getting along this afternoon?

a10a_1474457.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1474457.text: Pretty good.

a10a_1474457.speaker: Duke
a10a_1474457.text: Yes. Sounds good. Hey, we got a couple of items for you. If you'll break out your LCL recovery checklist, I'd like to go down where you've got the items returned and the stowage location, just by item number. Over.

a10a_1474457.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1474457.text: Yeah, Charlie. But we're not quite ready to do that yet. Can you hold on? It may be a couple of hours.

a10a_1474457.speaker: Duke
a10a_1474457.text: Roger. We'll hold off until tomorrow. Whenever you get ready, we're standing by, RETRO is interested. Also, the people in the back room have been working for 3 days on the water bag, and we got a procedure for you that has been refined on separating out the bubble, if you want a lot of exercise. Over. [Long pause.]

a10a_1474457.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1474457.text: Go ahead with your procedure there. Over.

a10a_1474457.speaker: Duke
a10a_1474457.text: Well, good. I didn't know whether you wanted that or not. First off, it's quite lengthy. It's a full page. I'll try to go through it slowly, and we can talk it through and then ask some questions. First off, fill the entire bag, both top compartment and bottom compartment, about half-full of water. Then, work the water and the gas to the lower compartment by either spinning it or just kneading it down. Then, after you get it all in the bottom, spin it up and then let it come to rest slowly; and if the ga - if possible, then squeeze the gas - if you have any gas in the upper compartment squeeze

a10a_1474457.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1474457.text: Hey, Charlie. With all due respect, would you play back Glynn's [Flight Director Glynn Lunney] tape recorder there on his desk and listen yourself, and then give us a call? [Pause.]

a10a_1474457.speaker: Duke
a10a_1474457.text: OK. I guess you couldn't understand that.

a10a_1474457.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1474457.text: No. We understood it.

a10a_1474457.speaker: Duke
a10a_1474457.text: (Laughing) I told you - I told you might not want this.

a10a_1474457.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1474457.text: Listen, babe, I'm glad that's all we got to worry about at the moment.

a10a_1474457.speaker: Duke
a10a_1474457.text: Me, too, Gene-o. We had this thing here, and if - That was the only recommendations we could come up with, and as I said, if you wanted lots of exercise you could do it, but if not - You know the general principle of the thing and it's your druthers [up to you]. Adios.

a10a_1474457.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1474457.text: We appreciate the homework that was done on it. Here we are with this thing, Charlie. Now, what do we do with that bag that's down in the bottom? I mean that bubble that's in the bottom?

a10a_1474457.speaker: Duke
a10a_1474457.text: Have you got all the water out of the top?

a10a_1474457.speaker: Young
a10a_1474457.text: Yes sir.

a10a_1474457.speaker: Duke
a10a_1474457.text: OK. Is the bottom part...

a10a_1474457.speaker: Young
a10a_1474457.text: I got all the water in the bottom and...

a10a_1474457.speaker: Duke
a10a_1474457.text: I understand, you got all the water in the bottom. Now is the bottom compartment completely full of water?

a10a_1474457.speaker: Young
a10a_1474457.text: Yes sir. Yeah.

a10a_1474457.speaker: Duke
a10a_1474457.text: And it's still got a bubble in it, right?

a10a_1474457.speaker: Young
a10a_1474457.text: Yes. It's still got a bubble in it.

a10a_1474457.speaker: Duke
a10a_1474457.text: OK. Then it's not completely full of water, and what you want to do is add some more water and spin it again. [Pause.]

a10a_1474457.speaker: Young
a10a_1474457.text: That's in work.

a10a_1474457.speaker: Duke
a10a_1474457.text: Hey, Apollo 10. Houston. You still swinging the bag? [Pause.]

a10a_1474457.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1474457.text: Stand by, Charlie. Over.

a10a_1480635.speaker: Young
a10a_1480635.text: Houston, this is 10. Over.

a10a_1480635.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1480635.text: Apollo 10, this is Houston. Go ahead.

a10a_1480635.speaker: Young
a10a_1480635.text: Roger. I've got the bag - the bottom half of the bag full of water, and there's some - a little water in the top of the bag. But every time I rotate and rotate and rotate, no matter by how much I rotate, that water in the top won't go down in the bottom, and that bubble in the bottom won't come up to the top.

a10a_1480635.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1480635.text: Stand by. I'll put the bagman on. [Laughter.]

a10a_1480635.speaker: Duke
a10a_1480635.text: [Laughing] This is your bagman. I think we ought to...

a10a_1480635.speaker: Young
a10a_1480635.text: [Garble].

a10a_1480635.speaker: Duke
a10a_1480635.text: Go ahead, 10.

a10a_1480635.speaker: Young
a10a_1480635.text: Go ahead, Charles.

a10a_1480635.speaker: Duke
a10a_1480635.text: I think I've said enough today about that water bag. I think we ought to forget the whole thing. [Pause.]

a10a_1480635.speaker: Young
a10a_1480635.text: Well, you know this doggone water and these bubbles, they stick to each other, or something! I get the feeling that is what is going on in there.

a10a_1480635.speaker: Duke
a10a_1480635.text: (Laughing) I think you're right, John. They tried - We tried it out in the back room there, in good old one-g, and if the thing won't work, fine. I apologize profusely for that procedure, and we - I think we ought to just forget it. Over.

a10a_1480635.speaker: Young
a10a_1480635.text: It's no problem.

a10a_1480635.speaker: Duke
a10a_1480635.text: OK. Fine. That's really...

a10a_1480635.speaker: Young
a10a_1480635.text: Look, we'd try it...

a10a_1480635.speaker: Duke
a10a_1480635.text: Go ahead.

a10a_1480635.speaker: Young
a10a_1480635.text: We'd try it. If it would work, we'd sure use it, I think. And we tried it; but like I say, we got a problem here with a bubble that's still down in the bottom, and the water being on the top. The two are just not going to mix.

a10a_1480635.speaker: Duke
a10a_1480635.text: Roger. Like I was saying, I think if you'd really rotate it for quite a while, the stuff would finally, eventually work its way down, but it takes a lot of exercise. At least it did down here in the backroom, and I don't really think it's - it's up to you guys if you want to continue to spin it. You've got the basic procedure down, and we'd better be quiet, Over.

a10a_1480635.speaker: Young
a10a_1480635.text: All I can - All I can think of when I look at this bag is: Is this what's going on in my stomach with these bubbles and this air? [Pause.] Because if it is, that stuff is just sitting in there floating.

a10a_1480635.speaker: Duke
a10a_1480635.text: Roger.

a10a_1480635.speaker: Young
a10a_1480635.text: It won't go to the top, and it won't go to the bottom. [Pause.]

a10a_1480635.speaker: Duke
a10a_1480635.text: Roger. It sounds like we've got a little problem there. Hey, I'd like to change the subject to talk about the LM cameras. We recommend wrapping up both cameras individually and putting them in compartment A5. That's the Hasselblad and the sequence.

a10a_1480635.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1480635.text: Roger.

a10a_1480635.speaker: Duke
a10a_1480635.text: And, for the ECS canister, we recommend you roll it up in any kind of a plastic material that you can get hold of to prevent it from, a term they call 'breathing' all over everything, and I guess that's just seeping out. And after you've done that you can - Recommend you roll the canister up in the third sleeping bag. And that's the one without the fittings on the end, and then stow it in food compartment L3. And the helmet that should have gone in L3, stow it on a suit, and put that under the left sleep restraint - correction - stow it in the left-hand sleep restraint, and stow with the helme

a10a_1480635.speaker: Young
a10a_1480635.text: With the helmet in towards the hatch. Roger.

a10a_1480635.speaker: Duke
a10a_1480635.text: OK. That's all we got.

a10a_1480635.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1480635.text: [Garble] Charlie, did you want the - Roger. We'll do that the final day. We were using these sleeping bags; they are really great at night. And you wanted to leave the suit in that restraint bag in its position. Over.

a10a_1480635.speaker: Duke
a10a_1480635.text: That's affirmative. Leave the - as it read here in the procedure: stow helmet, planned to be stowed in L3, on the suit, and the suit to be stowed in the left-hand sleep restraint attached to normal-use fittings. And stow the helmet end of the suit towards the hatch. Over. [Pause.]

a10a_1480635.speaker: Young
a10a_1480635.text: Understand.

a10a_1480635.speaker: Duke
a10a_1480635.text: 10, Houston. Just talking to the surgeon, and the concern with the canister is that the lithium hydroxide getting out into the cabin; so if you haven't already done so, we recommend you wrap the canister in some plastic material and tape it up. Over.

a10a_1480635.speaker: Young
a10a_1480635.text: Do you - Got any idea where we get this plastic material?

a10a_1480635.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1480635.text: Roger. We recommend food bags or fecal bags and tape as required. Over. [Pause.]

a10a_1480635.speaker: Young
a10a_1480635.text: OK.

a10a_1482342.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1482342.text: Hello, Houston. Apollo 10. Over.

a10a_1482342.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1482342.text: Go ahead, Apollo 10.

a10a_1482342.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1482342.text: Roger, Bruce. Is Charlie there? I want to talk to him for just a minute. Over.

a10a_1482342.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1482342.text: Yes, indeed.

a10a_1482342.speaker: Duke
a10a_1482342.text: Go ahead, Tom.

a10a_1482342.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1482342.text: Hey, Charlie. Right. I just wanted to - Before I get my chance to settle down, I just want to amplify one thing that happened back there in staging on Snoopy. You were right on that switch position, but you know on a three-position switch, we finally figured it out later on, up around CSI. We went through the procedures okay, but I was floating up a little bit and had one restraint harness down. You know how you can look in the simulator if you're in different positions and how the switch positions look in different positions? Over.

a10a_1482342.speaker: Duke
a10a_1482342.text: Rog.

a10a_1482342.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1482342.text: OK. Well, I put my finger on the switch and I was floating up a little bit and looked down, and it looked like it was in Att Hold, but if you stretched down a little bit you'd see it - It turned out it was in the other position. Anyway, as soon as it happened, we caught it and real fast it went into gimbal lock and got all squared away for the burn within about 30 seconds. So you might pass that on down to Chris and Deke. And we went through the procedure as outlined, and my finger was on the switch and everything, but just - In fact, you know, like in the Command Module, you look at the Att-1

a10a_1482342.speaker: Duke
a10a_1482342.text: Roger. We copy, Tom. We thought - There was a great recovery, and we'll pass this on. Over.

a10a_1482342.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1482342.text: Yeah. Roger. Our procedures were right, and we were - In the LM, with those hoses, you ride a little high, and I was held down with one restraint harness at the time. So I was kinda like on my tiptoes, and I looked down and put my finger on the switch, and the line was lined up with Att Hold. If you'd actually get down lower, you know quite a bit lower, you'll see that it is lined up there. And normally on three-position switches, you dont flip them back and forth all the way to justify the position. Over.

a10a_1482342.speaker: Duke
a10a_1482342.text: Roger, Tom. Copy that. It's - I know it is real easy to do, and we'll pass this on. And, just - it was - All you can add is it was just a great recovery. So everything was - came out real great. You guys did a great job. Over.

a10a_1482342.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1482342.text: Roger. Thank you, Charlie. Yeah. We were like Speedy Gonzales there. We were squared away in attitude and - real fast, and then made a pitch input avoid the red cherry, and bang! We were over in the attitude back again in about 30 seconds, 40 seconds, and all set to go. Over.

a10a_1482342.speaker: Duke
a10a_1482342.text: Roger.

a10a_1482342.speaker: Young
a10a_1482342.text: Like in here, right now. It looks like the BMAGs are uncaged, but they are in fact caged. It's just the way those switches look.

a10a_1482342.speaker: Duke
a10a_1482342.text: Roger. We copy. We figured something like that had happened.

a10a_1482342.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1482342.text: Charlie, things were getting...

a10a_1482342.speaker: Duke
a10a_1482342.text: I was just going to say, we figured something like that was going to happen. Go ahead, Gene. I'm cutting you out. Excuse me.

a10a_1482342.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1482342.text: That's all right. Things were getting a little slow at that point, anyway. We thought we'd add to the excitement.

a10a_1482342.speaker: Young
a10a_1482342.text: They really added to it, I'll tell you that.

a10a_1482342.speaker: Duke
a10a_1482342.text: [Garble].

a10a_1482342.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1482342.text: Charlie, this is Tom again. I want to say - Roger. Sorry about cutting you out, but I just wanted to say again, we thought you did a great job on CapCom and all of the support people getting the PADs up to both spacecraft and coordinated. I know that you're like the left-handed paperhanger and everything else, but it really worked out smooth that day and I think we really tested the total system. Over.

a10a_1482342.speaker: Duke
a10a_1482342.text: Thanks, Tom.

a10a_1482342.speaker: Young
a10a_1482342.text: [Garble]. It's really beautiful.

a10a_1482342.speaker: Duke
a10a_1482342.text: OK. Thanks gobs, you guys. I know that we had a lot of good guys in the room here looking at it that day, and it was a great team effort all the way around. You guys did a great job, and we're just real pleased to be part of the flight. It was really a great day last Thursday.

a10a_1482342.speaker: Young
a10a_1482342.text: Yeah. What I appreciate was that quick recovery from that state vector. They zapped me a new one like nothing flat. That's beautiful.

a10a_1482342.speaker: Duke
a10a_1482342.text: The Trench is all listening. We'll pass it on to the guys, and I agree with you. Those guys were really on top of everything throughout the whole day. [Long pause.]

a10a_1482342.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1482342.text: Charlie, another thing about the LM. We'll discuss it, of course at length, but you know that S-band antenna worked far, far better, than I ever thought it would. And I think it worked far better than a lot of people thought it would.

a10a_1482342.speaker: Duke
a10a_1482342.text: We were certainly pleased with the operation of the steerable. The comm was really fantastic. Our only bad pass was during phasing and we, of course, are disappointed in that pass of Comm. I've heard something that we might have had a side-lobe lock-on there, but it's not been confirmed yet. We were disappointed with the Omnis a little bit, but not too much. [Pause.]

a10a_1482342.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1482342.text: The capability of the High Gain to lock on and go to Auto Track with a fairly decent signal was great. That was just tremendous.

a10a_1482342.speaker: Duke
a10a_1482342.text: Well, it looks like old Snoop performed in a great style throughout the whole day. Over.

a10a_1482342.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1482342.text: How's he doing now? Is he still on his way?

a10a_1482342.speaker: Duke
a10a_1482342.text: Last we saw of him he was on his way toward the Sun, but we lost him at about 121 hours or thereabouts. He was still perking along.

a10a_1482342.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1482342.text: Well, we got an American flag, and every state in the Union has got a flag in Snoop going around the Sun.

a10a_1482342.speaker: Duke
a10a_1482342.text: That's great news, 10. Just went by to visit the gals, and everybody's in great shape on the home front. Over.

a10a_1482342.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1482342.text: Very good. Thank you. [Long pause.]

a10a_1482342.speaker: Duke
a10a_1482342.text: 10, Houston. If you got a couple of more minutes to talk, the back room would like to know - They've got some questions for you, so they can get one leg up on LM-5. The first one concerns on the operational - operation of the LM steerable antenna during the phasing burn pass. It has three parts to it. I'll ask the first part. What were the circumstances surrounding loss of S-band steerable from AOS to the phasing burn on Rev-13? Over.

a10a_1482342.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1482342.text: Charlie, I don't know what the circumstances were, but we had good lock when we came on down and - good S-band lock - and I could hear. You can hear that S-band tracking because of the noise it makes, and I heard it tracking. And then I got somewhere down in there in the process of our comments and photography work and what have you, I heard us losing lock and I went down there to look at it and then I tried to tune it up - went to Manual, tried to tune it up and the fact is - I'm not sure whether we had the capability to call Verb 64, but I played with it a little bit there for a minute or so

a10a_1482342.speaker: Duke
a10a_1482342.text: That's fine, Gene. Second part of the question was: what was your procedure when the antenna went into the stops and the circuit breaker popped? Over.

a10a_1482342.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1482342.text: Well, when it inadvertently went into stops, I put it at pitch 90, yaw 0, pushed in the circuit breaker and it popped right around to 90 and 0, and we started over again. That happened about three times. I think once during a P52 - twice during a P52 - and one other time. [Garble] that it stopped one time when it shouldn't have.

a10a_1482342.speaker: Duke
a10a_1482342.text: Roger. We copy. One further question on the antenna. When did you switch to the Auto mode? Was it within about 1 minute after AOS on that phasing burn pass? Over. [Pause.]

a10a_1482342.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1482342.text: [Garble] the horn, and procedurally, you know I came on in Omnis and I heard John give you a Go for DOI and then I gave you the DOI burn report and it was after that that we went to High Gain lock.

a10a_1482342.speaker: Duke
a10a_1482342.text: Roger...

a10a_1482342.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1482342.text: So you know we had a good High Gain lock there. We had a good High Gain lock there for a while. I believe you were getting high bit rate data.

a10a_1482342.speaker: Duke
a10a_1482342.text: That's affirmative, I'm pretty sure we were. The TELCOM's not here now, of course, but we can run that by them. Im pretty sure, if I recall the circumstances, we had high bit rate during the early part of that phasing pass. I know because - well, I know we did because we got you a state vector and then I read - correction - that was the rev before. But, anyway, I can remember seeing some high bit rate data and then at some time we lost it and I don't know why. That about exhausts our knowledge on that question. The other one was the two-part question on the drinking water. Was the gas noted in

a10a_1482342.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1482342.text: It was initially when I first went in on the first day. There's no question about it. It got less and less, but I think even after we egressed we took some big gulps of water and there was still some bubbles in it.

a10a_1482342.speaker: Duke
a10a_1482342.text: Roger. We copy. Second part: was any gas noted in the Command Module potable tank prior to diverting fuel cell water into the potable tank? Over.

a10a_1482342.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1482342.text: Charlie, did you read that?

a10a_1482342.speaker: Duke
a10a_1482342.text: Gene, I must have cut you out. I was asking B part, on the LM water - correction - on the Command Module potable water. Was any gas noted in the Command Module potable water prior to diverting fuel cell water into the potable tank? Over.

a10a_1482342.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1482342.text: Roger, Charlie. That was - In fact, when we started to take our first drink of the water that had been serviced at the Cape it was as bad as it's been ever since. In fact, it might have been worse on the first day. So the first servicing that they gave it at the Cape probably did not have deaerated water or was not deaerated properly because - the fact there was tremendous amounts of air in that water when we first started to drink it after TLI. Over.

a10a_1482342.speaker: Duke
a10a_1482342.text: Roger. We copy, 10. Final question that's written down here was on the VHF Simplex A. Did Simplex A come on immediately upon switching from Simplex B to Simplex A when you rechecked behind the Moon on the twelfth rev? Over.

a10a_1482342.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1482342.text: That's affirm...

a10a_1482342.speaker: Young
a10a_1482342.text: Sure did.

a10a_1482342.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1482342.text: That's affirm, Charlie. And as soon as we got Simplex A, we went ahead and tried the LM Duplex A, Command Module Duplex B capability from the LM, not in the voice range, there, but just the voice to make sure we could use that Duplex mode for the ranging capability; and that also worked.

a10a_1482342.speaker: Duke
a10a_1482342.text: Fine. Great show. I don't understand what was wrong with it when we first tried to check it, but we're sure happy that it fixed itself because the ranging really looked like it worked like a champ during the whole rendezvous. I've got a question. What exactly - had the AGS started you off in attitude before you staged, or as you staged, or right before you staged? Over.

a10a_1482342.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1482342.text: OK. You know our procedure. I throw the staging switch after Gene thrusts the [garble] P47 and Gene thrusts forward 2 feet per second [0.6 m/s]. As soon as he starts - starts 2 feet per second [0.6 m/s]. Then just as he starts forward, I throw the switch. OK. What happened: it started to go off a little bit as we started aft, and then as he started, forward and I threw the switch we got on the ascent stage, it just took off. And then that's when I grabbed the hand controller and avoided the gimbal lock and got squared away. But it was just - you know the LM is actually - It has sharper maneuve

a10a_1482342.speaker: Duke
a10a_1482342.text: OK, Tom. Thanks a bunch. It was really a fill in for just me, and also FIDO was curious as to what kind of Delta-V we gave to the descent stage when we separated, and that clears that point up. That's all we got for you for right now. If you guys can think of anything else that you'd like to pass on that we could get a leg up on, we'd appreciate it. Over.

a10a_1482342.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1482342.text: OK, Charlie. I've got one. It was the same squawk that was noted on Gemini 9 - pardon me - I mean Apollo 9; that kind of dates me doesn't it. [Laughter.] On the LM on the rate error needles - You know they squawked at - When the rate error needles were zero, actually you had some rates. Well, we tried to get that calibrated, you know, in the testing there at KSC. When I got in flight, I found that's why I used a little more fuel, particularly during the landing radar test. I pulsed the error needles into zero but on half rates. Right at the last, we calibrated them before docking, and when the

a10a_1482342.speaker: Duke
a10a_1482342.text: Roger. We got that. Thank you much, Tom. I was always under the impression that those needles were supposed to - should have been zero except when power off, but it looks like we had problems just like, as you say, just like 9 did. By the way the - I don't know whether you've heard, but the landing radar appears to have worked like a champ. We had - As far as I can tell, we still had indications of lock-on at about 68,000 feet [20,700 metres]. Over.

a10a_1482342.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1482342.text: Right. And a good show. You know, we had some time there, so what I did was turn the radar on early and pick up that attitude. And as soon as I pitch down, boom, I could see the tape meter started to drive and also the velocity started to go the other - Well, of course the velocity didn't lock on until later, but right away it looked like we had altitude lock-on way, way higher than we expected. Over.

a10a_1482342.speaker: Duke
a10a_1482342.text: Rog. Thank you much, 10. That's all we have for you right now. Out.

a10a_1482342.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1482342.text: Charlie, I've got another thing on the S-band - the LM S-band signal strength. It appeared that any time you call up the angles - and all the angles that we had preprogramed in the Flight Plan and the Verb 64s were excellent, but it appears that anywhere between 34 and 36 if you got that kind of signal strength and went to Auto, she'd acquire and pop right up to about 43 or 44 on the signal strength meter. But even better than that, if you call up the angles and you could tune it in manually very easy from that 34, 36 well into the 40 region and then, of course, go to Auto [garble] popped up t

a10a_1482342.speaker: Duke
a10a_1482342.text: Roger. We haven't found the answer to that one, Gene. You passed that on to us right at, as you came around AOS, and we've been working on it, but we haven't heard the answer for - on that one. We're still working that one. Over.

a10a_1482342.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1482342.text: OK. And in the lunar environment, never once did 407 go to 10000. It stayed zeros all the time, which was expected, but contrary to Earth orbit environment.

a10a_1482342.speaker: Duke
a10a_1482342.text: Roger. That's good news. Thank you much.

a10a_1482342.speaker: Mission Control
a10a_1482342.text: This is Apollo Control at 148 hours, 49 minutes. During that inflight debriefing there, Apollo 10 did pass the equal potential point between the Earth and the Moon. Has now left the lunar sphere of influence, and is in the Earth's sphere. That occurred at 148 hours, 39 minutes, 3 seconds. We copied the distance from the Earth at that time of 179,524 nautical miles [332,478 km]. Velocity, 4,869 feet per second [1,484 m/s]. Distance from the Moon at that time was about 33,820 nautical miles [62,635 km].

a10a_1482342.speaker: Mission Control
a10a_1482342.text: The Atlantic recovery force's ships and aircraft will be released at 153 hours elapsed time.

a10a_1482342.speaker: Mission Control
a10a_1482342.text: We have nothing further for the crew at this time so we will take down the loop now and come back up if there is air to ground conversation. This is Mission Control. Houston.

a10a_14849XX.speaker: Duke
a10a_14849XX.text: Roger. That's good news. Thank you much.

a10a_14849XX.speaker: Mission Control
a10a_14849XX.text: This is Apollo Control at 148 hours, 49 minutes. During that inflight debriefing there, Apollo 10 did pass the equal potential point between the Earth and the Moon. Has now left the lunar sphere of influence, and is in the Earth's sphere. That occurred at 148 hours, 39 minutes, 3 seconds. We copied the distance from the Earth at that time of 179,524 nautical miles [332,478 km]. Velocity, 4,869 feet per second [1,484 m/s]. Distance from the Moon at that time was about 33,820 nautical miles [62,635 km].

a10a_14849XX.speaker: Mission Control
a10a_14849XX.text: The Atlantic recovery force's ships and aircraft will be released at 153 hours elapsed time.

a10a_14849XX.speaker: Mission Control
a10a_14849XX.text: We have nothing further for the crew at this time so we will take down the loop now and come back up if there is air to ground conversation. This is Mission Control. Houston.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1491041.text: Hello, Houston. Apollo 10.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1491041.text: Hold your mike down a little bit.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1491041.text: Is it on?

a10a_1491041.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1491041.text: Yes. [Garble].

a10a_1491041.speaker: Young
a10a_1491041.text: Play that song over again, though, when you get to it. Zap it up a little bit.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1491041.text: Well, why, don't you get it reset, and then...

a10a_1491041.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1491041.text: Apollo 10, this is Houston. Did you call?

a10a_1491041.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1491041.text: Darn. This thing just doesn't want to move off 90 degrees, does it?

a10a_1491041.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1491041.text: You got my glove there, babe?

a10a_1491041.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1491041.text: Apollo 10, this is Houston. Did you call?

a10a_1491041.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1491041.text: I couldn't find them.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1491041.text: No.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1491041.text: Hey, let's put this in the purse. Let's keep all the LM - liberation stuff...

a10a_1491041.speaker: Young
a10a_1491041.text: Alright.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1491041.text: ...together.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1491041.text: You want to dump those batteries in that - you got a place for them?

a10a_1491041.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1491041.text: [Garble] those batteries [garble] I didn't use those.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Young
a10a_1491041.text: [Garble].

a10a_1491041.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1491041.text: I'll put my gloves on it, babe.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Young
a10a_1491041.text: [Garble] gloves [garble].

a10a_1491041.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1491041.text: You're - Let's see. Here's yours - let's put...

a10a_1491041.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1491041.text: But mine are - mine are in there deeper. Here's - here's mine.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1491041.text: OK.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1491041.text: It's not the batteries. It's the damn tape [garble].

a10a_1491041.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1491041.text: Oh, shit.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1491041.text: That's alright. It'll play. [Garble] rewind.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1491041.text: Yes. Fine. Just stick it in. It working?

a10a_1491041.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1491041.text: Yes.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Young
a10a_1491041.text: It'll work. The rewind don't want to work, though.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1491041.text: [Garble] have any problems [garble].

a10a_1491041.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1491041.text: I don't know what you're doing.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1491041.text: I think it's from the LM.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1491041.text: Call up Verb 64; you can't do that. Here we go - here it goes.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1491041.text: Okay, get the tape all [garble].

a10a_1491041.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1491041.text: You can't call up Verb 64, can you?

a10a_1491041.speaker: Young
a10a_1491041.text: [Garble].

a10a_1491041.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1491041.text: Huh?

a10a_1491041.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1491041.text: I wouldn't - Yes. - think theoretically you can. Just like we called up some - other stuff that one time, and...

a10a_1491041.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1491041.text: Look at the side [garble].

a10a_1491041.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1491041.text: Huh?

a10a_1491041.speaker: Young
a10a_1491041.text: Look at that!

a10a_1491041.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1491041.text: [Laughter.] Whose suit's that? That Gene-o's?

a10a_1491041.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1491041.text: Blow.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Young
a10a_1491041.text: [Blowing.]

a10a_1491041.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1491041.text: No. (Blowing) Now I do. Try it. [Blowing.] You - you hear me?

a10a_1491041.speaker: Young
a10a_1491041.text: [Garble].

a10a_1491041.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1491041.text: I don't hear you.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1491041.text: You hear me?

a10a_1491041.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1491041.text: I hear you, Gene-o.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Mission Control
a10a_1491041.text: 149:15:XX The is Apollo Control, and we've put in a call to the crew.

a10a_1491041.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1491041.text: Apollo 10, this is Houston. Over.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1491041.text: Roger, Houston. Apollo 10.

a10a_1491041.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1491041.text: Roger, 10. We lost contact with you there for a few minutes. Did you all go to Command Reset or otherwise change your Comm mode?

a10a_1491041.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1491041.text: No, Bruce. I saw the S-band hunting around, and then I went to Manual to get a hard lock. And we're in okay and back in Reacq, but I don't know where it was. Just hunting around and didn't want to get a signal for you.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1491041.text: How does it work?

a10a_1491041.speaker: Young
a10a_1491041.text: Beautiful. [Garble] ask him if he reads you?

a10a_1491041.speaker: Young
a10a_1491041.text: Alright.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1491041.text: Here you go.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Young
a10a_1491041.text: OK.

a10a_1491041.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1491041.text: Roger, 10. At that time, we had selected Omni Delta and, as the system is explained to me, the [High Gain] should not have been going to any particular position but it won't hurt itself. When we got ready to lose signal strength on Delta we would have ground commanded back to the High Gain Antenna, and it should then reacquire. Over.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1491041.text: OK. We didn't do anything up here.

a10a_1491041.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1491041.text: OK.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Young
a10a_1491041.text: Sure you did.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1491041.text: What are you doing?

a10a_1491041.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1491041.text: You - you talk to them. I [garble].

a10a_1491041.speaker: Duke
a10a_1491041.text: Hello, Apollo 10. Houston. Gene, we've got some preliminary word on that local vertical problem for you. The GUIDO's have been - Stand by one.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1491041.text: I'll tell him.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1491041.text: OK, go ahead. We'll wait until...

a10a_1491041.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1491041.text: OK. Go ahead.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Duke
a10a_1491041.text: Hey, we - The GUIDOs would like me to wait a couple of minutes until they get their story confirmed by MIT before we pass it up to you. We'll give it to you in a little while. Over.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1491041.text: OK. [Pause.] Over.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1491041.text: Are you ready? Got the music?

a10a_1491041.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1491041.text: [Garble].

a10a_1491041.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1491041.text: Go.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1491041.text: Hello, Houston. Apollo 10.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1491041.text: Turn it on so he can hear it when I'm talking to him.

a10a_1491041.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1491041.text: Go ahead, 10.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1491041.text: Roger. Just wanted to describe [garble] kind of the total situation here internal. We've got all the spacecraft restowed. Got the music playing, got a beautiful view out here as we rotate around slowly. We've got the Moon in one window and the Earth in the other window. We got it worked out where no thrusters are firing and we just feel in great shape. Over.

a10a_1491041.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1491041.text: That sounds like you have a better view than the one from the top of the Astroneedle.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1491041.text: [Laughter.] Right. Did you hear the music? Over.

a10a_1491041.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1491041.text: Yes, indeed. Actually our facilities down here for playing music in the MOCR are a little limited so you're about our only source of music.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1491041.text: Turn it on.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1491041.text: (Music) OK. We'll key a little bit in.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Mission Control
a10a_1491041.text: [Music changes to "Strangers on the shore" by Acker Bilk.]

a10a_1491041.speaker: Young
a10a_1491041.text: Houston, Apollo 10. Over.

a10a_1491041.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1491041.text: Roger, Apollo 10. This is Houston. Send your message.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Young
a10a_1491041.text: All right. Roger. We've got a little coat of moisture all over the upper hatch, and it's fanning out - oh, small bubbles in 1/8 to 3/16 in [3.2 to 4.8 mm] diameter, very flat against the whole underside of the hatch. And we've been wiping it down at intervals. And the temperature in the tunnel is 20 degrees cooler. And it's very nice.

a10a_1491041.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1491041.text: Roger. We copy. How is the overall cabin temperature?

a10a_1491041.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1491041.text: That's very nice, too.

a10a_1491041.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1491041.text: OK.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1491041.text: This is WAP 10, broadcasting from the strongest station in the world from 200,000 miles [370,000 km] out, saying hello to our favorite Flight Director and to one of the most outstanding teams in the world that we've ever been associated with. If you have any request, just give us a call. This is Tom, John, and Gene with your morning music.

a10a_1491041.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1491041.text: Oh! Roger to Tom, John, and Gene show. I don't know where you guys get this morning music bit though. I guess it's morning for you all.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1491041.text: Isn't it 6 o'clock in the morning? I have 10 after 6. Is that...

a10a_1491041.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1491041.text: Would you believe...

a10a_1491041.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1491041.text: Is that a.m. or p.m.?

a10a_1491041.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1491041.text: Would you believe it's p.m. down here?

a10a_1491041.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1491041.text: OK. This is Tom, John, and Gene evening show.

a10a_1491041.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1491041.text: [Laughter.] Roger. Out.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1491041.text: That's not bad, 200,000 miles for a volt and a half.

a10a_1491041.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1491041.text: Right. That's very good. You certainly...

a10a_1491041.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1491041.text: We can't handle all requests because our...

a10a_1491041.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1491041.text: You certainly got the...

a10a_1491041.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1491041.text: Our library is limited however, so we - I want to say we can't handle all requests because our library is somewhat limited, but we'll do our best when the occasion arises. Over.

a10a_1491041.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1491041.text: Roger. You certainly got the highest antenna around. Over.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1491041.text: Houston, Apollo 10. Did you give us something specific to wrap in the LCG?

a10a_1491041.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1491041.text: : Roger. We were looking for the - Stand by.

a10a_1491041.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1491041.text: : 10, this is Houston. Negative. We have nothing specific to be wrapped in the LCG with reference to the Hasselblad and the sequence camera. We ask you to put them temporarily in compartment Foxtrot 1 and Foxtrot 2, and after removal of the unsuited reentry provisions, to wrap individually those cameras in available garments and store them in compartment Alpha 5. Over.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1491041.text: Roger.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Mission Control
a10a_1491041.text: 149:25:56 The LCG is the liquid cool garment.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1491041.text: Here, T.P.; we'll take some internal movies.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1491041.text: Yes. Hey, that spotmeter is a good idea, babe.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1491041.text: Is there any Velcro on that spotmeter?

a10a_1491041.speaker: Young
a10a_1491041.text: There wasn't much.

a10a_1491041.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1491041.text: OK, here's - [garble].

a10a_1491041.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1491041.text: Use a lot?

a10a_1491041.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1491041.text: Yes.

a10a_1494011.speaker: Young
a10a_1494011.text: Houston, Apollo 10. Over.

a10a_1494011.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1494011.text: Go ahead, Apollo 10. [Pause.]

a10a_1494011.speaker: Young
a10a_1494011.text: Roger. I'm looking a little ahead in the Flight Plan to these star lunar landmark sightings, and I'm wondering what kind of W-matrix you want in there before we start that.

a10a_1494011.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1494011.text: Stand by. [Pause.]

a10a_1494011.speaker: Young
a10a_1494011.text: Is this the same W-matrix data for the set of P23 No Comm cases around about that time?

a10a_1494011.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1494011.text: Stand by a minute, please. [Long pause.]

a10a_1494011.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1494011.text: 10, this is Houston. On page G 1-72 in the checklist, we've got the W-matrix that they're looking for. Over. That's in the CMP section. You copy?

a10a_1494011.speaker: Young
a10a_1494011.text: Can't you...

a10a_1494011.speaker: Young
a10a_1494011.text: Roger.

a10a_1494011.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1494011.text: Houston. Roger. Out.

a10a_1494011.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1494011.text: Be better if you were laying on the couch.

a10a_1494011.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1494011.text: Why don't you lay on the couch? I think we'll take some time exposures.

a10a_1494011.speaker: Young
a10a_1494011.text: There you go.

a10a_1494011.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1494011.text: Hold the stuff still; it will be a l-second exposure. Alright.

a10a_1494011.speaker: Young
a10a_1494011.text: OK.

a10a_1494011.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1494011.text: John, get over there by Gene-o. I'll get back here as far as I can - Yes, you two get over there as far as you can. Ready?

a10a_1494011.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1494011.text: Take a couple of them.

a10a_1494011.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1494011.text: OK, I - just about as far back here - Yes, I can get back here a little ways farther. Yes, there you go; good show. Good show.

a10a_1494011.speaker: Young
a10a_1494011.text: There you go.

a10a_1494011.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1494011.text: We'll take some of you down in the LEB...

a10a_1494011.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1494011.text: Yes.

a10a_1494011.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1494011.text: We'll take some when the Sun comes around, too, Tom. Believe it's...

a10a_1494011.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1494011.text: What have we got left in this bugger? 160.

a10a_1494011.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1494011.text: We'll take a few of these, then we'll take [garble].

a10a_1494011.speaker: Mission Control
a10a_1494011.text: 149:46:06 Apollo 10's present distance from the Earth is 176,314 nautical miles [326,534 km]; velocity, 4,906 feet per second [1,495 m/s].

a10a_1494011.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1494011.text: 10, this is Houston. On that W-matrix, when you punch up Verb 67, we expect in R1 and R2, you get the values showing up in the Flight Plan. And we need a four balls 3 in R3. Over. [Pause.]

a10a_1494011.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1494011.text: Stand by.

a10a_1494011.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1494011.text: It's in there. I saw it.

a10a_1494011.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1494011.text: Where in the shit is the Flight Plan?

a10a_1494011.speaker: Young
a10a_1494011.text: Say that again. Over.

a10a_1494011.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1494011.text: Roger. On this W-matrix. When you call up Verb 67 on page 1-72 of the checklist, you'll get values in R1 and R2 which are the ones that are already in the Flight Plan, that is three balls 94, three balls 57. And we need loaded in R3 a plus four balls 3 to put you in cislunar W-matrix. Over.

a10a_1494011.speaker: Young
a10a_1494011.text: Roger.

a10a_1494011.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1494011.text: Houston, out.

a10a_1494011.speaker: Young
a10a_1494011.text: [Garble].

a10a_1494011.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1494011.text: (Laughing) That'll be classified. I'd like to use this little one in here. I don't know how.

a10a_1494011.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1494011.text: Yes. Yes. [Garble].

a10a_1494011.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1494011.text: I don't know. Really?

a10a_1494011.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1494011.text: Isn't that nice? Let's - Boy, I - we should make some reference to [garble] I bet you it would turn out to be a ball.

a10a_1494011.speaker: Young
a10a_1494011.text: [Garble].

a10a_1494011.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1494011.text: When we get back. Tom, take one like that [garble].

a10a_1494011.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1494011.text: OK. Keep your head there above the window.

a10a_1494011.speaker: Young
a10a_1494011.text: Above the window?

a10a_1494011.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1494011.text: [Garble] in the way of the window. See, that Sun's going to wash you out. No good.

a10a_1494011.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1494011.text: Too late; you got to catch it just...

a10a_1494011.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1494011.text: Yes.

a10a_1494011.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1494011.text: ...you got to catch it just when the Sun comes around. When it comes around to you or John around the hatch window. Try and catch it when the Sun comes in here and comes in there and comes...

a10a_1494011.speaker: Young
a10a_1494011.text: See what this says on - on the Moon. Freak it.

a10a_1494011.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1494011.text: Gee, I don't know how to work this thing.

a10a_1494011.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1494011.text: You believe that's just 1/250th at f:8? [Garble] use f:11.

a10a_1494011.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1494011.text: What? At the Moon?

a10a_1494011.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1494011.text: Yes. At the Sun [garble] at the Earth.

a10a_1494011.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1494011.text: Shoot 1/250 at f:8?

a10a_1494011.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1494011.text: [Garble] ASA 64. Look at it when it comes around to your side [garble].

a10a_1494011.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1494011.text: OK.

a10a_1494011.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1494011.text: SPS engine, I love your ass.

a10a_1494011.speaker: Young
a10a_1494011.text: [Garble].

a10a_1494011.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1494011.text: What?

a10a_1494011.speaker: Young
a10a_1494011.text: Yes, get that damn thing off my ears and head. You can't either.

a10a_1494011.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1494011.text: The only thing that bothers me about the whole rig is that, after a while, this little earpiece begins to bother me.

a10a_1494011.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1494011.text: Your headset? It's down in here. There's an earpiece on it - there's an earpiece on your headset. Yes, it's on it.

a10a_1494011.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1494011.text: Fuel cell's going to be able to bring her on the line again.

a10a_1494011.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1494011.text: Cooling down on him, huh?

a10a_1494011.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1494011.text: Huh? There's a left, center, right on that little tab on top.

a10a_1494011.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1494011.text: You know, I kind of like Snoop.

a10a_1494011.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1494011.text: Got an electric eye on it, doesn't it?

a10a_1494011.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1494011.text: Yes.

a10a_1494011.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1494011.text: Hey, we're trying some film in here.

a10a_1494011.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1494011.text: I've tried some - and I've tried and tried, and you're right, it doesn't...

a10a_1494011.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1494011.text: I know it. Do you have a time stop on it?

a10a_1494011.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1494011.text: No, that's the trouble, See. At least, I don't see it.

a10a_1494011.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1494011.text: What's all this in here? Have we [garble] that?

a10a_1494011.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1494011.text: Yes, it's got ASA at 400 in it.

a10a_1494011.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1494011.text: What's that - what do you then?

a10a_1494011.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1494011.text: You look at something like that light, and then you match that up to put it on it.

a10a_1494011.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1494011.text: Not if you got ASA at 400.

a10a_1500010.speaker: Young
a10a_1500010.text: [Blows on microphone.] Can you read me now?

a10a_1500010.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1500010.text: Loud and clear.

a10a_1500010.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1500010.text: Hello, Houston. Apollo 10. Over.

a10a_1500010.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1500010.text: Apollo 10, this is Houston. Go ahead.

a10a_1500010.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1500010.text: Roger, Bruce. On our Flight Plan at 150, I've got the temperatures on the Command Module RCS thrusters when you're ready to copy. Over.

a10a_1500010.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1500010.text: Roger. Go ahead.

a10a_1500010.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1500010.text: Roger. 5 Charlie, 4.90; 5 Dog, 4.45; 6 Alpha, 4.50; 6 Bravo, 4.80; 6 Charlie, 4.40; 6 Dog, 4.70. Over.

a10a_1500010.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1500010.text: This is Houston. Roger. I believe we copied it correctly one time through. Thank you.

a10a_1500010.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1500010.text: Roger. [Pause.]

a10a_1500010.speaker: Young
a10a_1500010.text: The babies are nice and warm. Don't need to heat them. [Pause.]

a10a_1500010.speaker: Duke
a10a_1500010.text: Right. [Long pause.]

a10a_1500010.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1500010.text: Hello, Houston. Charlie Brown.

a10a_1500010.speaker: Duke
a10a_1500010.text: Go ahead.

a10a_1500010.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1500010.text: I'm just interested in what your plan of attack is for the next day and a half on the use of fuel cell 1. Are we going to crank it up after it cools down to a certain point and use it for a while and then shut it off, or how do you want to handle it? I noticed it is getting down now to - it, I guess around 390 degrees - 80 or 90 degrees [°F, 200°C).

a10a_1500010.speaker: Duke
a10a_1500010.text: Stand by, 10. EECOM is coming. Over.

a10a_1500010.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1500010.text: OK, Charlie. I just wanted to sort of get the feel for what you're thinking about. [Long pause.]

a10a_1500010.speaker: Duke
a10a_1500010.text: 10, Houston. I got some words on the fuel cell. Over.

a10a_1500010.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1500010.text: Go ahead, Charlie.

a10a_1500010.speaker: Duke
a10a_1500010.text: Roger, Gene-o. We'd like you to put fuel cell 1 on Main A and Main B at this time and keep it online until we - for about an hour or so until we hit TC of 420 [°F, 216°C]. Then the thing has been decreasing about 4 degrees [F, 7.2°C] per hour. That means well have to cycle it again at about 165 hours for another hour. Over.

a10a_1500010.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1500010.text: OK, Charlie. Ill go ahead and put it on Main A and Main B now. Thank you.

a10a_1500010.speaker: Duke
a10a_1500010.text: Roger. It'll take about an hour and should be up to about 420 [°F, 215°C] or so.

a10a_1500010.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1500010.text: OK. [Long pause.]

a10a_1500010.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1500010.text: Looking good here, Charlie.

a10a_1500010.speaker: Duke
a10a_1500010.text: Roger. Looking good here.

a10a_1500010.speaker: Mission Control
a10a_1500010.text: This is Apollo Control at 150 hours, 12 minutes. Showing a distance from the Earth for Apollo 10 at 175,064 nautical miles [324,219 km]. Velocity, 4,920 feet per second [1,500 m/s].

a10a_1501716.speaker: Young
a10a_1501716.text: Houston, 10. Over. [Pause.]

a10a_1501716.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1501716.text: 10, this is Houston. Go ahead.

a10a_1501716.speaker: Young
a10a_1501716.text: Roger. I was just thinking about that landmark tracking yesterday. Were - were you guys taking - was that the two revs of tracking state vector that we were getting? And then we came around to the landing site and marked on it, that would give us an indication of how good our targeting was.

a10a_1501716.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1501716.text: Stand by.

a10a_1501716.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1501716.text: Roger, 10. The information that you requested was that your vector was based on the radar tracking from the two previous revolutions. Over.

a10a_1501716.speaker: Young
a10a_1501716.text: Roger. So if we were repeatable on that landmark on Site 130, that would be an indication of how close you were getting it, probably. Huh?

a10a_1501716.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1501716.text: Roger.

a10a_1501716.speaker: Young
a10a_1501716.text: Or not - I don't know. Probably not.

a10a_1501716.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1501716.text: : Oh, FIDO down here is nodding yes, that it would be an indication of how close you were getting it.

a10a_1501716.speaker: Young
a10a_1501716.text: OK. Thank you. [Long pause.]

a10a_1501716.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1501716.text: Right, 10, they had a local solution running down here at the same time, and the results that we were getting were consistent with the results that you were getting. And the landmark tracking exercises were set up so that if properly executed the values would be repeatable. Over.

a10a_1501716.speaker: Young
a10a_1501716.text: Understand. [Long pause.] I gue - I guess it was repeatable because that site never moved the whole time I was watching it. [Pause.]

a10a_1501716.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1501716.text: Roger, 10. That's what our reduction of your sextant data said, too. It gave us the site in a fixed location from rev to rev.

a10a_1501716.speaker: Young
a10a_1501716.text: Outstanding.

a10a_1501716.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1501716.text: Hello, Houston. 10. On that fuel cell, did you say you want me to go ahead and take it off the line at 420 (°F, 216°C) or you want me to wait for some word from you?

a10a_1501716.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1501716.text: Roger. We'll keep an eye on it down here, and give you a call. However, the value we're working towards is 420 (°F, 216°C) and if you see it first, why, I guess there's nothing to stand in your way of taking it off.

a10a_1501716.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1501716.text: OK, Bruce.  I'm reading - How about calibrating me right now. I'm reading about, oh, 390 (°F, 199°C).

a10a_1501716.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1501716.text: Roger. We've got 378.5 (°F, 192.5°C) on our TM here.

a10a_1501716.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1501716.text: OK. Fine. Thank you.

a10a_1501716.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1501716.text: We'll keep track of it for you.

a10a_1501716.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1501716.text: Hello, Houston. Apollo 10.

a10a_1501716.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1501716.text: Roger, 10.

a10a_1501716.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1501716.text: Roger. We're still just very gently rolling out here and have a beautiful view we'll be able to show you on our scheduled TV pass. And, again, from this distance as we look back out at the Moon there, the basic color of the highland light area is a tan and the mare area is a brown. And, again, that area I pointed out this morning, you can still see the difference. One looks more like a chocolate brown, the other looks like - more like a light, shall we say a chocolate milkshake, and, I say, the colors haven't changed out this far. Over.

a10a_1501716.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1501716.text: Roger. Those last ones you were referring to were the mare down in the southwest area of the Moon?

a10a_1501716.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1501716.text: That's right, Bruce. Where I showed you that, the line of demarcation between those two flows. Over. By the difference in color. Over.

a10a_1501716.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1501716.text: Roger. I caught that this morning, and that line of demarcation is really very clear down here. And just to confirm...

a10a_1501716.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1501716.text: Roger.

a10a_1501716.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1501716.text: ...the TV pass is still 152 hours, 35 minutes to 45 minutes. Is that correct?

a10a_1501716.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1501716.text: That's what we've got in the Flight Plan. It looks like were right on it, and everything's looking good. And John's going to go ahead with some of his work here. Over.

a10a_1501716.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1501716.text: Roger. [Pause.]

a10a_1501716.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1501716.text: 10, this is Houston. On your waste water dump, we currently have it scheduled at 152 hours GET. We're trying to get some photographic observations of this dump. The east coast of the U.S. is pretty well overcast, and we've received some requests to schedule it at 153:30. We're wondering how you feel about this and whether you were planning to go to sleep in accordance with the time line? Over.

a10a_1501716.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1501716.text: OK. Stand by. Yeah. Roger. That's no problem, and we really feel in great shape. And we might stay up a little bit later than the programmed sleep period today. Over.

a10a_1501716.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1501716.text: Roger. If it's agreeable with you, we'll schedule the waste water dump for 153 hours, 30 minutes. Over.

a10a_1501716.speaker: Stafford
a10a_1501716.text: Roger. Sounds good, Bruce.

a10a_1501716.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1501716.text: Houston, out. [Long pause.]

a10a_1501716.speaker: Young
a10a_1501716.text: OK, Houston. This is 10. We're going to stop the PTC right about here looking at the Moon so we can do some star/landmark tracking.

a10a_1501716.speaker: Duke
a10a_1501716.text: Rog.

a10a_1503724.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1503724.text: Houston, 10. What kind of High Gain have you got locked at this point?

a10a_1503724.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1503724.text: Stand by. Roger, 10. We're on Omni Delta right now. Your present attitude is not compatible for High Gain.

a10a_1505900.speaker: Young
a10a_1505900.text: Rog. I don't know if you can see my DSKY or not...

a10a_1505900.speaker: Young
a10a_1505900.text: ...but this thing never even - never even come close to pointing at Taruntius P, and I wonder if I should just go ahead and accept this mark. [Pause.]

a10a_1505900.speaker: Young
a10a_1505900.text: I marked it right in Taruntius P, I know.

a10a_1505900.speaker: Young
a10a_1505900.text: Do I have the - Did I have the latitude and longitude of the thing loaded right? I checked that.

a10a_1505900.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1505900.text: Roger, 10. We were watching you down here. All the loading seems to be correct. We suggest you go ahead and accept it. Over.

a10a_1505900.speaker: Young
a10a_1505900.text: OK, Houston. You had better throw out that first one. Somehow that Noun 89 got rewritten in there. [Long pause.]

a10a_1505900.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1505900.text: 10, this is Houston. Guido says that when you recycle, the data begins to write over what you've got in the cell and the program is performing as anticipated. Over.

a10a_1505900.speaker: Young
a10a_1505900.text: It's ain't performing as I anticipated.

a10a_1505900.speaker: Young
a10a_1505900.text: I mean anytime it writes over a Noun it's already - just finished putting in there, there's something wrong.

a10a_1505900.speaker: Young
a10a_1505900.text: Houston, do you want us to delay for this data that's coming down, or are you getting it anyway? [Long pause.]

a10a_1505900.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1505900.text: Roger, 10. If you could slow down just a little bit more at the Noun 49 point, we'd appreciate it. We're having a little trouble copying it.

a10a_1512436.speaker: Young
a10a_1512436.text: Yeah. The problem is that this thing don't - this thing - If youre marking on something that's been in there before, it's got the '0' mark in there on second vector. It has some other landmark Noun 89 in there rather than the first one.

a10a_1512436.speaker: Mission Control
a10a_1512436.text: This is Apollo Control at 151 hours, 39 minutes. Apollo 10's distance from the Earth is 170,829 nautical miles [316,375 km]. Its velocity is 4,974 feet per second [1,516 m/s].

a10a_1514444.speaker: Young
a10a_1514444.text: Houston, Apollo 10. Over.

a10a_1514444.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1514444.text: Roger, 10.

a10a_1514444.speaker: Young
a10a_1514444.text: That completes the star landmark - the first set. If I wasn't - If I hadn't messed up on that first one, that would have probably been pretty fair.

a10a_1514444.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1514444.text: Roger. We're writing the data now. We'll have an analysis of how it all worked out for you in a few minutes. Over.

a10a_1514444.speaker: Young
a10a_1514444.text: Well, from a pilots standpoint, it's far easier than star horizons. Boy!

a10a_1514444.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1514444.text: Roger. When you got a minute...

a10a_1514444.speaker: Young
a10a_1514444.text: It's just...

a10a_1514444.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1514444.text: Roger, 10. When you have a minute, we got a maneuver PAD for you.

a10a_1514444.speaker: Young
a10a_1514444.text: A maneuver PAD? I thought you scratched that last maneuver?

a10a_1514444.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1514444.text: Roger. We've had a minor revision, here. We have scratched midcourse correction 5. Over.

a10a_1514444.speaker: Young
a10a_1514444.text: OK.

a10a_1514444.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1514444.text: You ready to copy?

a10a_1514444.speaker: Young
a10a_1514444.text: Roger. Go ahead.

a10a_1514444.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1514444.text: Roger. This will be midcourse correction 5 Alpha. Waste water/G&N: 25240, pitch and yaw trim not applicable, GET ignition 153:30:00.00; Noun 81 NA; roll, 326, 171, 060; Noun 44: Lima, Alpha, Romeo, Golf, Echo; H P Bravo, Echo, Tango-Tango, Echo, Romeo; 00001; burn time is 10 minutes, 04 seconds; Delta-V C NA; sextant star, 23, 066.9 29.7; remainder of the PAD is NA. Knowledge remark: monitor in P00, do not trim residuals; shut down manually at 10 per cent on the waste-water purge. For your information, this will change your entry angle from approximately minus 6.9 degrees to approximately minu

a10a_1514444.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1514444.text: Roger. I got everything. Would you repeat the second line of Noun 44, Please?

a10a_1514444.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1514444.text: Which line? Roger...

a10a_1514444.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1514444.text: Noun 44.

a10a_1514444.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1514444.text: Roger. The second line of Noun 44: H P is Bravo, Echo, Tango, Tango, Echo, Romeo. Over.

a10a_1514444.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1514444.text: Roger. I had that. I just wanted to make sure.

a10a_1514444.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1514444.text: That's all right.

a10a_1514444.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1514444.text: OK. MCC-5 Alpha. MCC-5 Alpha is waste water/G&N: 25240, Noun 48 is NA; Noun 33 is 153:30:00.00; Noun 81 is NA; roll, 326, 171, 060; Noun 44 is Lima, Alpha, Rodeo, George, Echo; Bravo, Echo, Tango, Tango, Echo, Romeo; Delta-V T is four balls 1; Birdseye is 10:4; Delta-V C is NA; sextant is 23, 066.9, 29.7. There'll be no ullage; we'll monitor in P00; we will not trim. We'll shut down manually at 10 per cent, and - better not. Never mind.

a10a_1514444.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1514444.text: Roger. Readback correct except that due to the exceptionally long burn time here, the PAD entry doesn't take the amount of time we're looking for. We need 10 minutes and 04 seconds, approximately. We're working on your overburn cut-off criteria.

a10a_1514444.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1514444.text: Hey. Do you want to go over mission rules for this one?

a10a_1514444.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1514444.text: Roger. Did not burn to depletion. 10, what we're looking for is, if it's convenient to maneuver to this attitude, we think we can improve your entry angles just a little bit. If it's not convenient, why you can do the dump in any attitude you happen to be in. As it is set up, this will give you, I guess about a tenth of a foot per second translation plus X.

a10a_1514444.speaker: Young
a10a_1514444.text: My golly. We'll be glad to maneuver to the attitude. Anything to improve that angle.

a10a_1514444.speaker: Young
a10a_1514444.text: Oh, it sounds pretty darn good right this minute.

a10a_1514444.speaker: Young
a10a_1514444.text: Roger. And I - I understand the world is going to be watching on this one to try and track it.

a10a_1514444.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1514444.text: Supposed to be. [Garble]. And, we show fuel cell 1 skin temp at about 421 degrees [F, 216°C) now. You can take fuel cell number 1 off the line. And, I don't know if you put the potable water heater back on or not. It looks like you can carry that load with no problem if you want to warm up some water for meals. Over.

a10a_1514444.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1514444.text: OK, Jack. I'm taking - We've got the potable water heater, and I'm taking fuel cell 1 off at this time.

a10a_1514444.speaker: McCandless
a10a_1514444.text: Roger. Out.

a10a_1514444.speaker: Mission Control
a10a_1514444.text: 151:58:32 This is Apollo Control. That last transmission all concerned the waste water dump. I guess you could call that a combination of space age humor and a little test that the flight dynamics officer would like to perform. In the proper attitude, he thinks there'll be enough energy in this water dump to add about a tenth of a foot per second [0.03 m/s].

a10a_1514444.speaker: Young
a10a_1514444.text: Houston, 10. Over.

a10a_1514444.speaker: Duke
a10a_1514444.text: Go ahead, John.

a10a_1514444.speaker: Young
a10a_1514444.text: Could you give us an attitude that would be good for this TV pass, so we get the Moon out one window and the Earth out the other window, if feasible?

a10a_1514444.speaker: Duke
a10a_1514444.text: Roger. FAO just handed it to me. Recommend roll of 338; pitch, 270; yaw, 000. That puts the High Gain at pitch, 019; yaw, 272. This is pointing south, it gives us more time of the Earth in the windows. Over.

a10a_1514444.speaker: Young
a10a_1514444.text: Roger. We're going to go to the south orientation now, huh?

a10a_1514444.speaker: Duke
a10a_1514444.text: Well, it's your druthers, this will give us some more time. This orientation, we get the Earth in the windows more of the time with the High Gain. Over.

a10a_1514444.speaker: Young
a10a_1514444.text: Roger. Let's do it, then.

a10a_1514444.speaker: Duke
a10a_1514444.text: OK.

a10a_1514444.speaker: Young
a10a_1514444.text: Houston, this is an attitude to go for the TV pass, right?

a10a_1514444.speaker: Duke
a10a_1514444.text: Affirmative.

a10a_1514444.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1514444.text: Charlie, you don't want us to set up PTC until after the waste-water dump? Right?

a10a_1514444.speaker: Duke
a10a_1514444.text: That's affirmative. You can hold off on the PTC until after the dump.

a10a_1514444.speaker: Cernan
a10a_1514444.text: OK.

a10a_1514444.speaker: Mission Control
a10a_1514444.text: 152:00:44 Apollo 10's present trajectory gives an entry angle at the Earth atmosphere interface of minus 6.9 degrees. Perfect is minus 6.5 and it can be plus or minus 1 degree. With this water dump in the attitude we called for there, FIDO thinks he can add about a tenth of a foot per second [0.03 m/s] and perhaps get the angle down to minus 6.8 degrees from minus 6.9. Therefore, the water dump was passed up in the form of a maneuver PAD.

a10a_1514444.speaker: Mission Control
a10a_1514444.text: And at 152 hours, 3 minutes; we're showing Apollo 10's distance from the Earth to be 169,669 nautical miles [314,227 km]. Velocity 4,990 feet per second [1,521 m/s]. This TV transmission is scheduled for 152 hours, 35 minutes approximately 1/2 hour from now.

a10a-1521255.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1521255.text: Hello, Houston. This is 10.

a10a-1521255.speaker: Cooper
a10a-1521255.text: Go ahead, 10. Houston.

a10a-1521255.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1521255.text: OK. I just hit Command Reset so I can get my High Gain back, and you're locked on Auto Track, Narrow.

a10a-1521255.speaker: Cooper
a10a-1521255.text: Affirmative.

a10a-1521255.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1521255.text: Hello, Houston. Apollo 10.

a10a-1521255.speaker: Duke
a10a-1521255.text: Go ahead.

a10a-1521255.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1521255.text: Roger. At 52:30, could you give us - At 52:30 when we start this pass, could you give us our distance from the Earth, and also our distance from the Moon, and our relative velocity? Over.

a10a-1521255.speaker: Duke
a10a-1521255.text: Roger. Tom, we'll be with that - get that up to you just in a minute.

a10a-1521255.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1521255.text: Apollo 10, this is Houston. Over.

a10a-1521255.speaker: Young
a10a-1521255.text: Go ahead. Over.

a10a-1521255.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1521255.text: Roger. I've got your distances from Earth and Moon and velocities, when you're ready to copy.

a10a-1521255.speaker: Young
a10a-1521255.text: Go ahead. Over.

a10a-1521255.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1521255.text: Roger. Distance from the Earth, 168,375 nautical miles [311,830 km]; velocity with respect to the Earth, 5,008 feet per second [1,526 m/s]; distance from the Moon, 45,313 nautical miles [83,920 km]; velocity with respect to the Moon, 5,048 feet per second [1,539 m/s]. Over.

a10a-1521255.speaker: Young
a10a-1521255.text: Roger. So we're pulling away from it, huh?

a10a-1521255.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1521255.text: Yes, indeed. And are you all making plans to ensure any food before turning in this evening? We don't see it in the Flight Plan.

a10a-1521255.speaker: Young
a10a-1521255.text: That doesn't mean we won't do it, because he left it out of the Flight Plan.

a10a-1521255.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1521255.text: If we get hungry, we're going to eat. Over.

a10a-1521255.speaker: Young
a10a-1521255.text: Listen, there's no place in the Flight Plan to put snacks, either, but that's what we've been doing.

a10a-1521255.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1521255.text: Roger. The motivation for that is that Deke is sitting down here at the console, and he says he is hungry.

a10a-1521255.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1521255.text: Deke must have been using that Exer-Genie. Over.

a10a-1521255.speaker: Young
a10a-1521255.text: Tell him to see if he can find a good candy bar out there in the...

a10a-1521255.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1521255.text: [Laughing.] No. He's only going to eat if you all eat.

a10a-1521255.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1521255.text: OK. Well, we've consumed most of it up through, starting on day 6. We're about on meal B of day 6, and we have about two meals that are not consumed out of that total. Over.

a10a-1521255.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1521255.text: Roger. Understand. You...

a10a-1521255.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1521255.text: Also - Also, tell Deke he's really missing something if he doesn't combine that water - that food with water that's filled full of gas, because that's really a thrill. Over.

a10a-1521255.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1521255.text: [Laughing.] Roger.

a10a-1521255.speaker: Young
a10a-1521255.text: Hey, Bruce. That star landmark, we never did any of that in the simulator and we never had any way to practice it, and all we've ever done is star horizon. But, my opinion of that, as a task, is that it's far easier than star horizon, and it would probably be just the way to go for a no-comm nav case. You could pick a couple of good sites on the world which, like out there in Arabia and Baja California, usually always open; why, it would be a good way to go.

a10a-1521255.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1521255.text: Roger. We copy that. And we're still working on reducing the data from your sightings.

a10a-1521255.speaker: Young
a10a-1521255.text: Roger. I would think it would be more, at least as accurate as star horizons. The stars at this point - the brighter stars like Arcturus and Spica - filled up the entire crater, so it was really no problem. The smaller stars: Denebola, Gienah and - and Gienah, they didn't quite fill up the whole crater, but it was so easy to put those things in there and make a Mark that it's just no task.

a10a-1521255.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1521255.text: Roger. I understand that Gienah was bright enough against the background to be used for marking. Is that correct?

a10a-1521255.speaker: Young
a10a-1521255.text: Sure was.

a10a-1521255.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1521255.text: Roger.

a10a-1521255.speaker: Young
a10a-1521255.text: Hello, Houston. We're configured and waiting and standing by for your Go on the TV. Over.

a10a-1521255.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1521255.text: 10, this is Houston. Roger. We'll let you know in a minute.

a10a-1521255.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1521255.text: 10, this is Houston. We're Go for TV now. Over.

a10a-1521255.speaker: Young
a10a-1521255.text: OK. We'll be coming your way in about 30 seconds.

a10a-1521255.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1521255.text: Roger.

a10a-1522758.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1522758.text: Hello, Houston, this is 10. Are you seeing the TV?

a10a-1522758.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1522758.text: Negative, 10. It's not coming through the network yet.

a10a-1522758.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1522758.text: OK. It should be on the way.

a10a-1522758.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1522758.text: Roger.

a10a-1522758.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1522758.text: Roger, 10. We're receiving your signal now. It looks like you're showing us the Moon.

a10a-1522758.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1522758.text: Roger, 10. We've got you now on the monitor. It's coming in very clearly. Very good picture. Not much noise at all in the loop, and the color looks like it's in pretty good shape, also. Over.

a10a-1522758.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1522758.text: 10, this is Houston. We're getting a good picture now. Over.

a10a-1522758.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1522758.text: 10, this is Houston. At the present time we're getting good TV, but no downlink voice right now. Stand by.

a10a-1522758.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1522758.text: Hello, Houston. How do you read now?

a10a-1522758.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1522758.text: Roger, 10. This is Houston. Reading you loud and clear on the voice now and a clear TV signal. Over.

a10a-1522758.speaker: Cernan
