a10a-1522758.text: OK. The Moon and the Earth are the same relative size to us now. The planet Jupiter is easily visible about 5 diameters from the Moon. We can see stars within 6 diameters of the Moon. Anything within that is washed out. The maria areas are very easily visible. The Sea of Fertility, the Sea of Tranquility, where the basic landing sites are, the Sea of Serenity, are the large maria areas to the center part of the height of your screen as you approach the terminator. I don't know whether you heard me the first time, but the Moon is technically - to us it's upside down. The north pole is at the bo

a10a-1522758.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1522758.text: Houston. Roger.

a10a-1522758.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1522758.text: The Moon with the naked eye and through our monocular, we can still see very vividly some of the most important landmarks. We can see Apollo Ridge, which we crossed over and used as a basic IP [initial point] for our approach for landing Site 2; we can see some of the smaller craters that surround our landing site area, are clearly visible to us yet at this time and, I might add, that the Moon from this position is pointing off to the side. I hope that this picture is giving you the detail, the resolution that we see with the naked eye here.

a10a-1522758.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1522758.text: Roger. We are getting very good resolution on the black and white monitor here at the console, and I guess we all wish that we could be up there with you looking at it first-hand.

a10a-1522758.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1522758.text: Well, Jack, you and the folks that are seeing us - watching us leave the Moon, and we're moving away as you see this picture, Bruce, about 3,500 miles per hour [6,500 kph]. So, if the picture looks like it is getting smaller slowly, it really is.

a10a-1522758.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1522758.text: Roger, Gene.

a10a-1522758.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1522758.text: Let me take you over, Bruce, to show you the Earth from Tom's window.

a10a-1522758.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1522758.text: At this time, you should have the Earth coming through on your set down in Houston. Over.

a10a-1522758.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1522758.text: Roger. We've got it.

a10a-1522758.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1522758.text: OK. Houston, Apollo 10. We're looking at the Earth out of our left window. We now are approximately 168,000 miles [311,000 km] on our return journey to the Earth, and again relative to the Earth, we're traveling approximately 3,500 miles per hour [6,500 kph]. At this distance, as Gene has described, the Earth and the Moon look approximately of the same diameter. And, as we look at it here, the Earth is growing from, say slightly smaller than a tennis ball, where it looks about the size of an orange. As you can see the Earth there, actually it's upside-down with the white cap as the North Pole.

a10a-1522758.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1522758.text: Coming in beautifully, Tom.

a10a-1522758.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1522758.text: Roger.

a10a-1522758.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1522758.text: A good relative size for both the Earth and the Moon. Tom mentioned one and another one might be: if you took a nickel and held it about 18 inches from your eyeball, that's what the size of the Earth the diameter of the Earth and the diameter of the Moon, appear to us at the present time.

a10a-1522758.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1522758.text: Roger. Understand. This tennis ball - Is that a tennis ball at arm's length?

a10a-1522758.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1522758.text: It's more like a nickel at arm's length, for the average eyeball.

a10a-1522758.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1522758.text: Roger.

a10a-1522758.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1522758.text: A tennis ball is a good size just looking at it at a distance, but in a correlation, it would be to that. And, Houston, how is the color coming through? Mostly whitish browns to the right of the set and darkish brown in there towards the California coast, and the blue down in the South Pacific. Over.

a10a-1522758.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1522758.text: Roger. The color is in here with high fidelity.

a10a-1522758.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1522758.text: Sounds great. OK, Houston, we're going to take you inside the cockpit for just a couple of minutes here. 0ver.

a10a-1522758.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1522758.text: Roger.

a10a-1522758.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1522758.text: OK. We've got the interior scene. Looks like you are looking at the dosimeter or radiometer there.

a10a-1522758.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1522758.text: 10, this is Houston. We're not getting very much illumination. Is that John at the NAV base?

a10a-1522758.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1522758.text: Roger.

a10a-1522758.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1522758.text: We can make out the wall of the spacecraft clearly, as for John's back, it's pretty well shadowed right now.

a10a-1522758.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1522758.text: OK. John is using the optics in a rather unorthodox fashion right at the moment. He appears to be upside down. Just, just a second. I'll see if I can turn him right-side-up for you.

a10a-1522758.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1522758.text: OK. Now we have John right-side-up, but the spacecraft is upside-down. We've got - still got a problem here. Stand by.

a10a-1522758.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1522758.text: I guess we'll just have to accept the spacecraft right-side-up, and John upside-down. Here he comes.

a10a-1522758.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1522758.text: OK, that's a lot better.

a10a-1522758.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1522758.text: That's what the average space navigator looks like, after 543 marks.

a10a-1522758.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1522758.text: You can observe the patch over one eye to help him adapt.

a10a-1522758.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1522758.text: [Laughing.] Roger. You've really got a...

a10a-1522758.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1522758.text: You might think he was some ancient pirate, but actually this is what the modern day space navigator looks like after all the marks that he has been taking. He's done a fantastic job on determining the altitude of the Moon's surface, and shooting all the star sightings. Over.

a10a-1522758.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1522758.text: You can see John's star chart above his optics right there, and above that are some of the codes that are used to operate the computer - the guidance computer on board.

a10a-1522758.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1522758.text: Roger.

a10a-1522758.speaker: Young
a10a-1522758.text: OK. This is what happens to the optics in zero gravity.

a10a-1522758.speaker: Young
a10a-1522758.text: Once you start a screw or bolt turning up here, it just keeps right on going forever. There is just absolutely no friction associated with operation of moving parts. That's why we have to stick everything together with glue. And since they have been rotating like this, I have lost both of them at least once.

a10a-1522758.speaker: Young
a10a-1522758.text: If you don't think it's hard for a one-eyed guy to find something like this when it's running around in the cockpit, you're not with it.

a10a-1522758.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1522758.text: I'll back off and show TP here.

a10a-1522758.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1522758.text: OK. We've got Tom on the screen now.

a10a-1522758.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1522758.text: 10, this is Houston. Tom's voice isn't coming through.

a10a-1522758.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1522758.text: As you can see, all of us have grown a little bit of a beard in the 6 days since we left Cape Kennedy. It's been a fantastic voyage out here, and it's certainly been a sight, and we hope we've been able to share a part of it with you by sending back some pictures.

a10a-1522758.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1522758.text: Roger. They've been some very impressive pictures, too.

a10a-1522758.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1522758.text: Again, just like we showed you one time before, once you're in zero gravity and you're adapted to it, it makes no difference whether you're right-side-up or upside-down. And we have been floating all over the cockpit doing chores, making attitude maneuvers, shooting stars, as you can see John there. And we'll say we feel in really great health. In fact, we've felt great ever since we climbed aboard the Saturn V rocket on Sunday, and we're certainly looking forward to a return to the Earth, and I think we'll be about as healthy when we return as when we left. Over.

a10a-1522758.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1522758.text: Roger.

a10a-1522758.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1522758.text: Here you see a pair of our scissors that we open the food with, just slowly floating.

a10a-1524652.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1524652.text: OK. We'll go over to the right side of the cockpit, and here's Gene Cernan. Right now, Gene and John are vying for the basic contest of who's growing the best moustache.

a10a-1524652.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1524652.text: For Jack Schmitt's sake, this is how we take targets of opportunity.

a10a-1524652.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1524652.text: This has been a, it's been a great trip, so far. We've worked hard, but it's been very challenging and very, very rewarding to us as a team here, and, I hope, to our team down there; because we couldn't be where we are if it wasn't for all you guys down there, and we really appreciate it.

a10a-1524652.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1524652.text: Thank you, 10. And I'll pass it on to everyone here in the MOCR and on the other shifts; and I guess it goes without saying that we admire the fine performance that you all have turned in up there.

a10a-1524652.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1524652.text: Thank you, Bruce. It's really been great. That pass down to the lunar surface at 50,000 feet [15,240 metres], and the rendezvous, and then shooting the top part of Snoopy around the Sun, and all the landmark tracking, and viewing the Moon as we saw it. And also, that climb out this morning as we left the Moon. Now, that's something you just won't ever forget; and it was so fantastic, that we just wanted to share it there with you. Over.

a10a-1524652.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1524652.text: Roger.

a10a-1524652.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1524652.text: Here you see Gene turning around the flashlight that's turned on. Now, one thing we use in the spacecraft because we do have the problem of zero-g is some material called Velcro, and here you'll see Gene putting a light on one of the knobs, and John is also putting a pencil there. In fact, with just one small piece, he can hold this whole camera that we have. It's only less than 1 inch square, but yet it has the cohesive force to hold the desired object to the surface.

a10a-1524652.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1524652.text: Well, we're going to end our TV cast, now, by again just showing you the Earth and the Moon for one quick glance, and Gene will take the camera and point it out to the Moon.

a10a-1524652.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1524652.text: 10, this is Houston. Is there anything we could see in the vicinity of the tunnel regarding condensation, or anything up there?

a10a-1524652.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1524652.text: Yes. We'll take you up in our tunnel there. We've got a lot of gear stored in it.

a10a-1524652.speaker: Slayton
a10a-1524652.text: Looks like Snoopy up there to me.

a10a-1524652.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1524652.text: [Laughing.] You better believe, that may be a part of Snoopy.

a10a-1524652.speaker: Young
a10a-1524652.text: OK. You're looking at the edge of the hatch. There's the hatch handle right there; the basic mechanism of the hatch handle mechanism that opens. If you can see it, there's condensation all over there. It's all wet, and right up there under the tunnel vent lights around the seal is drops of water condensing out.

a10a-1524652.speaker: Young
a10a-1524652.text: Can you see that water on the tube? Does it show up on the monitor? And, there's condensation on the walls of the tunnel, as far down as the top of the hatch surface.

a10a-1524652.speaker: Young
a10a-1524652.text: But there's very little electrical wiring in the tunnel, so we're not really worried about that.

a10a-1524652.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1524652.text: Roger. We can't make out much in the way of water. We can see a little bit of glistening occasionally. That's about the size of it.

a10a-1524652.speaker: Young
a10a-1524652.text: That's it, that's it. Well, there's a thin, there's a thin film of drops all over the hatch, and...

a10a-1524652.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1524652.text: Roger. We caught something there.

a10a-1524652.speaker: Young
a10a-1524652.text: Can you see that?

a10a-1524652.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1524652.text: Roger.

a10a-1524652.speaker: Young
a10a-1524652.text: That's the same type of film that's all over the hatch and the tunnel walls. Saw a lot on the hatch - on the pressure equalization valve. Look at it, right there.

a10a-1524652.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1524652.text: Roger.

a10a-1524652.speaker: Young
a10a-1524652.text: Bright, shiny spots of water.

a10a-1524652.speaker: Young
a10a-1524652.text: And like I said before, this morning, it's 20 degrees cooler in the tunnel; very nice up there. The pressure equalization valve is covered with water well every piece of equipment in there, particularly the steel pieces around the rim of the seal and pressure equalization valve, are covered with a thin film of water drops. I think you can see some, even on the hatch mechanism. Can you see the alignment arrows...

a10a-1524652.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1524652.text: ...Yes. Just one...

a10a-1524652.speaker: Young
a10a-1524652.text: ...that we use to align the hatch with?

a10a-1524652.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1524652.text: Roger. The alignment arrow comes through nicely. In fact, we could read, I guess it was "gear box disconnect" a few minutes ago.

a10a-1524652.speaker: Young
a10a-1524652.text: Roger. This hatch weighs about 80 pounds [36 kg] or a little better, and in one g with - a man has very great difficulty to position this thing and install it, and locking it by himself. In zero gravity it's extremely easy to manipulate and operate, and it was even easy to wrestle it by these hoses the other day, which we had to take it out and put it in two or three times while we're checking out the lunar module, which was attached just above this hatch. But it was a piece of cake to haul it in and out.

a10a-1524652.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1524652.text: Reports like that are good news for our AAP [Apollo Applications Program-Skylab] package handling problem.

a10a-1524652.speaker: Young
a10a-1524652.text: I didn't say it would be easy for AAP, Bruce.

a10a-1524652.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1524652.text: I don't believe you can see it, but there's some big drops of water about the size of a quarter right where John is putting his hand up there, right now. Right opposite that tunnel light, and opposite the end of the hatch handle. It's on the vertical portion of the hatch.

a10a-1524652.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1524652.text: Right now, John has one of our absorbent towels and is mopping up the water around in that area on the hatch handle.

a10a-1524652.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1524652.text: Roger.

a10a-1524652.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1524652.text: OK. We're getting an outside view, again.

a10a-1524652.speaker: Young
a10a-1524652.text: Roger. As a matter of fact, I was just up in the tunnel feeling of that. That stuff on the outer hatch seal is not water. It's ice.

a10a-1524652.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1524652.text: Roger. Ice.

a10a-1524652.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1524652.text: OK. Gene is going to focus it on the Moon. There, I think he's got it. Over.

a10a-1524652.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1524652.text: Roger.

a10a-1524652.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1524652.text: OK. Like Tom did with the Earth, I've turned the Moon over for you and you're looking at the North Pole at the top; the east is to the right; and the south is to the bottom of your screen. You're looking at the main area that we were interested in as far as landing site operation is concerned, the dark area in the middle: the maria, Sea of Tranquility, Sea of Fertility area. As I say, with the naked eye this is still very plain and very visible, and this is full zoom on the lens. The relative size again at - some - about 40,000 miles [74,000 km] away from the Moon about 45,000 miles [83,000 km

a10a-1524652.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1524652.text: Roger, Apollo 10. We're looking forward to having you all back in about 2 days here. We're standing by.

a10a-1524652.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1524652.text: Roger, Bruce.

a10a-1524652.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1524652.text: 152:58:52 The duration of that transmission was 29 minutes, 5 seconds.

a10a-1524652.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1524652.text: Hello, Houston, Apollo 10.

a10a-1524652.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1524652.text: Go ahead, 10.

a10a-1524652.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1524652.text: Roger. You've heard our report, how we feel healthy and very hardy up here. Just want a report on how our boss is doing, going through the same simulation with the food on the ground. Over.

a10a-1524652.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1524652.text: Stand by a second. The boss just walked out - to go eat, we believe...

a10a-1524652.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1524652.text: What did you say, Houston?

a10a-1524652.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1524652.text: [Laughing.] Roger. We're speculating he went out to eat. He came over here to watch the pass, and I guess it was a secondary objective to find out whether you all were inserting a meal in the Flight Plan for today or not.

a10a-1524652.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1524652.text: He had some other conveniences to go with that food that we don't have that might make it taste better.

a10a-1524652.speaker: CapCom
a10a-1524652.text: [Laughing.] Roger.

a10a-1524652.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1524652.text: 153:01:26 The boss is Donald K. Deke Slayton, Director of Flight Crew Operations. ... And Deke Slayton was in the viewing room talking to Mrs. John Young at the time the crew asked for the status report from him. I believe he's coming into the Control Center now and will probably talk with the crew very shortly.

a10a-1524652.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1524652.text: Hello, Houston. Apollo 10. Over.

a10a-1524652.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1524652.text: Go ahead, 10.

a10a-1524652.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1524652.text: Roger. For the G&N water Delta-V, want to reconfirm that the yaw angle is 060 degrees. Over.

a10a-1524652.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1524652.text: Stand by.

a10a-1524652.speaker: Young
a10a-1524652.text: You know, Houston, if it's 060 degrees according to the book on one of these burns, you got to realign the platform. That's too close to the middle gimbal. Over.

a10a-1524652.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1524652.text: Roger. We don't want you to have to do that, so we'll waive the 060 bit.

a10a-1524652.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1524652.text: 10, Houston. Correction there. We will waive the platform realignment and use yaw 060.

a10a-1524652.speaker: Young
a10a-1524652.text: I was afraid you were going to say that.

a10a-1524652.speaker: Slayton
a10a-1524652.text: 10, Houston.

a10a-1524652.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1524652.text: Go ahead, Houston.

a10a-1524652.speaker: Slayton
a10a-1524652.text: Roger. Understand you wanted a food report from the one-g test sample down here.

a10a-1524652.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1524652.text: Roger. We're doing real good up here, Deke, and feel real healthy. Wondering how you were surviving down there on it. Over.

a10a-1524652.speaker: Slayton
a10a-1524652.text: I'm surviving real well, except I'm starving to death. That hydrogen up there must be real filling.

a10a-1524652.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1524652.text: [Laughing.] It is, and I guess that's the only factor that you're missing there, boss, because this water really seems to fill you up. Over.

a10a-1524652.speaker: Slayton
a10a-1524652.text: Well, we save some weight on food that way.

a10a-1524652.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1524652.text: Right. Good reducing diet also. I guess our total BTU's per day is probably a little bit less, particularly after that rendezvous day here, as far as our movements and everything; and you start to use the Exer-Genie right away, you build up a heat load that 5 psi can't circulate out very well. Over.

a10a-1524652.speaker: Slayton
a10a-1524652.text: Roger. I expect that's true.

a10a-1524652.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1524652.text: Houston, Apollo 10. Again, I mentioned earlier today, and I guess it got relayed on to you, that we're still itching quite a bit from all the insulation that we got in here from the tunnel hatch; and at least after that microbiology, the next thing we want to do after we get aboard the carrier is going to be to take a shower. Over.

a10a-1524652.speaker: Slayton
a10a-1524652.text: Roger. Got that message, Tom, and the medics are shaking their heads "yes." That sounds like a reasonable plan to them.

a10a-1524652.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1524652.text: OK. Real good. I wish we'd had a camera going inside. It looked like three people scrambling around in a snowstorm here when that vent valve was opened up there. And the same way over in Snoopy. Snoopy was completely covered with the snowstorm but we got it fairly well policed-up, but it still is settling around all over. And so, we're taking care of it the best we can, but I think that's the best way to get rid of the rashes we have. Over. There's no problem, but we just want a shower as soon as we get out.

a10a-1524652.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1524652.text: 10, have you...

a10a-1524652.speaker: Young
a10a-1524652.text: We keep cleaning the inflow valve out at regular intervals.

a10a-1524652.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1524652.text: Roger. Have you tried using the wet-wipes? Do they help any?

a10a-1524652.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1524652.text: Oh, yes. We've taken about the best type of shower we can, and all skin treatment - everything else, and we keep cleaning the inflow valve to the ECS system - oh, at least three or four times a day, and still just finding fibers - lint from the fiberglass in there. But we've got everything under hand, but in the meanwhile, we just itch a little bit. Over.

a10a-1524652.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1524652.text: Roger. We copy. And we'll work on lining up some showers for you.

a10a-1524652.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1524652.text: OK. Thank you, now.

a10a-1530840.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1530840.text: Houston, Apollo 10. You can relay on to Deke that we aren't going to eat another meal before we go to bed. Over.

a10a-1530840.speaker: Slayton
a10a-1530840.text: Roger. Got that message. I'll start making the line-up right now.

a10a-1530840.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1530840.text: Tell him not to get hungry, now, down there.

a10a-1530840.speaker: Young
a10a-1530840.text: Roger. Should we be in Narrow Deadband for this water dump? Over.

a10a-1530840.speaker: Young
a10a-1530840.text: What quads do you want enabled and disabled today?

a10a-1530840.speaker: Duke
a10a-1530840.text: Roger, Apollo 10. Wide Deadband is satisfactory, and your DAP is configured properly. Over.

a10a-1530840.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1530840.text: And would you give us a Mark at 9 minutes to the maneuver? Over.

a10a-1530840.speaker: Young
a10a-1530840.text: So we can get our clocks Synced.

a10a-1530840.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1530840.text: Roger. Our clocks are Synced, and we're counting down to the maneuver. Thank you.

a10a-1530840.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1530840.text: Roger. We just got informal word from the Princeton that they've got plenty of hot water and soap available on board for you.

a10a-1530840.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1530840.text: Well, thank you very much. Certainly appreciate the effort, there.

a10a-1530840.speaker: Young
a10a-1530840.text: Are you sure they're hot on water?

a10a-1530840.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1530840.text: They would make an exception for you all.

a10a-1530840.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1530840.text: OK. Tell them thanks a lot. Over.

a10a-1530840.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1530840.text: Roger. For John, Barbara was in here in the viewing room watching the show, and she enjoyed the production and hearing you very much.

a10a-1532545.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1532545.text: Houston, Apollo 10. We're in the maneuver altitude and counting down, coming up on 3 minutes to maneuver. Over.

a10a-1532545.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1532545.text: Roger. Coming up on 3 minutes.

a10a-1532545.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1532545.text: Mark.

a10a-1532545.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1532545.text: Three minutes.

a10a-1532545.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1532545.text: Roger.

a10a-1532545.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1532545.text: 153:27:09 And this manuever, is a waste water dump.

a10a-1532545.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1532545.text: Mark.

a10a-1532545.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1532545.text: One minute to the maneuver.

a10a-1532545.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1532545.text: Roger. Fifty-four seconds and counting.

a10a-1532545.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1532545.text: Roger. Would you count us down to the last 5 seconds, please, Houston? Make sure we're accurate there when we start it. Over.

a10a-1532545.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1532545.text: Roger.

a10a-1532545.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1532545.text: Roger. Stand by. 5, 4, 3, 2, 1.

a10a-1532545.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1532545.text: Flush. [Laughter.]

a10a-1532545.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1532545.text: Roger. And we're on the way.

a10a-1532545.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1532545.text: We've got a good ignition. The valves are open; the pressure's good.

a10a-1532545.speaker: Young
a10a-1532545.text: Man, it's raining out there.

a10a-1532545.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1532545.text: Houston, at 1 minute, the maneuver looks good. Over.

a10a-1532545.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1532545.text: Roger out.

a10a-1532545.speaker: Young
a10a-1532545.text: Steering is straight and true.

a10a-1532545.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1532545.text: We've got a pull 0.0000015 g, at the moment.

a10a-1532545.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1532545.text: Houston, if Deke's still there, ask him what he thought of that rate of climb this morning after we lit the big afterburner. Over.

a10a-1532545.speaker: Slayton
a10a-1532545.text: That was pretty impressive, Tom. I've never seen anything quite like that.

a10a-1532545.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1532545.text: Yes. Neither have I, Deke. All three of us just sat there in amazement. We just went vertically right out from it. It was really amazing ... like you really pulled back on the pole after the burner was lit and you're up to V MAX .

a10a-1532545.speaker: Slayton
a10a-1532545.text: Yes. I'll have to take that ride with you someday.

a10a-1532545.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1532545.text: Sure love to have you.

a10a-1532545.speaker: Young
a10a-1532545.text: Boy, that engine really runs. I tell you that three-quarters of a g were getting felt like about 7 g's. It's hard to get your head off the headrest.

a10a-1532545.speaker: Young
a10a-1532545.text: I think the real impressive thing about it, though, is the accuracy with which it controls and ends up. Once you get done with a burn, by golly, it doesn't look like we got any work to do much now.

a10a-1532545.speaker: Slayton
a10a-1532545.text: Yes. That was fantastic, that cut-off.

a10a-1532545.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1532545.text: Yes. The guidance systems have really performed for us on this whole mission, in fact, even including the Saturn there. Over.

a10a-1532545.speaker: Slayton
a10a-1532545.text: Roger. No question about it.

a10a-1532545.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1532545.text: Say, Deke, I'm trading John one shrimp cocktail for two chicken soups, but you don't have that advantage down there. So you just have to stay with what you've got.

a10a-1532545.speaker: Slayton
a10a-1532545.text: Yes. I'm eating Tom's menu so I don't have much variety there.

a10a-1532545.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1532545.text: Sorry about that.

a10a-1532545.speaker: Slayton
a10a-1532545.text: Actually, the flavor is pretty good down here, Tom. I don't know how it affects you up there, but my opinion it's probably the gas is giving you the most problem, and not the basic food.

a10a-1532545.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1532545.text: Right, Deke. Yes. The food itself tastes real good and those wet packs are good. Man, they've made a real great effort. And the only thing is I'm sure just the water has filled us up so much and the lack of total activity in here, we just - We're staying completely filled up. There's no doubt about that, but we're just lagging a little bit behind in the total number of meals consumed. Over.

a10a-1532545.speaker: Slayton
a10a-1532545.text: Roger. Understand.

a10a-1532545.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1532545.text: 10, Houston. We show you about 12.0 percent now.

a10a-1532545.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1532545.text: Roger. I'm reading about 15. I'll bias it and cut if off at 10.

a10a-1532545.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1532545.text: Yes. We show 10 now.

a10a-1532545.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1532545.text: Say again.

a10a-1532545.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1532545.text: Roger. We show 9½ percent now. You're overburning.

a10a-1532545.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1532545.text: Roger. Manuals cut off - shut off. We got it. Residuals look like about 0.05 percent plus.

a10a-1532545.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1532545.text: Houston. Roger. Out.

a10a-1532545.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1532545.text: Houston, this is 10. It looks as if the I sp might have been a little bit low as far as the total burn time was concerned. Over.

a10a-1532545.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1532545.text: Roger. Actually in defense of the EECOMs, shortly before the burn they came up with a revised burn time about 10 plus 58, so looks like they were right about in the middle on it.

a10a-1532545.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1532545.text: Roger.

a10a-1532545.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1532545.text: Oh, EECOM is doing the trench work now, huh?

a10a-1532545.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1532545.text: For a maneuver of this sort, yes.

a10a-1532545.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1532545.text: 10, Houston. When it's convenient for you, we can take your onboard readouts, crew status report, and things of this sort. Over.

a10a-1532545.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1532545.text: OK. Stand by. It will be a little while yet. We are right in the middle of this meal. Over.

a10a-1532545.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1532545.text: Oh, Roger. No rush. We're going to be here for a while, yet.

a10a-1532545.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1532545.text: OK.

a10a-1532545.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1532545.text: 153:42:25 I sp is specific impulse, and Apollo 10 dumped about 33 pounds [15 kg] of waste water during this maneuver.

a10a-1534348.speaker: Young
a10a-1534348.text: Houston, this is 10. We're going to PTC attitude, heads down tonight, and look at the southern constellations for morning realign. OK?

a10a-1534348.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1534348.text: Fine with us.

a10a-1534348.speaker: Young
a10a-1534348.text: Houston, this is 10. Over.

a10a-1534348.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1534348.text: Go ahead, 10.

a10a-1534348.speaker: Young
a10a-1534348.text: Roger. It is kind of - mighty cold in this tunnel area. If it really starts to freeze things up, we might want to orient this thing - hatch toward the Sun for a little bit one of these days. We'll keep an eye on it. That be all right?

a10a-1534348.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1534348.text: Roger. We copy.

a10a-1534348.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1534348.text: Hello Houston, this is 10.

a10a-1534348.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1534348.text: Go ahead, 10.

a10a-1534348.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1534348.text: I got some RAD readings for you in this order: 26044, 05044, and 15045. I got Battery C 36.8; PYRO BATT's are both 37; RCS 54, 66, 67, and 64.

a10a-1534348.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1534348.text: Roger. Readback...

a10a-1534348.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1534348.text: That's all right, Bruce. I've got them written down. I'm sure you got them right. I'm cycling the fans, and I'm going into an O 2 purge at this time.

a10a-1534348.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1534348.text: Roger. Like to confirm the RAD readings. 26044, 05044, 15045. Over.

a10a-1534348.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1534348.text: That's it. You got them.

a10a-1534348.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1534348.text: Roger.

a10a-1534348.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1534348.text: 10, this is Houston. Over.

a10a-1534348.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1534348.text: Go ahead. Over.

a10a-1534348.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1534348.text: Roger. Looking ahead in the Flight Plan, there's nothing very critical immediately following your rest period. If required we could slip the P22 work by a couple of hours and if you want to go ahead and sleep in it's your option. Over. Sunday morning and all that.

a10a-1534348.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1534348.text: OK. I'll leave that - whatever John wants to do - Roger. Whatever John wants to do on that. Over.

a10a-1534348.speaker: Young
a10a-1534348.text: OK. It doesn't make any difference to me. Whatever is convenient with you all.

a10a-1534348.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1534348.text: Well, we're going to be here one way or the other and - your option.

a10a-1534348.speaker: Young
a10a-1534348.text: Well, I figured you wouldn't turn loose the MOCR. How about we play it if we wake up we do it; if we sleep, we don't. Would that be fair?

a10a-1534348.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1534348.text: That's fair.

a10a-1534348.speaker: Young
a10a-1534348.text: In other words, we do it when we wake up, if that'll be all right.

a10a-1534348.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1534348.text: Roger.

a10a-1534348.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1534348.text: Hey, Bruce. The purge is complete; the canister has been changed. What comm mode do you want me in tonight, Omni or High Gain? Omni again?

a10a-1534348.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1534348.text: OK. We'd like you in Omni comm mode. We'd like you to select Omni Bravo on board with the rest of the comm configuration per the Flight Plan, that is S-band squelch, Enable; S-band nominal mode voice, Off; and the arch tape Off.

a10a-1534348.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1534348.text: OK. Fine. I'll stay High Gain here for a little bit.

a10a-1534348.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1534348.text: Roger. We'd also like you to terminate the charge on battery A and Optics Power switch to Off.

a10a-1534348.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1534348.text: OK. We got that. Thank you.

a10a-1534348.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1534348.text: And then I've got your heater configuration for the Cryo tanks.

a10a-1534348.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1534348.text: Stand by one. ... OK, Jack. Why don't you take them one at a time, and I'll just go through them - Bruce, I'm sorry.

a10a-1534348.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1534348.text: OK. Oxygen tank number 2, Auto; oxygen tank number 1, Off; hydrogen tank number 1, Auto; hydrogen tank number 2, Off.

a10a-1534348.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1534348.text: OK, Bruce. Here's what I got. I got hydrogen 1, Auto; 2, Off; oxygen 1, Off; 2, Auto.

a10a-1534348.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1534348.text: Roger. And we have an inquiry from Joe Garino as to what sort of utilization, if any, you're getting on the inflight exerciser? Over.

a10a-1534348.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1534348.text: Roger. We've been using it after TEI, and it's working out real good. Would you pass the word on to Joe. We have been - All three of us have been using it and it's working out fine. And we were rather busy there all the time before TEI up on the whole mission, and now we're using it on the way back. Over. It works good.

a10a-1534348.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1534348.text: Roger. You're not having any problems with it are you, or anything like that?

a10a-1534348.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1534348.text: Negative. It works as prescribed. It's real good. Over.

a10a-1534348.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1534348.text: Very good. I'll pass it on.

a10a-1540455.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1540455.text: Houston, this is 10. I'm going Omni's now. I'll power down the S-band.

a10a-1540455.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1540455.text: Roger. On the High Gain antennas we'd prefer you to leave the antenna powered up but in the manual mode overnight. Over.

a10a-1540455.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1540455.text: 10, Houston. When you're through with your computer, we'd like to give you a NAV - a state vector update, and update the CMC clock. And do you have any comments on the EMS [Entry Monitoring System] check? Over.

a10a-1540455.speaker: Young
a10a-1540455.text: No. We haven't done it yet. Over.

a10a-1540455.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1540455.text: 154:15:07 This is Apollo Control at 154 hours, 15 minutes. We're showing Apollo 10's distance as 163,186 nautical miles [302,220 km]. Velocity, 5,082 feet per second [1,549 m/s]. We're estimating the change of shift news conference for 10:30 pm central daylight time.

a10a-1541436.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1541436.text: Apollo 10, this is Houston. We've completed the state vector and clock Delta-T uplink. We've performed the Verb 66 for you. Over.

a10a-1541436.speaker: Young
a10a-1541436.text: Houston, we're in a 20-minute wait period with our C and D [SM RCS] jets disabled, prior to setting up a three-tenths of a degree roll rate.

a10a-1541436.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1541436.text: Roger. We copy. We're through with the computer. We did a Verb 66, state vector update, and clock update.

a10a-1541436.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1541436.text: Apollo 10, this is Houston. Reading you loud and clear. Over.

a10a-1541436.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1541436.text: Houston, this is Apollo 10. Over. How do you read?

a10a-1541436.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1541436.text: Apollo 10. Apollo 10, this is Houston. Reading you loud and clear. Over.

a10a-1541436.speaker: Young
a10a-1541436.text: Roger. We're not reading you, Bruce. We know you're trying, but we can't make it out.

a10a-1541436.speaker: Young
a10a-1541436.text: OK. Read you loud and clear now.

a10a-1541436.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1541436.text: OK. We're through with the computer. We gave you a state vector update, a clock update, and we did the Verb 66 for you. Over.

a10a-1541436.speaker: Young
a10a-1541436.text: Thank you. I was just saying we're in our 20-minute hold period prior to setting up a three tenths degree rate and going to a wide deadband.

a10a-1541436.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1541436.text: Roger. We copy. We'll stick with you until you get set up in PTC, and then I guess we'll bid you a good night.

a10a-1541436.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1541436.text: 10, Houston. On our displays down here, we show your rates nulled out sufficiently to proceed with setting up the desired roll rate. Over.

a10a-1542941.speaker: Young
a10a-1542941.text: Roger. The EMS test was completed, worked just like it's supposed to.

a10a-1542941.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1542941.text: And 10, this is Houston. If you all want to sign off now, we have nothing further for you. I guess we'll expect to hear from you in the same way - I guess Downvoice Backup - as in the past.

a10a-1542941.speaker: Young
a10a-1542941.text: Roger. We'll be talking to you.

a10a-1542941.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1542941.text: 154:36:47 This is Apollo Control. You heard CapCom Bruce McCandless bid the crew goodnight. At the present time, Apollo 10 is 162,122 nautical miles [300,249 km] from Earth, traveling at a speed of 5,098 feet per second [1,554 m/s]. This rest period is scheduled to last for 9 hours until about 163 hours, Ground Elapsed Time. During the night, we'll give you periodic status reports on the condition of the spacecraft and the position and we'll be continuing to monitor systems and also the biomedical information on the crew. At 154 hours, 38 minutes; this is Apollo Control.

a10a-1542941.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1542941.text: This is Apollo Control 155 hours, 24 minutes. Flight Surgeon reports that the crew apparently are still awake. The last time we heard from them was about 50 minutes ago. And CapCom Bruce McCandless bid the crew good night. We have biomedical data on Tom Stafford and Gene Cernan. John Young is apparently in the sleep station under the right couch. We don't have biomedical data on him, but the information we're getting from telemetry from Stafford and Cernan indicates that they have not gone to sleep at this time. Apollo 10 is now 159,739 nautical miles [295,836 km] from Earth. That's more than

a10a-1625427.speaker: Spacecraft
a10a-1625427.text: (Music: Come Fly With Me")

a10a-1625427.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1625427.text: [Whistling.]

a10a-1625427.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1625427.text: Good morning, good morning! This is Tom, John, and Gene from KAT 10, broadcasting again from approximately 140,000 miles [259,280 km] out into the universe. It's a beautiful day out here, and it appears that it might be a beautiful day down in Mother Earth country. For those of you who are not just ready for work or are just getting up: Get up lazy bones! It's time you got up! Big day ahead! And the thought for today is: Remember, National Secretarys Week was last month!

a10a-1625427.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1625427.text: Good morning, Apollo 10. You managed to wake everybody up early down here, and thank you for your brief program. And, we'll be giving your advice due consideration down here. And we've got a little bit of music for you.

a10a-1625427.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1625427.text: Wonderful, Jack. Let's hear it.

a10a-1625427.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1625427.text: (Music: "Zippity-do-da")

a10a-1625427.speaker: Unidentified Crew member
a10a-1625427.text: [Applause.]

a10a-1625427.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1625427.text: Roger. Thank you for the applause. And watch out for migratory bird season.

a10a-1625427.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1625427.text: That was a couple of seals up here.

a10a-1625427.speaker: Engle
a10a-1625427.text: You might have recognized Deke Slayton, as solo, on that song we sent up to you. 10.

a10a-1625427.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1625427.text: Roger. [Laughter.]

a10a-1625427.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1625427.text: If he's eating that food, he's zipptty-do-da-ed all right.

a10a-1625427.speaker: Engle
a10a-1625427.text: He's not in here yet, and I'm going home. I'll see you guys later.

a10a-1625427.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1625427.text: Hey, Joe. We haven't had a chance to say hello to you.

a10a-1625427.speaker: Engle
a10a-1625427.text: I know that. I hung around to wait until you wake up. It was an exciting night last night. I'm glad we SIM'ed it.

a10a-1625427.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1625427.text: We just figured it out. We were rotating from three times an hour, and it's just 3 days and 3 nights every hour now. What day is it? That makes it about the middle of August, I think.

a10a-1625427.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1625427.text: Hello, Houston. Apollo 10.

a10a-1625427.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1625427.text: Morning, Tom.

a10a-1625427.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1625427.text: Roger. Is Joe still there? Over.

a10a-1625427.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1625427.text: Roger. He's still here.

a10a-1625427.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1625427.text: Yes, Joe. How about doing me a favor, will you, old buddy, over?

a10a-1625427.speaker: Engle
a10a-1625427.text: You name it.

a10a-1625427.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1625427.text: OK. We're kind of out of town for church today, and the minister - You know Reverend Parrot - wanted my - you know, reflections or something that might be appropriate to read in the service since I won't be around there. Have you got a pencil? I just had copied down a couple of things that I thought might be appropriate. Over.

a10a-1625427.speaker: Engle
a10a-1625427.text: Roger. Go ahead.

a10a-1625427.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1625427.text: Roger. Psalm 8, Psalm 122, Psalm 148, and Isaiah 2:4. Over.

a10a-1625427.speaker: Engle
a10a-1625427.text: OK. Readback: Psalm 8, 122, 148 and Isaiah 2:4.

a10a-1625427.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1625427.text: Right. Just tell the congregation hello for me and that I thought that those might be appropriate since he was asking for something that - you know - to go along with the mission. Over.

a10a-1625427.speaker: Engle
a10a-1625427.text: Roger that, Tom. That is very appropriate; I'll see that the word gets around.

a10a-1625427.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1625427.text: Joe knows them all, right off the top of his head.

a10a-1625427.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1625427.text: [Laughter.] OK. Right.

a10a-1625427.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1625427.text: Hey, Jack, we're sorry to keep you off the golf course this morning.

a10a-1625427.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1625427.text: I gave up the game a long time ago.

a10a-1625427.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1625427.text: We'll have to try it again after we get back.

a10a-1625427.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1625427.text: That's a good idea. Like to take it up.

a10a-1630607.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1630607.text: Hey, Gene. I've got your astrocast here. We're trying to whip up some news, but I think it will be a while. Yours is...

a10a-1630607.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1630607.text: This Sunday may find you in some quandary over home conditions. There should be some help available. Don't make smart remarks about Marines.

a10a-1630607.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1630607.text: Who wrote that? Did the great philosopher write that?

a10a-1630607.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1630607.text: The unemployed philosopher. He's got the day off today.

a10a-1630607.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1630607.text: Im still waiting for that special song.

a10a-1630607.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1630607.text: And here's John's. His money has to be spent today on institutions and the use of them for various purposes. Take the time to check everything out before doing anything drastic. Finding out the "why" in a situation may be more important than any other determination.

a10a-1630607.speaker: Young
a10a-1630607.text: They got me there, all right.

a10a-1630607.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1630607.text: Yes. And, Tom. Your relatives and neighbors expect to see you this Sunday. Do the amenities gratefully. Make the rounds; there are gifts for you here and there. Then seek solitude. Reprimand all those in your command who make smart remarks about Marines. Over.

a10a-1630607.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1630607.text: Hey, Jack. Don't you call us. We'll call you.

a10a-1630607.speaker: Young
a10a-1630607.text: Are you just coming on duty, or are you leaving?

a10a-1630607.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1630607.text: I've been out guarding the gate all night, of course.

a10a-1630607.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1630607.text: 163:24:29 This is Apollo Control. The crew of Apollo 10 apparently, at this time, having breakfast. They were to have slept a little bit longer, although they did wake up about the premission Flight Plan wake up time. Here at Mission Control it had been decided to let them sleep until they called back here. Their call was in the form of music being piped down from the spacecraft from a small cassette tape recorder. Lunar Module pilot Gene Cernan followed up with a disc jockey bit, and there was a certain amount of repartee between the ground and the spacecraft communicator here in Mission Cont

a10a-1631845.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1631845.text: Hello, Houston. This is Charlie Brown.

a10a-1631845.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1631845.text: Jack, I'd like to hold off on this ECS redundant component check until we get fuel cell number 1 back on the line, which I assume won't be too long, judging from the temperature. The main reason is I'd just rather do that when I turn on the secondary pump.

a10a-1631845.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1631845.text: OK, Gene-o. That will work out good.

a10a-1631845.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1631845.text: 163:33:55 This is Apollo Control. Circuit is getting quite noisy as the spacecraft rotates around where the Omni antennas tend to break lock. Present position of Apollo 10; 134,041 nautical miles [248,244 km] above Earth, out from Earth. Velocity steadily increasing, now 5,609 feet per second [1,710 m/s]. Here in Mission Control, the maneuver PAD for midcourse number 6 and state vector updates and all the other information that must be passed up to the crew today are being generated. The crew apparently still in the midst of breakfast. We will now rejoin the static from the air-to-ground circu

a10a-1631845.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1631845.text: 163:48:46 This is Apollo Control still standing by for resumption of communications with Apollo 10 as they settle down for the day's business. We'll continue to monitor the circuit as hopefully the conversation will resume. Here it goes.

a10a-1633345.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1633345.text: Apollo 10, Houston. I've got the Orange Bugle, here, when you're ready to listen.

a10a-1633345.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1633345.text: OK. Hilo, Hawaii: Kilauea Volcano on the Island of Hawaii erupted shortly before dawn Saturday, spewing lava 200 feet [60 metres] into the air. Dr. Howard Power, scientist in charge of the US Geological Surveys Volcano Observatory said it was the 14th eruption of Kilauea since 1960. The last one occurred February 22 and one lasted for 55 hours. Aboard the Yacht Duchess: The first men scheduled to land on the Moon practiced Earth splashdown procedures in the Gulf of Mexico Saturday and sprayed each other with disinfectant that will be used to guard against any unexpected moonbug contamination.

a10a-1635452.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1635452.text: Hello, Houston. This is 10.

a10a-1635452.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1635452.text: Go ahead.

a10a-1635452.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1635452.text: Jack, I don't know whether we lost you or not, but the last we heard was the mountain climbing.

a10a-1635452.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1635452.text: OK. you lost me. Let's just pick up the baseball scores. That's all I had left. Chicago 7, San Diego 5; Houston 5, Mets 1; Phillies 8, Braves 3; and still no baseball team in Oklahoma.

a10a-1635452.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1635452.text: Roger.

a10a-1635452.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1635452.text: Looks like the Cubs and the Astros are the hottest ball clubs in the league this week.

a10a-1635452.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1635452.text: Yes. The Cubs are quite a ways out in front and Houston really needs it.

a10a-1635452.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1635452.text: Yes. I've got two loyalties there, and so I'm for both teams. Hey, listen, our heartiest and sincere personal congratulations to Miss Virginia.

a10a-1635452.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1635452.text: Roger. We copy. Sincere congratulations to 19-year-old Miss Virginia.

a10a-1635452.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1635452.text: Thank you for the news, Jack. How's the weather back there these days?

a10a-1635452.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1635452.text: Well, the weather around Houston has been real nice. It's getting rather warm, up to about 90 each day. The old humidity is starting to climb, too.

a10a-1635452.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1635452.text: We meant the recovery area.

a10a-1635452.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1635452.text: I have a request in for weather and we'll get that to you pretty soon.

a10a-1635452.speaker: Young
a10a-1635452.text: OK.

a10a-1635452.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1635452.text: And, Jack, you might pass on to the Governor down there in Samoa that we're certainly looking forward to the reception and seeing his beautiful island. Over.

a10a-1635452.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1635452.text: Roger, Tom. We'll pass that on.

a10a-1635452.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1635452.text: OK, 10. Houston. Here's the weather forecast for the landing area. Essentially no change from the weather I gave you yesterday. 1,800 [feet, 550 metres] scattered, 10,000 [feet, 3,000 metres] broken, high broken 10 miles [24 km]. Wind 120 at 15 knots [7.7 m/s], wave height is 5 feet [1.5 metres], 81 degrees, widely scattered showers. Over.

a10a-1635452.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1635452.text: Jack, we missed the first part of that.

a10a-1635452.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1635452.text: OK. The weather conditions are no different than forecast yesterday. 1,800 [feet, 550 metres] scattered, 10,000 [feet, 3,000 metres] broken, high broken in 10 [miles, 24 km], wind 120 at 15 [knots, 7.7 m/s], wave height 5 feet [1.5 metres], 81 degrees, widely scattered showers. Over.

a10a-1635452.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1635452.text: OK. Thank you.

a10a-1635452.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1635452.text: Houston, this is 10.

a10a-1635452.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1635452.text: Go ahead.

a10a-1635452.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1635452.text: As we played "Fly Me To The Moon" about 4 days ago on our way out to remind you of help we needed, we'd like to play you one more song in its entirety to remind you of our determinations.

a10a-1635452.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1635452.text: OK. Go ahead. We're listening.

a10a-1635452.speaker: Spacecraft
a10a-1635452.text: (Music: "Going Back To Houston")

a10a-1635452.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1635452.text: Roger, 10. We can see you're really determined to get here. As a matter of fact, if you want, we probably could arrange it so as you didn't have to stop at Samoa on the way. Over.

a10a-1635452.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1635452.text: Jack, after careful consideration here, we voted that you should go back and guard the gate.

a10a-1635452.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1635452.text: 164:08:13 This is Apollo Control. A little more disk jockey type music out of the spacecraft, Dean Martin's "Going Back to Houston. " Continuing to monitor air to ground here for resumption of the day's activities. Here we go.

a10a-1635452.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1635452.text: Apollo 10, Houston. We would kind of like to go to High Gain antenna, and during PTC mode, if you would go to Reacq and Narrow Beam, your settings are pitch plus 30 and yaw 270. Over.

a10a-1635452.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1635452.text: OK. How soon do you expect us to pick that up, Jack? I'm in Narrow and Reacq right now and I will go to High Gain on my switches, here. And you can switch us whenever you think we will get ACQ.

a10a-1635452.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1635452.text: Roger. And during the times that you are not in PTC today, go High Gain to Manual and select Omni B. Over.

a10a-1635452.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1635452.text: Omni B. Roger.

a10a-1635452.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1635452.text: 164:11:04 This is Apollo Control. Circuit noise building up as the spacecraft rotates around to here it's breaking lock with the Omni antenna. We will continue to monitor for resumption of conversation.

a10a-1640952.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1640952.text: Hello, Houston. This is 10.

a10a-1640952.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1640952.text: Howdy, 10. Reading you loud and clear, now.

a10a-1640952.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1640952.text: Yes. That - let me get that antenna set up for you, and then I'll put it in Reacq because it doesn't want to pick it up and lock onto you and reacq you. Let me know when you want to make that switch over to High Gain, and I'll set it up for you and then put it in Reacq, and then we'll let it run. Otherwise, I don't think it's going to lock on for us. And I've got some RAD readings for you if you'd like them.

a10a-1640952.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1640952.text: OK. Let's go with the RAD readings.

a10a-1640952.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1640952.text: Roger.

a10a-1640952.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1640952.text: Proper report from yesterday - proper reports from yesterday: the Commander and the CMP both had [garble].

a10a-1640952.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1640952.text: Roger. We copy.

a10a-1640952.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1640952.text: And, 10, Houston. You can select High Gain now. Over.

a10a-1640952.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1640952.text: OK. Will do.

a10a-1640952.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1640952.text: Apollo 10, Houston. How do you read now?

a10a-1640952.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1640952.text: OK, Jack. I'll give it to you now. It's in Reacq at plus 30 and 270.

a10a-1640952.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1640952.text: OK, Good.

a10a-1640952.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1640952.text: OK, 10. On the High Gain antenna then, you can leave her hands off and we'll take her from there. Over.

a10a-1640952.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1640952.text: It's all yours. I didn't mean to hit Command Reset but since there's nothing critical, I'd play with it for a while and get it set up because the first time around it didn't want to acquire. It was banging all over the place when we were trying to come back around, so I thought I'd get you a good lock on. So we're at Reacq narrow plus 30, 270 and youve got them.

a10a-1640952.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1640952.text: OK, Gene-o. We weren't quite in the High Gain attitude there, and we weren't able to get our command in.

a10a-1640952.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1640952.text: Okey doke.

a10a-1640952.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1640952.text: Jack, what do you think about putting Fuel Cell 1 on, and I'll get on with that redundant component check and start the battery charge and what have you?

a10a-1640952.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1640952.text: OK, Gene. Let's crank up fuel cell 1 and put it on both buses and give it a chance to warm up, and in about 1 hour we'll go with the redundant component check. Over.

a10a-1640952.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1640952.text: OK. Is it OK then to go ahead and put start charging battery B at this time after I get it on?

a10a-1640952.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1640952.text: Affirmative, Gene-o. You can start your battery B recharge.

a10a-1640952.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1640952.text: Thank you.

a10a-1640952.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1640952.text: And when you're ready to copy I've got consumables and Flight Plan. Over.

a10a-1640952.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1640952.text: OK, Jack. Go ahead on the consumables. Over.

a10a-1640952.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1640952.text: OK. On the consumables, Tom, at 162 hours we had total RCS, 55 percent; A, 44 60 56 58: H 2 and O 2 is 24.7 and 315. Your RCS is 18 percent above the Flight Plan.

a10a-1640952.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1640952.text: OK. I got all those. Thank you.

a10a-1640952.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1640952.text: And, Apollo 10, we've got you out there at about 130,000 miles [240,000 km] at about 5,700 feet per second [1,740 m/s], and got a nominal entry angle of minus 6.52.

a10a-1640952.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1640952.text: Roger. You mean that last maneuver we made with the - using the G&N and the water put us in the corridor there? Over.

a10a-1640952.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1640952.text: Roger.

a10a-1640952.speaker: Young
a10a-1640952.text: Fantastic!

a10a-1640952.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1640952.text: Roger. We'll...

a10a-1640952.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1640952.text: Well, from that I take it we don't - Pardon me. What I take from that is we don't make any more midcourses? Over.

a10a-1640952.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1640952.text: OK, 10. The numbers that I gave you were with a midcourse, would be minus 6.52. So we're going to do a midcourse 6. Over.

a10a-1640952.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1640952.text: Roger. Understand midcourse 6. Thank you.

a10a-1640952.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1640952.text: And in our present status without a midcourse, we'd be up around 6.95, so we're right in there anyway pretty close, but we ought to sweeten it up a little.

a10a-1640952.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1640952.text: Roger. We agree. Over.

a10a-1643513.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1643513.text: And Apollo 10, Houston. We have a state vector for you when we can get your computer and we also have a minor Flight Plan update. Over.

a10a-1643513.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1643513.text: Roger. Computer is in Accept at this time and go ahead.

a10a-1643513.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1643513.text: Roger. Flight Plan update. Here's a note first. The P23's scheduled for today are designed to determine the minimum Sun angle. However, you may have a little difficulty with one or more of these sets due to the Sun angle. However, the attempt should be made anyway on schedule. At 168 hours, consideration is being given to an S-band reflectivity test and the test procedures are on page 3-19A of the Flight Plan.

a10a-1643513.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1643513.text: OK, Apollo 10. Apollo 10, Houston. Understand we didn't key, so I'll repeat.

a10a-1643513.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1643513.text: Roger. We're trying to follow.

a10a-1643513.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1643513.text: How much did you copy, Tom?

a10a-1643513.speaker: Young
a10a-1643513.text: Nothing.

a10a-1643513.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1643513.text: OK. The site wasn't keying...

a10a-1643513.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1643513.text: We didn't copy at all.

a10a-1643513.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1643513.text: Roger. The site wasn't keying and they're keying for us now. So the P23's that are scheduled for today are designed to determine the minimum Sun angle. You may have a little difficulty with one or more of these tests because of the Sun angle. However, the attempt should he made anyway on schedule. At 168 hours, we're giving consideration to making an S-band reflectivity test and these test procedures are on page 3-19A of the Flight Plan. But - We'll come through with more word on this later. At 170:30, delete the ECS redundant component cheek. This check is duplicated in about an hour anyway,

a10a-1643513.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1643513.text: Roger. We have the ECS redundant component check deleted.

a10a-1643513.speaker: Young
a10a-1643513.text: Houston, with that state vector you just gave us, would it be OK to run through P37 to see what that midcourse is going to be? Just to see what this thing thinks it's going to be?

a10a-1643513.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1643513.text: Stand by one, John.

a10a-1643513.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1643513.text: OK. Apollo 10, Houston. Uplink complete; you can go the Block, and we'd like to see you do some P37's. And the time you can use is 176:50, and we would like to follow you through on it. Over.

a10a-1643513.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1643513.text: Apollo 10, Houston. Did you copy?

a10a-1643513.speaker: Young
a10a-1643513.text: Roger. We're going to run through P37 right now.

a10a-1643513.speaker: Young
a10a-1643513.text: Are you guys copying all this OK, Jack?

a10a-1643513.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1643513.text: That is affirmative, John. We've got it.

a10a-1643513.speaker: Young
a10a-1643513.text: Time of transfer: 14 hours, 58 minutes and 44.78 seconds.

a10a-1643513.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1643513.text: Roger. We see it.

a10a-1643513.speaker: Young
a10a-1643513.text: Wow!

a10a-1643513.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1643513.text: Houston, 10.

a10a-1643513.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1643513.text: Go ahead.

a10a-1643513.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1643513.text: Jack, can you get me a recommended exposure setting to use the interior 16-millimeter film outside at distant Earth, please?

a10a-1643513.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1643513.text: Stand by one.

a10a-1643513.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1643513.text: Just want to check it against my stop-meter here.

a10a-1643513.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1643513.text: Roger.

a10a-1643513.speaker: Young
a10a-1643513.text: Gee whiz! Just two passes.

a10a-1643513.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1643513.text: That's great.

a10a-1644816.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1644816.text: Apollo 10, Houston. We noticed you got Delta-V - correction, inertial velocity 36,314 [fps, 11,069 m/s]. We had difference by 1 foot per second, and you got minus 6.5. We got minus 6.52. Over.

a10a-1644816.speaker: Young
a10a-1644816.text: Well, I don't know why. You guys sent me the data. I wouldn't argue over a 200th of a degree anyway; nobody knows it that well.

a10a-1644816.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1644816.text: Roger. We were just trying to tell you how well off you are.

a10a-1644816.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1644816.text: What did you guys get for Delta-V?

a10a-1644816.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1644816.text: Well we're looking a 1.2 on the Delta-V.

a10a-1644816.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1644816.text: 164:53:22 This is Apollo Control. Spacecraft now 129,835 nautical miles [240,454 km] from Earth, traveling at a velocity of 5,701 foot per second [1,738 m/s]. We'll be passing up to the crew the maneuver PAD, all the numbers needed for preparing to do the midcourse correction burn number 6 which will be in the neighborhood of 1.2 feet per second [0.36 m/s]. Also the entry PAD which will have all the numbers needed for the ranging and spacecraft steering during entry, as well as times of entry events such as drogue chute deploy, main parachute deploy and splashdown and so on. These numbers will

a10a-1644816.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1644816.text: Apollo 10, Houston. We have some dope on the exposure setting for you. Turns out the whole film, of course, has to be processed the same way, so if you are going to use a whole magazine for exterior shots, that is a whole magazine, your exposure settings should be film at 1/250. If you want to use part of the film for - part of the magazine for interior shots, then do you exterior shots at f:22 and 1/500. Over.

a10a-1644816.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1644816.text: Jack, I missed part of that. I understand exterior shots with the 69- and 60-millimeter interior is f:22 at 1/500. That's all I heard.

a10a-1644816.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1644816.text: OK, 10. How do you read me now? Over.

a10a-1644816.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1644816.text: OK. Why don't you repeat that for us, Jack? Would you?

a10a-1644816.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1644816.text: OK. Since the whole film has got to be processed in one batch, if you want to use the whole magazine for exterior shots, your setting should be f:11 at 1/250. But if you want to use part of the magazine interior, then do the exteriors at f:22 and 1/500, so that all the pictures will come out all right when they are processed. Over.

a10a-1644816.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1644816.text: OK. I got that. Thank you very much, Jack.

a10a-1650004.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1650004.text: Apollo 10, Houston. It turns out that it's quite important that we do this P23 midcourse navigation drill pretty much on time to get the appropriate data and solutions, and so would like to recommend that we get on with it pretty soon. Over.

a10a-1650004.speaker: Young
a10a-1650004.text: Roger. We're going on with it right now.

a10a-1650004.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1650004.text: 165:28:50 This is Apollo Control. We've had no recent communications with the spacecraft and while the entry and midcourse correction number 6 information is being compiled to pass up to the crew, we'll take this circuit down for the time being and bring it back up when conversation does resume. And at 165 hours, 29 minutes Ground Elapsed Time this is Apollo Control.

a10a-1650004.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1650004.text: This is Apollo Control, 165 hours, 39 minutes Ground Elapsed Time; we have an accumulation of tapes and we'll join the live conversation as the tape is played out.

a10a-1652928.speaker: Young
a10a-1652928.text: Houston, we are wondering from that first look if the W-matrix is OK,

a10a-1652928.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1652928.text: Stand by one. We'll have somebody look at it.

a10a-1652928.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1652928.text: Apollo 10, Houston. Turns out the only way we can look at the W-matrix is to have you call up a verb 67. Over.

a10a-1652928.speaker: Young
a10a-1652928.text: Roger. Well according to the instructions, we're not supposed to change it from what it was the other day, but I was wondering if when you uplink a state vector that doesn't reshuffle it some way or another.

a10a-1652928.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1652928.text: Apollo 10, Houston. If you call up a Verb 67, all that does is let you look at the W-matrix - doesn't do anything to it and when we send you a state vector, it would just reinitialize it. Over.

a10a-1652928.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1652928.text: And, John, when your buddies wake up there, I've got a maneuver PAD and an entry PAD anytime you are ready for it.

a10a-1652928.speaker: Young
a10a-1652928.text: Roger. Go. They are not quite ready.

a10a-1652928.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1652928.text: ... Only with you down there can we feel so secure, Jack, and we're ready to copy, babe.

a10a-1652928.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1652928.text: OK. I've got a midcourse 6 maneuver PAD. Midcourse 6, RCS/G&N: 25240 176 49 5728, plus three balls 12, plus all balls, plus all balls, 088 354 351, NA. H P is plus 00212 00012 005 00012 40 2744 340 033 Delta 003, Lima 12. The rest is NA. Your set stars are Deneb 43, Vega 36. Roll align 148 013 018. Your ullage is a two- quad burn; use Bravo and Delta. How do you copy? Over.

a10a-1652928.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1652928.text: I think I got it all, Jack. It's midcourse 6, it's an RCS/G&N burn: 25240, then we'll go to Noun 33: 176 49 5728, plus three balls 12, plus all balls, plus all balls, roll is 088, 354, and 351. Perigee is plus two balls 212, three balls 12, two balls 5, three balls 12 40 2744 340 033 Delta 003 and Lima 12. Deneb 43, and Vega 36; 148 013 and 018; two quads: Bravo and Delta.

a10a-1655032.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1655032.text: Jack, I'm also starting a fuel cell purge at this time.

a10a-1655032.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1655032.text: Roger. We copy.

a10a-1655032.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1655032.text: Apollo 10, Houston.

a10a-1655032.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1655032.text: 10, Roger. Go ahead with the fuel cell purge.

a10a-1655032.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1655032.text: Houston, Apollo 10. Do you want us to remain in approximately this attitude for the next 2 hours; and where we're going to be picking up sextant navigation stars horizon marks? Over.

a10a-1655032.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1655032.text: Stand by one, Tom.

a10a-1655032.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1655032.text: Apollo 10, Houston; We suggest going back to PTC after the redundant component check is completed, and we'd like to have some words from John as to Sun interference in his P23. Over.

a10a-1655032.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1655032.text: He'll talk to you in a minute. Over.

a10a-1655032.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1655032.text: Hello, Houston. Apollo 10.

a10a-1655032.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1655032.text: Go ahead 10.

a10a-1655032.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1655032.text: Say, Jack, we're starting to get pretty cold in the cabin since we've got to blank out all the windows here for John to do that tracking, and we'd like to get some Sun in this cockpit. Over. So how about delaying here for a few minutes to put the Sun in one of the windows? Over.

a10a-1655032.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1655032.text: Sure, this whole attitude business is at your convenience, Tom.

a10a-1655032.speaker: Young
a10a-1655032.text: Houston, on that P23, I dont think the problem was interference with the Sun. The problem was to try to determine how close to the terminator you could mark stars, wasn't it?

a10a-1655032.speaker: Young
a10a-1655032.text: So you can relax some those star selection sightings for no comm.

a10a-1655032.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1655032.text: Stand by, John.

a10a-1655032.speaker: Young
a10a-1655032.text: I think that the purpose of it was to be able to improve the star selection sighting schedules for the no comm cases. And I didn't have any problem tracking those close to the terminator. ...

a10a-1655032.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1655032.text: Roger. We copy. Yes, John. You're right.

a10a-1655032.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1655032.text: Apollo 10, Houston. Secondary coolant loop check looks good here, and you can go to Reset on your secondary Evap. Over.

a10a-1655032.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1655032.text: OK.

a10a-1655032.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1655032.text: 166:00:00 This is Apollo Control. While waiting for resumption of air-to-ground, to review the two maneuver PADs, or actually, one maneuver PAD and the entry update, the midcourse correction number 6 is now planned for 176 hours, 49 minutes, 57.28 seconds Ground Elapsed Time. It'll be a 1.2-foot per second [0.36 m/s] burn using the RCS thrusters. This will adjust the entry corridor to the proper angle. And then following that the entry information was passed to the crew, which would bring a splash point at 15 degrees, .07 minutes south, or actually 15.07 degrees south latitude by 164.68 west l

a10a-1655032.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1655032.text: Apollo 10, Houston. Your secondary Evap backpressure looks OK now, and you can turn your secondary pump off. This will help you out in that cabin temperature some, there.

a10a-1655032.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1655032.text: Thank you, Jack. We've got it cleaned up, now.

a10a-1661903.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1661903.text: Apollo 10, Houston. I have some Flight Plan information for you.

a10a-1661903.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1661903.text: Stand by for a minute, Houston. Over.

a10a-1661903.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1661903.text: Roger.

a10a-1661903.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1661903.text: Houston, Apollo 10. Go ahead on that Flight Plan. Over.

a10a-1661903.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1661903.text: This is Apollo Control. Let's join the conversation in progress.

a10a-1661903.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1661903.text: OK, 10. Before we go ahead with the Flight Plan, we'd like you to turn on your H 2 purge line heaters now, and start an H 2 purge on fuel cell 1 in 20 minutes. And here's the Flight Plan update. A good time to perform this S-band reflectivity test would be after the completion of P23. And we mentioned that the procedure is on page 3-19A of your Flight Plan. Your acquisition angle for beginning this test is roll 033, pitch 196, yaw 337. And your High Gain angles are pitch minus 010 and yaw 300. In addition, I have roll, pitch, and yaw attitudes and High Gain angles for tests 1, 2, and 3, if you

a10a-1661903.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1661903.text: OK. Stand by.

a10a-1661903.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1661903.text: OK. We're looking at 3-19A now, and go ahead for tests 1, 2, and 3. Over.

a10a-1661903.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1661903.text: OK. For test 1: roll 027, pitch 196, yaw 298. Your High Gain angles will be pitch minus 010, yaw 340. For test number 2: roll is 065, pitch is 196, yaw 298. High gain angles are pitch minus 020 and yaw 350. Test number 3: roll 090, pitch 196, Yaw 306. And your High Gain angles are pitch minus 30 degrees, and yaw is 360 degrees. Over.

a10a-1661903.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1661903.text: Roger. On the callback here. For test 1: roll 027, pitch 196, yaw 298. High gain: pitch minus 010, yaw 340. Test 2: roll 065, pitch 196, yaw 298. High gain: pitch minus 020, yaw 350. Test 3: roll 090, pitch 196, yaw 306. High gain: pitch minus 030, and yaw is 360. Over.

a10a-1661903.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1661903.text: Thats affirmative, Tom.

a10a-1661903.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1661903.text: OK, Jack. And then we'll pick this up around 168 hours. Over.

a10a-1661903.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1661903.text: Roger. 168 hours. And did you copy turning on your H2 purge line heaters? Over.

a10a-1661903.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1661903.text: Roger. You wanted that done in 20 minutes, or do you want it done now for a period of 20? Over.

a10a-1661903.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1661903.text: We would like you to turn on your H2 purge line heaters now, and then start your H2 purge in 20 minutes on fuel cell 1. Over.

a10a-1661903.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1661903.text: OK. Mark the purge line heaters on.

a10a-1661903.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1661903.text: And that will be a continuous purge on each - on fuel cell 1. Over.

a10a-1661903.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1661903.text: Roger. In 20 minutes well start - In other words, you want us to continue to purge fuel cell 1 from now on, then? Over.

a10a-1661903.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1661903.text: That's affirmative. We'll let you know when to terminate the purge on it.

a10a-1661903.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1661903.text: OK.

a10a-1663305.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1663305.text: Apollo 10, Houston. We have a request. We'd like you to - during the reflectivity test, to punch up Verb 64 for us so we can read out the High Gain pitch and yaw angles down here on the ground. Over.

a10a-1663305.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1663305.text: Hello, Houston. This is 10.

a10a-1663305.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1663305.text: Go ahead, 10.

a10a-1663305.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1663305.text: Get your LCL recovery checklist, if you would, Jack.

a10a-1663305.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1663305.text: Go ahead.

a10a-1663305.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1663305.text: OK. The items I call out are the items that we will stow. That's 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 18, 20, 21, 22.

a10a-1663305.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1663305.text: Roger. Copy.

a10a-1663305.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1663305.text: OK. Items 20 and 21 are stowed in the tissue section of A-1.

a10a-1663305.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1663305.text: Understand. Tissue section of A-1.

a10a-1663305.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1663305.text: 20 - 22 is in A-8 with the exerciser.

a10a-1663305.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1663305.text: Go ahead.

a10a-1663305.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1663305.text: All other items are stowed is a single bag. They will be on the onboard side of A-6 strapped down. They'll be between A-6 and the bulkhead.

a10a-1663305.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1663305.text: Roger.

a10a-1663305.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1663305.text: That's it for the LCL. We're not sure exactly yet where we're going to put the canister.

a10a-1663305.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1663305.text: Roger.

a10a-1663305.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1663305.text: You might pass on to - to Joe that items 9 and 10, which were highly cherished, were unavailable.

a10a-1663305.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1663305.text: Roger. We'll pass the word.

a10a-1663305.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1663305.text: Tell him the LCL recovery checklist procedure was not applicable for those two items.

a10a-1663305.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1663305.text: Roger.

a10a-1663305.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1663305.text: Apollo 10, Houston. We have s stowage - a recommended stowage location down here for the lithium hydroxide canister. It says to wrap it in plastic, and wrap it in a sleeping bag, and put it in L-3. Did you get that word? Over.

a10a-1663305.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1663305.text: Well, that's OK. But we're not eating that much food. L-2 and L-3 are still just about full of food. Over.

a10a-1663305.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1663305.text: Roger. We copy, Tom. Did you wrap the canister up to prevent breathing that hydroxide? Over.

a10a-1663305.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1663305.text: Roger. We wrapped it.

a10a-1663305.speaker: Young
a10a-1663305.text: It looks to us like turning the cabin into the Sun increases the cabin temperature about 3 degrees.

a10a-1663305.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1663305.text: Roger, John. We copy.

a10a-1663305.speaker: Young
a10a-1663305.text: Maybe it was 1 degree. Would you believe a half a degree?

a10a-1663305.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1663305.text: Roger. We copy. It didn't do much good.

a10a-1663305.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1663305.text: Hello, Houston. This is 10.

a10a-1663305.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1663305.text: Go ahead,10.

a10a-1663305.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1663305.text: On that - On that LCL recovery checklist, I did make one mistake. You want to get it out again?

a10a-1663305.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1663305.text: Sure, I got it.

a10a-1663305.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1663305.text: I said we brought back items 20, 21, and 22 for stowage. Actually, it was 19, 20, and 22. 21 was really not in condition to bring back.

a10a-1663305.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1663305.text: Roger. We copy.

a10a-1663305.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1663305.text: Think about that one.

a10a-1663305.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1663305.text: Roger. I'll pass the word on to the appropriate people and let them think about it.

a10a-1663305.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1663305.text: You may not have to go too far.

a10a-1663305.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1663305.text: Does super RETRO want to know how many tons of gear we left in the LM?

a10a-1663305.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1663305.text: That's affirmative. How many tons did you leave in the LM?

a10a-1663305.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1663305.text: Seemed about like 20 or 30. We took a temporary stowage bag, three helmet bags full of fluid, materials, and insulation, which probably doesn't weigh very much, and - and - and I would and the hatch stowage bag was full of a lot of gear -the hatch stowage bag. Actually, the weight of that stuff was probably - it was a lot in volume, but it didn't seem to be - You know, it didn't feel like much. But there's a lot of weight. We took one temporary stowage bag and three helmet bags - not helmet bags, but those inner bags in the helmets that you keep your gloves in. We had those full of gear, and o

a10a-1663305.speaker: Lousma
