a10a-1663305.text: Roger. We copy.

a10a-1663305.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1663305.text: Also, it seems like the docking target got misplaced and went with Snoopy.

a10a-1663305.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1663305.text: Roger. Copy. And we'd like you to start the purge on fuel cell 1 now, please.

a10a-1663305.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1663305.text: OK.

a10a-1663305.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1663305.text: But the hatch bag turned out to be a very convenient waste disposal stowage thing. We had that thing just crammed full of stuff.

a10a-1663305.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1663305.text: OK.

a10a-1663305.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1663305.text: Jack, it's after the fact, and as far as LM stowage for that c.g. on that burn was concerned, but it was stowed opposite the probe and drogue on the right-hand side. But like John said, it was big and bulky, but I'm sure it didn't weigh but a couple or 3, 4, or 5 pounds, maybe. And at that time, I didn't think it significant to mention because of the LM c.g., and apparently it wasn't.

a10a-1663305.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1663305.text: OK. Stowed opposite the probe and drogue. And that was the hatch stowage bag?

a10a-1663305.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1663305.text: That's affirmative.

a10a-1663305.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1663305.text: Apollo 10, Houston. We've got some configurations to do on the H 2 and O 2 tank heaters. H 2 tank 1 heater Off, tank 2 heater Auto; O 2 tank 1 heater Auto, mud tank 2 heater Off.

a10a-1663305.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1663305.text: OK, Jack. Ive got those. You know, you're the first guy that's ever passed those up in order of H 2 1 and 2 and O 2 1 and 2? I always get them in some other order. But that's the way I've got them now.

a10a-1663305.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1663305.text: That's left to right, isn't it?

a10a-1663305.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1663305.text: I knew it would have to be different from you, but it seems right this way.

a10a-1665814.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1665814.text: Apollo 10, Houston. Here's something that I didn't get acknowledgment on. If you're not using the computer during the S-band reflectivity test, we'd like you to do a Verb 64 so we can watch the High Gain pitch and yaw angles down here. Over.

a10a-1665814.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1665814.text: Roger. We copied that, Jack, and we'll give it to you.

a10a-1665814.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1665814.text: We will be using the computer to make Automaneuvers to those angles. Over.

a10a-1665814.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1665814.text: Apollo 10, Houston. We've got another news item here. In the Atlanta Classic, Bruce Crampton is leading. In second place by two strokes, Bert Yancy, Bruce Develin, and Gary Player. And the unemployed local philosopher- He just showed up unexpectedly, and he says that color TV is on its way back, just as he predicted, and it's going to make a real splash around here pretty soon.

a10a-1665814.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1665814.text: [Laughter.] Roger. Thank you very much for the news there, Jack.

a10a-1671818.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1671818.text: Apollo 10, Houston: We note down here that you are using only one RCS quad. Unless you'd rather do it otherwise, unless you'd rather continue to do it this way, we'd prefer to use two quads because it does perturb the trajectory somewhat to use only one quad at a time. Over.

a10a-1671818.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1671818.text: OK. Will do. I was just reducing the usage on A. We've got plenty of fuel; just trying to balance it out. I'll go do that. OK. Got them.

a10a-1671818.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1671818.text: And, 10, according to our charts down here, they look pretty well balanced. The requirements are such that A should be looking about the way it is right now.

a10a-1671818.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1671818.text: OK. The onboard indicators are pretty much off then. Over.

a10a-1671818.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1671818.text: OK, Tom.

a10a-1671818.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1671818.text: Now, these folks down here tell me that you guys have so far set the economy record on the fuel usage so far.

a10a-1671818.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1671818.text: Roger. Thank you. We've been watching it real close. We did use quite a bit in the landmark tracking's to really pulse and make sure everything was on there since we knew how important that was, but other than that, we've been watching it as tight as we could. Over.

a10a-1671818.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1671818.text: Roger, Tom.

a10a-1671818.speaker: Mitchell
a10a-1671818.text: Put you in the Mobil Economy Run next year, Tom.

a10a-1671818.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1671818.text: Yes. Right, Ed. Hello there.

a10a-1671818.speaker: Cooper
a10a-1671818.text: Watch who'll get you for a commercial.

a10a-1671818.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1671818.text: Good morning, Gordo. How are you?

a10a-1671818.speaker: Cooper
a10a-1671818.text: Fine, Tom. We enjoyed your readings this morning.

a10a-1671818.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1671818.text: Roger.

a10a-1671818.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1671818.text: 167:36:36 This is Apollo Control. While we are waiting for our conversation to resume. a few numbers here. Distance of Earth from Apollo 10 is now 120,555 nautical miles [223,268 km]; approach velocity now up to 5,921.9 feet per second [1,805 m/s]. Spacecraft weight computed to be 25,200 pounds [11,430 kg]. Continuing to monitor air to ground. Pretty quiet now. The crew should be involved in midcourse navigation exercise in which stars and Earth horizon, either near or far horizon, here goes a call.

a10a-1671818.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1671818.text: Houston, Apollo 10. That completes the star horizon check. I guess the next activity will be about 168 hours when we come up for the reflectivity test. Over.

a10a-1671818.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1671818.text: Roger, 10. We copy.

a10a-1671818.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1671818.text: And we are going to open all shades now and get some heat in this place. Over.

a10a-1671818.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1671818.text: Roger.

a10a-1671818.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1671818.text: And I notice our quad A temperature has gone up quite a bit, even though it is still lower than what we had in lunar orbit. We'll go ahead and start maneuvering into these attitudes for the S-band reflectivity test. Over.

a10a-1671818.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1671818.text: Roger, Tom.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1674346.text: Houston, this is 10. I'll go ahead and record step 5 and if there's any difference, just make note of it. I'll just go ahead and follow through with it.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1674346.text: Roger.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1674346.text: Jack, just one other quick question. Step 2, where I've got the control values, I used the new control values that you read up to Tom here a little while ago for test 1, 2, and 3. Is that correct?

a10a-1674346.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1674346.text: Stand by one.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1674346.text: OK, Gene. In step 1, we gave you the attitudes to which to go to get the pitch and yaw angles as specified in tests 1, 2, and 3. And then we still want you to set your High Gain control to those settings which are listed in step 2, which are all 20 degrees off in yaw.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1674346.text: Jack, you gave us a roll, pitch and yaw attitude and a High Gain pitch and yaw for tests 1, 2, and 3. I'm just a little bit confused. On step 2, do you want me to use the printed numbers in the book or do you want me to use the pitch and yaw that you gave us before with the roll, pitch, and yaw for tests 1, 2, and 3?

a10a-1674346.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1674346.text: OK. The attitudes that I gave you were just a convenience number. Those are the attitudes to which you should go to set up your antenna as specified in step 1. Then we want you to slew the - -

a10a-1674346.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1674346.text: OK. Fine...

a10a-1674346.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1674346.text: Roger. Copy now?

a10a-1674346.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1674346.text: OK. Yes. I'll use your pitch and yaw for acquisition and then I'll go right through steps 1, 2, 3, and so forth just as written with the numbers.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1674346.text: Right. And then when you go to step 3, this causes you to slew off and then you go to step 4 back to Auto. This will tell us how well the antenna comes back to the position to which we want it to come.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1674346.text: OK.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1674346.text: And if we get the same numbers in step 5, why, then we know that the antenna is doing what we want it to, and if not, why, we want to know what those numbers are and reduce the data later.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1674346.text: Okey doke.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1674346.text: Apollo 10, we're handing over the High Gain. You may get a burst of noise.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1674346.text: OK, Houston. We're at the first attitude and I'm going to my ranging switch off and we do have a good lock at this attitude.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1674346.text: Roger.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Young
a10a-1674346.text: OK, now I maneuver to High Gain, here.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1674346.text: [Garble] High Gain [garble] High Gain.

a10a-1674346.text: Minus 10 and 340.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1674346.text: [Garble].

a10a-1674346.text: It said High Gain Antenna control to minus 10 and 320. ... High Gain ... ?

a10a-1674346.speaker: Young
a10a-1674346.text: It is.

a10a-1674346.text: [Garble]. Right?

a10a-1674346.text: Yes.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1674346.text: [Garble].

a10a-1674346.text: Yes.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1674346.text: High Gain Antenna ... High Gain. Can High Gain be ... compared?

a10a-1674346.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1674346.text: High Gain control.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Young
a10a-1674346.text: Shit, they always compare.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1674346.text: I mean manually.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Young
a10a-1674346.text: [Garble] High Gain [garble] High Gain control. Shit, when you're in Manual, they always ...

a10a-1674346.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1674346.text: Hello, Houston. This is Apollo 10. [Garble] on this reflectivity test Im rolling right [garble].

a10a-1674346.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1674346.text: No, I think they want us to get all through with it, Tom.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Young
a10a-1674346.text: You don't have to hold attitude to proceed, Tom.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1674346.text: OK.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Young
a10a-1674346.text: Proceed to CMC in Auto.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1674346.text: Yes. But the heater configuration switch is Off.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1674346.text: Apollo 10, Houston. We've got lots of background noise. Stand by on your transmission.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Young
a10a-1674346.text: OK, what'd you do? What's your - fuel - cryo pressure?

a10a-1674346.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1674346.text: I'll get [garble], Tom.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Young
a10a-1674346.text: Have we got the other fuel cell on the line? Huh?

a10a-1674346.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1674346.text: Is fuel cell 1 heating?

a10a-1674346.speaker: Young
a10a-1674346.text: Huh? Is it on the line?

a10a-1674346.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1674346.text: Yes.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Young
a10a-1674346.text: Turn the freaking heater on.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1674346.text: Apollo 10, Houston. You have a caution and warning on the H 2 Press Cryo tank. Don't worry about it. In fact, the heater's going to cycle momentarily to bring that pressure back up.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1674346.text: OK. Looks like it's tank 1 to us. Tank 2 is well in the green.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1674346.text: Roger. We copy tank 1. It'll cycle and come on up.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1674346.text: But that's the configuration I gave you 30 minutes ago.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Young
a10a-1674346.text: I just flipped the heater switch to Auto. Okay.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1674346.text: Roger, 10. They tell us that tank 1 is going to follow the tank 2 heater cycle. Over.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1674346.text: Tank [garble] is off.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Young
a10a-1674346.text: OK.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1674346.text: I don't understand that one.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Young
a10a-1674346.text: [Garble] is lower. It cuts on [garble].

a10a-1674346.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1674346.text: [Garble] High Gain meter to High Gain control. High Gain [garble] Auto...

a10a-1674346.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1674346.text: Let's turn [garble]. We got the Cryo pressure again. Over.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1674346.text: We're in High Gain.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1674346.text: We're really banging or freaking this damn antenna back [garble] uplink on the Omni [garble].

a10a-1674346.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1674346.text: Apollo 10, Houston. Let's put heaters in both H 2 Cryo tanks to Auto. Over.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1674346.text: OK, there both Auto. And we're in step 5, test 1.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1674346.text: Roger.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Young
a10a-1674346.text: [Garble] zero, zero, zero.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1674346.text: Hello, Houston, Houston. How do you read test 1?

a10a-1674346.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1674346.text: We're reading you, 10. A little background noise.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1674346.text: OK. Very good. I'm going on to step 2 and Ill give you a reading test when it's all over.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1674346.text: Roger.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1674346.text: Maneuver to High Gain. Minus 20 and 320.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Young
a10a-1674346.text: You got to go to that different attitude, don't you?

a10a-1674346.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1674346.text: Yes. Tom, how about roll 065...

a10a-1674346.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1674346.text: I've got to roll 065? You mean, after I get him, I go to a different attitude on test 1?

a10a-1674346.speaker: Young
a10a-1674346.text: Yes.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1674346.text: Well, we're on test 2 now.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1674346.text: Oh, this is the second test. OK, [garble] let's go here.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Young
a10a-1674346.text: Do you want me to do that for you?

a10a-1674346.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1674346.text: Yes. Why don't you...

a10a-1674346.speaker: Young
a10a-1674346.text: OK. What's the numbers there, Gene-o?

a10a-1674346.speaker: Young
a10a-1674346.text: Same thing, huh? 065, 196, and 298, huh? Go.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Young
a10a-1674346.text: I wished I knew what the freak we're doing.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1674346.text: Tell you what - I'd better talk...

a10a-1674346.speaker: Young
a10a-1674346.text: I know it.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1674346.text: Apollo 10, Houston. We need the fans on in both H 2 Cryo tanks. Over.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Young
a10a-1674346.text: [Garble] the shit out of our cryo's.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1674346.text: OK. The fans are on.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1674346.text: [Garble] fuel cell off?

a10a-1674346.speaker: Young
a10a-1674346.text: [Laughter.] Keeps it running, doesn't it, by God; keeps the damn temperature down there...

a10a-1674346.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1674346.text: That's where it is.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1674346.text: That's right.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1674346.text: Heater's broken off-scale, and we're purging off-scale high. How about that?

a10a-1674346.speaker: Young
a10a-1674346.text: We still got the Fuel Cell 1 light now, but for a different reason. Hell, we've got it for three reasons.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1674346.text: That's right, three reasons, three out of the six not bad (yawn).

a10a-1674346.speaker: Young
a10a-1674346.text: Oh! 91 from 168. That sure is an interesting test you're running there, Gene-o, but I [garble] if I understand it. Uh-oh, where is the entry checklist?

a10a-1674346.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1674346.text: I've got it.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Young
a10a-1674346.text: Can I bum it from you?

a10a-1674346.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1674346.text: Sure can.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Young
a10a-1674346.text: Want to-look over some of that good stuff here before we [garble]?

a10a-1674346.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1674346.text: [Garble] make you hungry, John?

a10a-1674346.speaker: Young
a10a-1674346.text: [Garble].

a10a-1674346.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1674346.text: [Garble] should just be exquisite.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1674346.text: OK, we're there.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1674346.text: Yes, I know.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1674346.text: Hello, Houston, Houston. This is Apollo 10. How do you read on test 2?

a10a-1674346.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1674346.text: Read you loud and clear.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1674346.text: OK. We'll Proceed to test 3.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1674346.text: Roger on 3.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1674346.text: [Garble] OK, roll is 090.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1674346.text: Yes.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1674346.text: OK, pitch?

a10a-1674346.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1674346.text: OK, roll is 090, pitch is 196, yaw is 30 [garble] OK.

a10a-1674346.text: What you got this thing here up here for?

a10a-1674346.text: What thing?

a10a-1674346.text: That thing here.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1674346.text: I've never - Must have done that [garble].

a10a-1674346.text: That was that one we launched.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1674346.text: It was?

a10a-1674346.speaker: Young
a10a-1674346.text: Yes, because I never touched it.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1674346.text: I never touched it.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1674346.text: I never touched it.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Young
a10a-1674346.text: Oh, shit.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1674346.text: [Laughter.]

a10a-1674346.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1674346.text: [Garble] have to abort.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Young
a10a-1674346.text: I'm glad we didn't, too.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1674346.text: I never touched it. I didn't even notice the damn thing.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Young
a10a-1674346.text: I - You know - I said, well, you know, one of [garble].

a10a-1674346.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1674346.text: Well, that'll help attenuate [garble] shock and [garble] pull that thing in tension.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Young
a10a-1674346.text: Pull it right out of the freaking wall [Laughter.].

a10a-1674346.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1674346.text: I had assumed you put it up there when you did the [garble] check.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Young
a10a-1674346.text: Hell, no; I didn't need it. Zero g. It was up when I - you know - it was up. I figured you'd already put it up.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1674346.text: Let me know - how close we are, Tom.

a10a-1674346.speaker: Stafford

a10a-1680758.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1680758.text: You know, I bet when we splash down out there, this water - cold water runs all out in that [garble].

a10a-1680758.speaker: Young
a10a-1680758.text: Bet you're right. That's probably where all the water comes from.

a10a-1680758.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1680758.text: I bet - I bet there'll be water galore [garble] cold now.

a10a-1680758.speaker: Young
a10a-1680758.text: Well, a lot of it's condensing up the hatch, too.

a10a-1680758.speaker: Young
a10a-1680758.text: That's a good place for it; there ain't no wires up here. I don't give a shit if we get ice up here as long as there ain't no wiring up there [garble] as long as we don't have to live up there.

a10a-1680758.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1680758.text: That shit will come raining down...

a10a-1680758.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1680758.text: Good place to put your feet up [garble].

a10a-1680758.speaker: Young
a10a-1680758.text: If I was designing the spacecraft, I'd make the bastard get the water out of it before it ever starts; but once it's designed, that's probably as good a place to have a water separator as anywhere.

a10a-1680758.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1680758.text: Did the other spacecraft notice water under there?

a10a-1680758.speaker: Young
a10a-1680758.text: I don't know if they ever noticed ice or not. We've got a lot of water up there now, a lot, a lot. Let me get my rag and go up in there and clean it out, as a matter of fact. Here, let me look at this here.

a10a-1680758.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1680758.text: [Garble].

a10a-1680758.speaker: Young
a10a-1680758.text: 5-C and -D. [Garble] at 168 hours 5-C...

a10a-1680758.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1680758.text: This is Apollo Control, 118,670 nautical miles [219,777 km] out from Earth. Velocity now 5,969 feet per second [1,819 m/s]. Air-to-ground still live for any possible conversation with the crew of Apollo 10.

a10a-1680758.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1680758.text: Hello, Houston. This is 10. How do you read?

a10a-1680758.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1680758.text: Loud and clear. How me?

a10a-1680758.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1680758.text: I'm reading you the same. I've got your readings if youd like them for 1, 2, and 3.

a10a-1680758.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1680758.text: Go ahead.

a10a-1680758.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1680758.text: Roger 10. Go ahead with the reading.

a10a-1680758.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1680758.text: Test 1 is pitch minus 10, yaw 360, and the percent signal is 65, and it was oscillating about two needles' width. Two is minus 25, 360, 65 percent, and steady. Three is minus 30, meter flipped to 000, 90 percent, and steady.

a10a-1680758.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1680758.text: Roger. Me copied all that. Thank you.

a10a-1680758.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1680758.text: OK, Jack?

a10a-1680758.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1680758.text: Houston, Apollo 10. We're all set to go back to PTC at this time. Over.

a10a-1680758.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1680758.text: Roger, Tom. Set yourself up in PTC.

a10a-1680758.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1680758.text: Jack, two added comments on the first and second tests: it appeared to me that the High Gain antenna did not regain a signal strength. However, in the third test, it appeared that it did 90 percent.

a10a-1680758.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1680758.text: Roger. We copy, Gene. Thank you.

a10a-1680758.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1680758.text: I tell you, though, in the last 3 or 4 days, I've become a High Gain fan.

a10a-1680758.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1680758.text: Roger. And the High Gain sure sounds a lot clearer and a lot better down here than the Omni's do.

a10a-1680758.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1680758.text: Sounds like you're sitting in the cockpit with us, Jack.

a10a-1680758.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1680758.text: Apollo 10, Houston. We're going to do another High Gain handover here in about 20 seconds; you might expect another burst.

a10a-1680758.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1680758.text: Roger.

a10a-1680758.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1680758.text: Hey, Jack, is it 12 o'clock noon down there?

a10a-1680758.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1680758.text: That's pretty darn close; I've got 12:04.

a10a-1680758.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1680758.text: Apollo 10, Houston. We'll need the S-band nominal ranging switch Ranging, please.

a10a-1680758.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1680758.text: Sorry about that, Jack.

a10a-1682602.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1682602.text: Apollo 10, Houston. We expect that you are in the 20-minute wait period for setting up PTC and we notice that we have all four quads. We'll need Alfa and Bravo. Over.

a10a-1682602.speaker: Young
a10a-1682602.text: Roger. I'm still thumbing through my book trying to find out how to do this.

a10a-1682602.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1682602.text: It's all right.

a10a-1682602.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1682602.text: Houston, will you give us a call when you think we've spent enough time waiting?

a10a-1682602.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1682602.text: That's affirmative. We'll tell you.

a10a-1682602.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1682602.text: Hello, Jack. This is Charlie Brown.

a10a-1682602.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1682602.text: Go ahead, Charlie.

a10a-1682602.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1682602.text: We're in the process now of commencing scientific experiment Sugar Hotel Alpha Victor Echo. And it's going to be conducted like all normal human beings do it.

a10a-1682602.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1682602.text: Atta boy. Roger. We copy. That'll impress the folks in Pago Pago.

a10a-1682602.speaker: Young
a10a-1682602.text: I don't know whether we're all going to make it. We're going to take a look at it one at a time, and we may decide that we'll have one test subject.

a10a-1682602.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1682602.text: Roger. I hope well get a chance to take a look at that on TV tonight, or tomorrow.

a10a-1682602.speaker: Young
a10a-1682602.text: You will for sure. We'll have it recorded for posterity also.

a10a-1682602.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1682602.text: Roger. Can't be worse than fiber glass.

a10a-1682602.speaker: Young
a10a-1682602.text: Would you believe what the shaving cream packed at 14.7 looks like when you open it up a 5 psi?

a10a-1682602.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1682602.text: Yes. Bet that looks colorful.

a10a-1682602.speaker: Young
a10a-1682602.text: It's white, but colorful.

a10a-1682602.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1682602.text: And, 10, Houston. We haven't come up with any better ideas on stowing that hydroxide canister. We want to make sure it's well protected, doesn't get damaged, so the only suggestion we've now got is to either find a place for it or have a big Sunday dinner and pack it in the L-3, or take the stuff out of L-3 and put it somewhere else, and pack the container in there. That's it. Over.

a10a-1682602.speaker: Young
a10a-1682602.text: OK.

a10a-1682602.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1682602.text: If you come up with a different location, we'd like to know what it is, so we can tell RETRO.

a10a-1682602.speaker: Young
a10a-1682602.text: We'll let Gene hold it on his lap.

a10a-1682602.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1682602.text: We'll find someplace for it and let you know, Jack.

a10a-1682602.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1682602.text: OK. Thanks.

a10a-1682602.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1682602.text: Houston, this is 10. The test is proceeding very successfully.

a10a-1682602.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1682602.text: Roger. Copy. Just as planned.

a10a-1682602.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1682602.text: Say, Tom, are those Navy guys getting themselves properly configured to keep up this immaculate Navy image? Over.

a10a-1682602.speaker: Young
a10a-1682602.text: He's off the headset right now, configuring.

a10a-1682602.speaker: Young
a10a-1682602.text: Jack, I hope you got John and my shoes done early enough to get sent out to the ship.

a10a-1682602.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1682602.text: I was going to say I wondered if you guys had a set of whites up there, or something like that. Maybe you've got some of those short pants they wear around.

a10a-1682602.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1682602.text: Houston, how does that look to you for 20 minutes?

a10a-1682602.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1682602.text: Wed like to hold off about another minute to complete the dump.

a10a-1682602.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1682602.text: OK, 10. It's complete. You can start PTC now.

a10a-1682602.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1682602.text: Thank you.

a10a-1682602.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1682602.text: Just to Break the monotony of this PTC, we're going to roll left this time.

a10a-1682602.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1682602.text: OK. Copy left-hand pattern.

a10a-1685038.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1685038.text: Apollo 10, Houston. Since you're rolling left this time, we'll have to give you some new High Gain angles and here they are: pitch minus 50 and yaw 90. Over.

a10a-1685038.speaker: Young
a10a-1685038.text: I'm afraid we may have messed this one up. It looks for some reason like we got an operator error when we punched that last button, and it started to rate and went back some way or other.

a10a-1685038.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1685038.text: It looks all right down here, 10.

a10a-1685038.speaker: Young
a10a-1685038.text: OK. But there was a lot of jet firing in there when I was trying to initiate the - to start this thing while I was making the entries, which I don't understand.

a10a-1685038.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1685038.text: You probably just have a right-handed spacecraft and he doesn't want to go that way.

a10a-1685038.speaker: Young
a10a-1685038.text: Houston, can you check and see that the deadband is opened up? I think it is.

a10a-1685038.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1685038.text: We've got you in wide deadband. We don't see anything different than the way it's supposed to be.

a10a-1685038.speaker: Young
a10a-1685038.text: OK, Jack. The only thing that I notice is that we're starting with both rates in both the - pitch and yaw a little and we're a little further off than we usually are by this time in the PTC. Usually it's gone for a couple of hours before it gets out 5 degrees.

a10a-1685038.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1685038.text: Yes. We're copying that too, but what I'm saying is, you did everything right.

a10a-1685911.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1685911.text: 10. Negative. Houston, 10. Do we have Goldstone acquisition? Over.

a10a-1685911.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1685911.text: Apollo 10, Houston. We're off Madrid right now and expect to get Goldstone about 171 30 Over.

a10a-1685911.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1685911.text: Apollo 10, Houston. We'd like you to turn the H 2 tank heaters off and tell us what position they're in at this time. Over.

a10a-1685911.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1685911.text: Stand by. We're kind of scattered all over the spacecraft. H 2 tank heaters are in Auto 1 and 2, and well turn them off at this time.

a10a-1685911.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1685911.text: The fans are both on - on. Over.

a10a-1685911.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1685911.text: Roger. And fans on. Leave them on.

a10a-1685911.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1685911.text: This is Apollo Control - no recent contact with Apollo 10, conversation wise. Now showing a distance of 113,516 nautical miles [210,232 km] distance; velocity, 6,106 feet per second [1,861 m/s]; showing now about 22 hours, 11 minutes until splash; this number likely will change somewhat when they do the midcourse correction burn number 6 which is now some 7 hours, 11 minutes from now. If and when the conversation does pick up again, we'll come back up live. And at 169 hours, 37 minutes Ground Elapsed Time, this is Apollo Control.

a10a-1685911.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1685911.text: This is Apollo Control; 169 hours, 56 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. Apollo 10 now 112,350 nautical miles [208,072 km] out from Earth, approaching at a velocity of 6,139 feet per second [1,871 m/s]. We have about 3 and a half minutes of accumulated tape of brief transmissions that have taken place since last the circuit was up live. We'll play that back at this time.

a10a-1694034.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1694034.text: Apollo 10, Houston. We weren't able to get High Gain the last time around. Want you to confirm that you are in the Reacq mode on the High Gain. Over.

a10a-1694034.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1694034.text: OK. We're in Reacq, now. So we were We were in Auto before.

a10a-1694034.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1694034.text: Roger. We copy, Tom. Thank you.

a10a-1694034.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1694034.text: Roger. What angles do you want for Reacq? Over.

a10a-1694034.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1694034.text: 10, that's pitch minus 50 and yaw 90. Over.

a10a-1694034.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1694034.text: Pitch minus 50 and yaw minus 90, right?

a10a-1694034.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1694034.text: Roger. Your yaw is 90 and pitch is minus 50. Over.

a10a-1694034.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1694034.text: Roger, Tom. Pitch minus 50 and yaw 90.

a10a-1700424.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1700424.text: Apollo 10, Houston. We'd like to get a little bit of - a little better handle on what's going on in the H 2 tanks, so we'd like you to make sure the fans are off in both H 2 tanks and the heaters in Auto for both H 2 tanks. Over.

a10a-1700424.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1700424.text: OK, Jack. We've got the fans off now and the heaters in Auto. Is there something unusual going on? You looking at the total quantity?

a10a-1700424.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1700424.text: No. We had reason to believe that one of the heaters may have stayed on one tank a while ago.

a10a-1700424.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1700424.text: OK, fine. My hydrogen purge now is coming down to 0.05. My flow rates are excellent. It's going to hit zero.

a10a-1700424.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1700424.text: Yes. I don't think you heard me earlier, but the experiment is proving to be a three-way huge success and you can pass on to the Governor of Pago Pago that we're ready to kick up our heels.

a10a-1700424.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1700424.text: Roger. We'll assure that you're probably escorted there, to Pago Pago. And the experiment came off successfully. Thank you.

a10a-1700424.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1700424.text: It really did, Jack. It came off very well, as a matter of fact.

a10a-1700424.speaker: Young
a10a-1700424.text: That's right. Just like we expected.

a10a-1700424.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1700424.text: This is Apollo Control; 170 hours, 21 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. Apollo 10 presently 110,871 nautical miles [205,333 km] out from Earth, coming in 6,180 feet per second [1,884 m/s]. Approximately an hour and a half from now, at 171 hours, 50 minutes, 49 seconds; Apollo 10 will be exactly midway on the return trip from the Moon. Mileage both ways will be 105,410 nautical miles [195,220 km]. We have an accumulation of tape of perhaps 2 minutes. It's been recorded within the last half hour. Let's listen to that now.

a10a-1704107.speaker: Young
a10a-1704107.text: Roger. Wonder if we shouldn't knock this off. This seems to be a little too much rates here.

a10a-1704107.speaker: Young
a10a-1704107.text: I'm wondering if you shouldn't knock this PTC off, and do some star landmark or something.

a10a-1704107.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1704107.text: OK, 10. This is Houston. Why don't we knock off the PTC now and start working on the P23 again. Over.

a10a-1704107.speaker: Young
a10a-1704107.text: OK. Because it'll take us that long to get started on it anyway.

a10a-1704107.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1704107.text: This is Apollo Control, 170 hours, 45 minutes. The Black Team of Flight Controllers has relieved the Orange Team. Apollo 10 is 109,413 nautical miles [202,633 km] from Earth; velocity, 6,222 feet per second [1,896 m/s]. Apollo 10 has discontinued the Passive Thermal Control mode and is now preparing to take another set of midcourse star Earth/horizon marks. Here's a brief bit of conversation on that subject.

a10a-1705531.speaker: Duke
a10a-1705531.text: Hello, Apollo 10. Houston. We'd just like for you to turn both H 2 Cryo tank heaters Off. It looks like they're stuck on in the Auto position. Over.

a10a-1705531.speaker: Duke
a10a-1705531.text: And, 10. Houston. We'd like you to verify that the Cryo fans are off also. Over.

a10a-1705531.speaker: Duke
a10a-1705531.text: Apollo 10, Houston. Bruce and I are just sitting here looking at your weather tomorrow. It looks like it's going to be about 1,800 [feet, 550 metres] scattered, 15-knot [7.71 m/s] winds at 5-foot [1.5 metres] seas. Beautiful day out there, and it's a beautiful day in Houston here today with about 90 degrees. There's so many people on Clear Lake you can't even see the water. Over.

a10a-1705531.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1705531.text: Roger, Charlie. Thanks for the weather report. John's getting started on his optics calibration at this time. Over.

a10a-1705531.speaker: Duke
a10a-1705531.text: Roger. We see that. Thank you, Tom.

a10a-1705531.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1705531.text: And, also, all three of us shaved today just using a very new technique called shaving cream and a razor, and it worked beautiful. Over.

a10a-1705531.speaker: Duke
a10a-1705531.text: Roger. That's what Jack passed on to us, Tom. That's really good news. Thanks a lot.

a10a-1705531.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1705531.text: This is Apollo Control at 171 hours, 40 minutes. Apollo 10 is 106,026 nautical miles [196,360 km] from the Earth approaching a velocity of 6,322 feet per second [1,927 m/s].

a10a-1705531.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1705531.text: We're about 9 minutes away from the time when Apollo 10 will be half-way home. The mid-point coming at 171 hours, 50 minutes, 49 seconds. We expect the distance-that time to be 105,410 nautical miles [195,219 km] to the Earth and to the Moon.

a10a-1712506.speaker: Duke
a10a-1712506.text: Hello, Apollo 10. Houston. John, could you pause for about - just 5 more seconds on the Noun 49? You're a little too speedy for the guys.

a10a-1712506.speaker: Young
a10a-1712506.text: Roger.

a10a-1712506.speaker: Young
a10a-1712506.text: Houston, that completes the sightings.

a10a-1712506.speaker: Duke
a10a-1712506.text: Roger, 10. Thank you much. Out.

a10a-1712506.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1712506.text: While we've got a couple of minutes here, is there anymore news out today?

a10a-1712506.speaker: Duke
a10a-1712506.text: Say again.

a10a-1712506.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1712506.text: I said, we got a couple of minutes here to listen. Is there any news today of any sort?

a10a-1712506.speaker: Duke
a10a-1712506.text: Stand by. We'll - -

a10a-1712506.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1712506.text: We heard some news early this morning.

a10a-1712506.speaker: Duke
a10a-1712506.text: Stand by. We'll see if we can get you something.

a10a-1712506.speaker: Duke
a10a-1712506.text: Hello, 10. Houston. John, your marks put you within 10 miles of MSFN's best estimate of ... perigee. And it was very good. PAO is coming up with some news for you. We'll have it for you in a little while.

a10a-1712506.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1712506.text: OK.

a10a-1712506.speaker: Young
a10a-1712506.text: Yes. But is it good enough, Charlie?.

a10a-1712506.speaker: Duke
a10a-1712506.text: Roger. Everybody's real satisfied with your marking. Over.

a10a-1712506.speaker: Young
a10a-1712506.text: Well, I ain't too happy with it.

a10a-1712506.speaker: Duke
a10a-1712506.text: Let me get you some exact figures. Stand by. I'll talk to FIDO.

a10a-1712506.speaker: Duke
a10a-1712506.text: Hello 10, Houston. John, you're improving your perigee from set to set. We feel like, on the next set, it'll be very close to a MSFW prediction. Right now, we have 15 nautical miles for a perigee, and you're coming up with 5. Last time - That's a 35-mile improvement over the last set of marks. Over.

a10a-1712506.speaker: Young
a10a-1712506.text: That's a step in the right direction, huh?

a10a-1712506.speaker: Duke
a10a-1712506.text: Roger that.

a10a-1712506.speaker: Young
a10a-1712506.text: Charlie, what I want to do when I finish this next set is go through P37 for the ignition time of the burn and see what it says I ought to do. Would that be fair?

a10a-1712506.speaker: Duke
a10a-1712506.text: Roger. That's affirmative.

a10a-1714939.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1714939.text: Hey, Charlie, where do you estimate Snoopy is these days?

a10a-1714939.speaker: Duke
a10a-1714939.text: 10, Houston. FIDO hasn't updated his estimate since the last time we passed it up. He'll work you out one, and we'll pass it up in a little bit.

a10a-1714939.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1714939.text: At the midpoint, velocity was 6,341 feet per second [1,933 m/s].

a10a-1714939.speaker: Duke
a10a-1714939.text: Hello, Apollo 10. Houston. Could you give us a Verb 74? We'd like to look at your erasable.

a10a-1714939.speaker: Young
a10a-1714939.text: Why don't you fix anything I messed up in there while you're at it.

a10a-1714939.speaker: Duke
a10a-1714939.text: Roger. We can't find anything you've messed up. It's all looking great.

a10a-1714939.speaker: Young
a10a-1714939.text: Listen, as many times as I punched them buttons, if theres not something wrong, it'll be a miracle.

a10a-1720447.speaker: Young
a10a-1720447.text: Houston, Apollo 10. Over.

a10a-1720447.speaker: Duke
a10a-1720447.text: Go ahead, 10.

a10a-1720447.speaker: Young
a10a-1720447.text: Roger. We have reached low enough to start PTC this time?

a10a-1720447.speaker: Duke
a10a-1720447.text: That's affirmative.

a10a-1720447.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1720447.text: This is Apollo Control. At 172 hours, 14 minutes. Apollo 10's distance from the Earth is 103,963 nautical miles [192,539 km]. Velocity is 6,386 feet per second [1,946 m/s]. We understand there has been some confusion about the form of shaving cream used by the crew. The shaving cream was in a tube. It was a tube of brushless shaving cream.

a10a-1720447.speaker: Young
a10a-1720447.text: OK, Charlie. I think we've got a good one going this time.

a10a-1720447.speaker: Duke
a10a-1720447.text: Roger, John.

a10a-1720447.speaker: Young
a10a-1720447.text: It doesn't have any of the rates in pitch and yaw like we started out with last time.

a10a-1720447.speaker: Duke
a10a-1720447.text: Roger. This thing's been working really good since - ever since the first thing.

a10a-1720447.speaker: Young
a10a-1720447.text: Well, last time we did one, we did one to the left and it got out of hand and went into deadband - spent about the entire hour and one half in the deadband.

a10a-1720447.speaker: Duke
a10a-1720447.text: Oh, that's a new one on me. I hadn't heard about it.

a10a-1720447.speaker: Young
a10a-1720447.text: Yes. I don't know what caused it; maybe some way I pushed the buttons wrong. Anyway, we had rates when we started into it, which is very peculiar.

a10a-1720447.speaker: Duke
a10a-1720447.text: Roger.

a10a-1720447.speaker: Young
a10a-1720447.text: This thing sure - The guy that thought that up was really smart. Was it anybody back there in the back room?

a10a-1720447.speaker: Duke
a10a-1720447.text: Yes. I think it was the CMS procedures and the SPAN guys back there that - or AGC or whatever they call themselves that came up with it. Looks - I got it in the checklist so we'll go pass it on to the other guys.

a10a-1720447.speaker: Young
a10a-1720447.text: That's just - Boy, that's just great. Looks like it saved you about 100 pounds [45 kg] a mission.

a10a-1720447.speaker: Duke
a10a-1720447.text: Roger. Hey, 10, We're considering a slip in the midcourse a half hour to give FIDO another half hour's tracking so he can get a little bit more confidence in his solution. If that's agreeable with you guys, we'd like to proceed that way. Over.

a10a-1720447.speaker: Young
a10a-1720447.text: OK with us.

a10a-1720447.speaker: Duke
a10a-1720447.text: OK. We'll plan then about 177:20 for the midcourse.

a10a-1720447.speaker: Young
a10a-1720447.text: Roger.

a10a-1720447.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1720447.text: Houston, Apollo 10. The world is just coming around in our left window, and it's really starting to get big now. Over.

a10a-1720447.speaker: Duke
a10a-1720447.text: Roger, 10. We got you out about 150,000 miles [277,800 km] right now.

a10a-1720447.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1720447.text: Roger, Charlie. When I say big I mean big compared to when we were around the Moon. Over.

a10a-1720447.speaker: Duke
a10a-1720447.text: Roger.

a10a-1720447.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1720447.text: Still looks like the North Pole has that socked in solid cloud deck. It's been there ever since we launched. Over.

a10a-1720447.speaker: Duke
a10a-1720447.text: Roger. We copy, Tom.

a10a-1720447.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1720447.text: Houston, Apollo 10. We're taking documentary sequence and still photos about every 4 or 5 hours of both the Moon and the Earth, so we should have a pretty good history of how they look all the way back. Over.

a10a-1720447.speaker: Duke
a10a-1720447.text: Roger. Thanks a lot. I'll pass that on to Jack.

a10a-1722551.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1722551.text: Hello, Houston. Apollo 10.

a10a-1722551.speaker: Duke
a10a-1722551.text: Go ahead, 10.

a10a-1722551.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1722551.text: Roger. Are you working with Goldstone now, Charlie? Over.

a10a-1722551.speaker: Duke
a10a-1722551.text: Roger. We just had a handover to Goldstone, Tom. Over.

a10a-1722551.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1722551.text: Roger. We're sitting up here and we have already gone through our entry-state - our entry phase for tomorrow and were just loafing here. And if you'd like to see what three clean-shaven looking individuals look like after 7 days, we could crank up the tube for you and also show you what the world looks like as it starts to grow, and the Moon really starts to shrink away. Over.

a10a-1722551.speaker: Duke
a10a-1722551.text: Roger. Stand by. See if we can get the network up. We'd like to see what you look like after yesterday's view of John down there with his patch on and almost we thought the camera was going to break. So, we'd like to see what you look like all fresh, Tom.

a10a-1722551.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1722551.text: OK.

a10a-1722551.speaker: Duke
a10a-1722551.text: And, Tom, we just - the PAO people just said that they were in contact with your mother and she's doing great and in great spirits and following the flight very closely.

a10a-1722551.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1722551.text: Real good. Tell them I sure appreciate it and thanks a lot. Over.

a10a-1722551.speaker: Duke
a10a-1722551.text: Roger.

a10a-1722551.speaker: Duke
a10a-1722551.text: 10, Houston. The network is working on the - see if we can get the lines up from Goldstone. Stand by.

a10a-1722551.speaker: Duke
a10a-1722551.text: 10, Houston. It'll take us 30 minutes to get the lines up so we can see it back here, but Goldstone is configured to record. You can transmit now. We have the High Gain, and we'll look at it in 30 minutes. Over.

a10a-1722551.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1722551.text: OK. I'm looking ahead in their Flight Plan. The next thing coming up is 174 and we are in no hurry here. When you get the lines up, we'll shoot it to you live. Over.

a10a-1722551.speaker: Duke
a10a-1722551.text: OK. That's fine, Tom. We'll give you the word.

a10a-1722551.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1722551.text: OK. Thank you now.

a10a-1722551.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1722551.text: Hello, Houston. This is 10.

a10a-1722551.speaker: Duke
a10a-1722551.text: Go ahead, 10.

a10a-1722551.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1722551.text: You might pass on appropriately that our CSM 16-millimeter camera finally failed. It's been trying for 2 days, and it just finally gave up the ghost. The fuse has been changed, but it just won't accept any cartridges and will not run at all. I'm using the 75-millimeter lens we have in the Command Module on the LM's 16-millimeter camera. This combination works, although I appreciate the fact that the masking for the lens might be inappropriate, but it's the last ditch effort. That's all we have left.

a10a-1722551.speaker: Duke
a10a-1722551.text: Roger. Understand. Your CSM 16-millimeter has failed and you've taken the 75-millimeter lens off the LM camera - correction - Command Module and put it on the LM camera. Over.

a10a-1722551.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1722551.text: That's affirmative. I just wish you'd - It's awful frustrating, Charlie. I wish you'd pass those words on appropriately.

a10a-1722551.speaker: Duke
a10a-1722551.text: Roger.

a10a-1724558.speaker: Young
a10a-1724558.text: Houston, Apollo 10. Over.

a10a-1724558.speaker: Duke
a10a-1724558.text: Go ahead.

a10a-1724558.speaker: Young
a10a-1724558.text: Roger. We're looking at Florida through the optics. The Cape's open today. Looks like y'all may have some clouds out there, little scattered clouds around Houston. Is that right?

a10a-1724558.speaker: Duke
a10a-1724558.text: It was like that when we came in 4 or 5 hours ago - correction - about 3 hours ago, John. Let me see if anybody's been outside lately.

a10a-1724558.speaker: Young
a10a-1724558.text: Oh, it's no real problem, we're just sightseeing. Boy, it's a beautiful view. You can see the subsolar pointing's in the Gulf of Mexico right about between the Yucatan peninsula and Mexico proper. And with these optics, I can look all the way into South America as far south as Chile.

a10a-1724558.speaker: Duke
a10a-1724558.text: Sounds great. Not much happening in the world today. No real significant news to pass on this afternoon. We've got the ball scores and that's about all; I can read you up those. We've got about 10 or 12. In the National League: Cincinnati 7, Montreal 2; Atlanta 4, Phillie 1; St. Louis 4, LA 0 - after four innings; San Diego 7, Chicago 1 - after four; New York 1, Pittsburgh 1 - after seven and one-half; Houston 5, New York 3 - after six and one half innings. In the American League: Detroit 10, California nothing; Seattle 3, Cleveland 2; Baltimore 5, Oakland 3; Kansas City 3, Washington 2; Bosto

a10a-1724558.speaker: Young
a10a-1724558.text: Wow!

a10a-1724558.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1724558.text: Hey, that's - That's dangerous work, babe. That's too fast.

a10a-1724558.speaker: Duke
a10a-1724558.text: Roger. You want to be on your way to getting airborne at that speed, I think.

a10a-1724558.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1724558.text: You want to have wheels in the ...

a10a-1724558.speaker: Duke
a10a-1724558.text: 10, Houston. At 173 hours and 10 minutes, you'll be 100,490 miles [186,107 km] out. Velocity relative to the Earth of 6,498 feet per second [1,980 m/s]. You'll be 109,847 miles [203,437 km] from the Moon. Velocity relative to the Moon is 5,776 feet per second [1,761 m/s]. Your sunset time is 191 19 55. And your sub-satellite point is at 173 [should read 73 degrees west], will be between Caracas and Panama. Over.

a10a-1724558.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1724558.text: Roger. We got those down, Charlie.

a10a-1724558.speaker: Young
a10a-1724558.text: That's how it looks, Charlie. I can tell we're directly between Caracas and Panama. That's what you said, wasn't it?

a10a-1724558.speaker: Duke
a10a-1724558.text: That's affirmative.

a10a-1724558.speaker: Young
a10a-1724558.text: It's quite obvious up here. Next time we go on one of these trips, we're going to take that big display down there with us.

a10a-1724558.speaker: Duke
a10a-1724558.text: OK. It's real pretty today. We got blue background and yellow lines and a green spacecraft and an orange Snoopy just dancing around up on the top of the board. FIDO's really outdoing himself.

a10a-1724558.speaker: Young
a10a-1724558.text: Every time we make a successful water dump, does he light up?

a10a-1724558.speaker: Duke
a10a-1724558.text: Oh boy; the top of his head just glows. You ought to see him.

a10a-1724558.speaker: Young
a10a-1724558.text: I wish I could.

a10a-1724558.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1724558.text: Yes. I bet that's a great sight down there. Over.

a10a-1724558.speaker: Duke
a10a-1724558.text: It really is. He's been grinning the whole flight. He's going to be impossible to live with. 10, a little update on the Atlanta Classic. Bert Yancey and Gary Player are now tied for the lead with about six to play on the last round.

a10a-1724558.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1724558.text: Very good. Thank you. They'll all be coming to Houston here before long.

a10a-1724558.speaker: Duke
a10a-1724558.text: Yes. Just a couple of weeks. It should be fun.

a10a-1724558.speaker: Duke
a10a-1724558.text: Hello, 10. Houston. We'd like you to leave the H 2 Cryo heaters off until sleep period tonight, and at that time we'll bring on one fan to stir them up. And that should bring the pressure up all right. Over.

a10a-1724558.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1724558.text: OK, Charlie.

a10a-1724558.speaker: Duke
a10a-1724558.text: Hello,10. Houston. Hey, Tom, it looks like it's going to take us an hour or more to get building 8 cranked up on the color converter. We're configured for black and white, if you want to give us that. We can look at the color later. Over.

a10a-1724558.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1724558.text: OK. Stand by one.

a10a-1724558.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1724558.text: Roger, Charlie. We'll just hold off because you will be able to see more of the United States, the longer we wait here.

a10a-1724558.speaker: Duke
a10a-1724558.text: Roger. We'll get building 8 cranked up, and we'll let you know then. Over.

a10a-1724558.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1724558.text: OK. We've got the optics calibration coming up. I think about 173 to 174. [garble] pardon me...

a10a-1724558.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1724558.text: Charlie, if it's going to be more than an hour, let us know, will you, because that will be pushing into P23.

a10a-1724558.speaker: Duke
a10a-1724558.text: Roger. We copy, Gene-o. We'll give you a word.

a10a-1724558.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1724558.text: Actually - actually you know, 45 minutes or an hour - 30 minutes to an hour would be a little bit better because more of the US continent will come into view at that time.

a10a-1724558.speaker: Duke
a10a-1724558.text: Roger.

a10a-1724558.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1724558.text: It's really beautifully clear - clear down there right now. It's just tremendous.

a10a-1724558.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1724558.text: I can almost make Tracy splashing around in the back yard.

a10a-1724558.speaker: Duke
a10a-1724558.text: I bet you that's what she's doing this afternoon, too, boy. It's about, as I said earlier, about 90 to 93 degrees out there. And we concur on holding off - We should be ready to go in an hour. Over.

a10a-1724558.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1724558.text: Okey doke.

a10a-1730525.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1730525.text: It's really beautifully clear - clear down there right now. It's just tremendous.

a10a-1730525.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1730525.text: I can almost make Tracy splashing around in the back yard.

a10a-1730525.speaker: Duke
a10a-1730525.text: I bet you that's what she's doing this afternoon, too, boy. It's about, as I said earlier, about 90 to 93 degrees out there. And we concur on holding off - We should be ready to go in an hour. Over.

a10a-1731430.speaker: Duke
a10a-1731430.text: Hello, Apollo 10. Houston. We're to lose the High Gain. We'll come back around again at 173:25, and at that time we will be Go for High - the TV. Over.

a10a-1731430.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1731430.text: OK. Sounds real good, Charlie. Thank you.

a10a-1731430.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1731430.text: 173:19:55 That's approximately 5 minutes from now. We will be getting another television transmission from Apollo 10 in about 5 minutes.

a10a-1731430.speaker: Young
a10a-1731430.text: Roger. Do you have a picture?

a10a-1731430.speaker: Duke
a10a-1731430.text: We're on the Omnis there, 10, and we'll - We'll be about another minute.

a10a-1731430.speaker: Duke
a10a-1731430.text: Hey, and we got some information on Snoop at 173:30, 5 minutes from now. He's 208,966 nautical miles [387,005 km] above the Moon, and he's 405,188 nautical miles [750,408 km] above the Earth. And stand by on his hyperbolic.

a10a-1731430.speaker: Duke
a10a-1731430.text: And he's going hyperbolic with respect to the Earth and the Moon, so he's moving out away from us. And his velocity with respect to the Earth is 7,530 feet per second [2,295 m/s], and he's going into solar orbit.

a10a-1731430.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1731430.text: Wonderful. Looks like Snoop's going to take a long trip. Over.

a10a-1731430.speaker: Young
a10a-1731430.text: Houston, do you have a picture? Over.

a10a-1731430.speaker: Duke
a10a-1731430.text: Roger, 10. We got the picture now.

a10a-1731430.speaker: Young
a10a-1731430.text: Roger. Looks like this is the Moon, and we're about 110,000 miles [204,000 km] from it. It still has a sort of a brownish cast to it, and it's still rotating very slowly. You can see when you look out your window tonight, you'll see it's only a three-quarter Moon or so.

a10a-1732713.speaker: Young
a10a-1732713.text: Houston, Apollo 10. Over.

a10a-1732713.speaker: Duke
a10a-1732713.text: Roger, 10. We got the picture now.

a10a-1732713.speaker: Young
a10a-1732713.text: Roger. Looks like this is the Moon, and we're about 110,000 miles [204,000 km] from it. It still has a sort of a brownish cast to it, and it's still rotating very slowly. You can see when you look out your window tonight, you'll see it's only a three-quarter Moon or so.

a10a-1732713.speaker: Duke
a10a-1732713.text: OK. We just got it up - We just got it up on the...

a10a-1732713.speaker: Young
a10a-1732713.text: Roger.

a10a-1732713.speaker: Duke
a10a-1732713.text: ...on the telemonitor now.

a10a-1732713.speaker: Young
a10a-1732713.text: This is...

a10a-1732713.speaker: Duke
a10a-1732713.text: Excuse me, John. Go ahead. Over.

a10a-1732713.speaker: Young
a10a-1732713.text: This is a full zoom on the lens, so it actually is a little smaller than it is on your screen. It's hardly enough to make any definition out of it at all.

a10a-1732713.speaker: Duke
a10a-1732713.text: 10, Houston. We can apparently make out the mare, the colors on our Vidicon are - has a greenish cast to it, but I think the color quality for the commercial is a little bit better than this, but we [garble] see the maria on it. Over.

a10a-1732713.speaker: Young
a10a-1732713.text: Roger. And at about 110,000 miles [204,000 km], I don't think you expect to see very much.

a10a-1732713.speaker: Young
a10a-1732713.text: It'll be a couple of minutes before - before the Earth comes around, so let us show you the interior.

a10a-1732713.speaker: Duke
a10a-1732713.text: Roger. We're standing by for your smiling face. I've heard of the big eye before, but the big hand is ridiculous.

a10a-1732713.speaker: Duke
a10a-1732713.text: OK, 10. I think we're looking at Tom's right - left shoulder there now, and the Sun coming in his window. Yes. There's his old grinning face, clean shaven.

a10a-1732713.speaker: Young
a10a-1732713.text: Roger. This is a remarkable innovation. After spending a lot of money on mechanical shavers which always manage to leave the whiskers flying around in the atmosphere, somebody finally came out with the idea of using a straight razor and brushless shaving cream. You rub it on, it keeps the whiskers when you shave it off, you put it in a towel and dispose of it, and you end up clean shaven. And after 8 days of wearing a beard, I guess you're looking at a couple of guys who aren't much hippies.

a10a-1732713.speaker: Duke
a10a-1732713.text: That's amazing, 10. Absolutely. That's what the space age does for you.

a10a-1732713.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1732713.text: I'll tell you, Charlie. That's one of the most refreshing things that's happened in the last couple of days. That was really great.

a10a-1732713.speaker: Duke
a10a-1732713.text: You guys really look good, Gene. Over.

a10a-1732713.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1732713.text: You know, actually - you know, it feels a lot different. We were getting where we could barely stand ourselves there for a while.

a10a-1732713.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1732713.text: We'll take you down to the Lower Equipment Bay and show you how different our navigator looks today compared to yesterday. On the panel in front of me, you can see the Lower Equipment Bay with the guidance and navigation panel that John works all the time to determine our position and attitude.

a10a-1732713.speaker: Duke
a10a-1732713.text: There's old one-eye. We got him.

a10a-1732713.speaker: Young
a10a-1732713.text: There's really not much difference today, is there?

a10a-1732713.speaker: Duke
a10a-1732713.text: You're - You're right, boy. You're right.

a10a-1732713.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1732713.text: John likes to play in here. Every time he gets something in his hand, he has to do something different to it.

a10a-1732713.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1732713.text: How's the color coming in now, Charlie? Over.

a10a-1732713.speaker: Duke
a10a-1732713.text: Roger. The interior colors are fine. Little greenish tints, but I think that's a problem we got, Tom, with our converter here in building 30. The exterior also had a - quite a greenish tinge to it. It's better than the black and white. The black and white has a lot better definition, however, though.

a10a-1732713.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1732713.text: OK. We'll take you outside now and show how the Earth looks today. It's starting to get bigger as we approach 100,000 miles [185,200 km].

a10a-1732713.speaker: Duke
a10a-1732713.text: Roger. We'll stand by for your commentary.

a10a-1732713.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1732713.text: Charlie, we'll have it in a minute, and it's just coming right over the window edge. Here it comes now.

a10a-1732713.speaker: Duke
a10a-1732713.text: Roger. We have it, 10. Out.

a10a-1732713.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1732713.text: OK. Again as you look at the - pardon me Again as you look at the Earth, it's upside down, so to keep all of you from standing on your heads, we'll just turn the camera upside down for the convenience of your viewing pleasure here.

a10a-1732713.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1732713.text: Charlie, we'll be looking at - at the east coast of - of the United States. Primarily down from - off the tip of Florida. Actually to us here we can see the Grand Bahama Banks. You can see the color changes in the water. You can see most of Florida. It looks like almost all the Gulf of Mexico is extremely clear. The Gulf Coast of the United States, Florida, Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana, on down through Texas all looks clear. We can look on across from Houston all the way into the San Joaquin Valley, all the way into the Los Angeles area coming over the horizon into Baja California.

a10a-1732713.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1732713.text: We're vertically right now above the Earth, somewhere between Caracas and Panama. Charlie, how does the TV look to you down there?

a10a-1732713.speaker: Duke
a10a-1732713.text: Roger, 10. It's looking real good. Black and white is excellent. Definition of color is coming through on the commercial real fine. Our vidicon here on the big screen has got a lot of greens to it, but on commercially, it's looking great. Over.

a10a-1732713.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1732713.text: Is it saturating right now?

a10a-1732713.speaker: Duke
a10a-1732713.text: Negative. Only in the North Pole area where the cloud banks are pretty heavy, and then only partially up there so - We've got one clear spot up towards the Arctic Circle that we can't figure out what it is. Could you give us a little run-down on that? Over.

a10a-1732713.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1732713.text: OK. Wait just a minute. It's starting to disappear out the left hatch window, and John will take the camera there and go right and take it out through our center hatch window. And here you can see the Earth as it starts to go out the left side window.

a10a-1732713.speaker: Duke
a10a-1732713.text: Roger.

a10a-1732713.speaker: Duke
a10a-1732713.text: 10, Houston. We got just 30 seconds left on the High Gain on this pass.

a10a-1732713.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1732713.text: Looks like we won't catch you this time, Charlie, but that big low-pressure cloud so very distinctive over the Alaskan area, Aleutian area is very distinctive to us with the naked eye. We can't quite get it for you out the hatch window at this time, as we're going.

a10a-1732713.speaker: Duke
a10a-1732713.text: Roger. We'll stand by then. We got about 20 seconds left or so and if you want to show us, it will be - Standby. Eight more minutes and we'll have the High Gain back, if you want to keep the camera up. Over.

a10a-1732713.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1732713.text: OK. We just wanted to get a - show you how things are going aboard Apollo 10 today. So after shaving we all feel refreshed. In fact, we feel just great up here, and looking forward to splashdown tomorrow. We got about 100,000 miles [185,200 km] more to go, but we really pick up the majority of it in the last few hours. Over.

a10a-1732713.speaker: Duke
a10a-1732713.text: Roger, 10. We copy. Thank you very much for the show. Over.

a10a-1732713.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1732713.text: 173:37:58 Duration of that transmission was 10 minutes, 22 seconds. And Apollo 10's distance is now 98,650 nautical miles [182,700 km]. Velocity, 6,558 feet per second [1,999 m/s].

a10a-1732713.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1732713.text: Roger. And we just wanted again to show you the relative size of the Moon and the Earth today, as we see it here nearly equidistant between the two, about 110,000 miles [204,000 km] from the Moon and 100,000 miles [185,200 km] from the Earth. And we'll see you tomorrow. Over.

a10a-1732713.speaker: Duke
a10a-1732713.text: Roger. Thank you much again, 10, for the show. See you later. Out.

a10a-1732713.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1732713.text: Houston, this is 10.

a10a-1732713.speaker: Duke
a10a-1732713.text: Go ahead.

a10a-1732713.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1732713.text: For my own long-range planning, do you anticipate bringing fuel cell 1 up once more tomorrow, prior to entry?

a10a-1732713.speaker: Duke
a10a-1732713.text: Stand by, Gene.

a10a-1732713.speaker: Duke
a10a-1732713.text: Apollo 10, Houston. We don't plan to bring fuel cell 1 back on the line for the rest of the flight. And we got your E-memory dump and it's Go. No mistakes after 7 days. And on your entry checklist, we got a couple of minor changes if you'd like to break that book out, and we'll talk to you about it. Over.

a10a-1732713.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1732713.text: OK. Stand by.

a10a-1732713.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1732713.text: Hello, Houston. Apollo 10. Go ahead on that entry checklist. Over.

a10a-1732713.speaker: Duke
a10a-1732713.text: Roger, 10. We'd like on page 2.2 correction 2.2 step 6, about the middle of the page; we say, "fuel cell 2 main A and B Off." We'd like to change that, of course, to fuel cell 1. Over.

a10a-1734903.speaker: Duke
a10a-1734903.text: Hello, Apollo 10. Houston. We've had second thoughts on the fuel cell. We'd like you to bring it on for the midcourse, and we'll let you know. If we didn't bring it on, it would die out on us at about 180 hours and we don't want to do that. We'd like to keep it for - until SEP. So, we'll give you a minimum time around the midcourse to have it on. Over.

a10a-1734903.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1734903.text: Roger, Houston. This is 10. We're standing by to set up the optics calibration at this time. Over.

a10a-1734903.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1734903.text: Roger. Since we've slipped the midcourse correction number 6 about 30 minutes, to roughly 177:20, we suggest that you stay in PTC for about another one-half hour and slip your P23 by half an hour, to something on the order of 174:50, commencement or thereabouts. Over.

a10a-1734903.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1734903.text: Houston. We're all configured for it, and John's getting pretty weary of making all these sights; and we want to go ahead and get it over with. Over.

a10a-1734903.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1734903.text: This is Apollo Control at 174 hours, 20 minutes. Apollo 10 is 96,025 nautical miles [177,838 km] from Earth. Velocity is 6,649 feet per second [2,027 m/s] and we're about 3 hours away from the midcourse correction burn.

a10a-1740916.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1740916.text: Yes. John's put it right on the money.

a10a-1762704.speaker: Young
a10a-1762704.text: Houston, were going into our REFSMMAT Realign now.

a10a-1762704.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1762704.text: This is Houston. Roger. Out.

a10a-1762704.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1762704.text: Apollo 10, this is Houston. Over

a10a-1762704.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1762704.text: Houston, go ahead.

a10a-1762704.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1762704.text: Roger, 10. We'd like to make a correction to our scheduled midcourse correction plan of operations here, by canceling midcourse correction number 6 and definitely having midcourse correction 7. A little background on this is that with the long fuel cell purge and the secondary evaporator checkout, the tracking still hasn't stabilized to the point where we can give you a midcourse correction number 6 and be confident 100 percent that midcourse 7 will not be required. And if there is a possibility of having to burn 7, the tracking people would like to consider - would like to continue their trac

a10a-1762704.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1762704.text: OK. Roger. Stand by.

a10a-1762704.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1762704.text: Roger.

a10a-1762704.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1762704.text: Roger. Houston, Apollo 10. That's what we practiced all along in the simulator, so it really doesn't matter to us one way or the other. We can sure do it. Over.

a10a-1762704.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1762704.text: Roger,10. Then we'll go with not burning 6 and definitely planning on having a midcourse correction 7, at 188:50 GET.

a10a-1762704.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1762704.text: Roger. As nominal.

a10a-1762704.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1762704.text: Roger.

a10a-1762704.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1762704.text: Apollo 10 is going back to the PTC mode. Over.

a10a-1762704.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1762704.text: 10, this is Houston. Roger. Out.

a10a-1762704.speaker: Young
a10a-1762704.text: You're definitely getting larger in diameter there, Earth.

a10a-1762704.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1762704.text: Roger. We understand you see us growing larger. We can't see you yet with the naked eye, but hope to tomorrow. We're showing you about 90,000 miles [166,700 km] out at the present time.

a10a-1762704.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1762704.text: Roger. Got a beautiful view here of the Earth. It seems like there is a little - from here like a cumulus thunderstorm up on the cloud cover that covers up near the polar ice cap. It really is beautiful, the way it stands out. We got a couple of pictures of it. Over.

a10a-1762704.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1762704.text: Roger. Out.

a10a-1762704.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1762704.text: Hello, Houston. Apollo 10. Can you check and see at what GET should we hit night time just before we approach the Entry Interface? Over.

a10a-1762704.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1762704.text: Roger. Stand by a second.

a10a-1762704.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1762704.text: Apollo 10, this is Houston. Time of local sunset will be 191:19:51 GET. Over.

a10a-1762704.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1762704.text: Roger. Could you say again, Bruce, please?

a10a-1762704.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1762704.text: Roger. 191 hours, 19 minutes, 51 seconds GET. Over.

a10a-1762704.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1762704.text: Roger. Copy. Sunset at 191:19:51.

a10a-1762704.speaker: Young
a10a-1762704.text: Houston, this is Apollo 10. Over.

a10a-1762704.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1762704.text: Go ahead, 10. We can hear you over the jukebox.

a10a-1762704.speaker: Young
a10a-1762704.text: OK. Would it be OK to run P37 through, taking your midcourse 7 time and see what we come up with? With this state vector we've got now?

a10a-1762704.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1762704.text: Apollo 10, this is Houston. Affirmative, and we'll run it down here, too. We can compare results if you like. Over.

a10a-1762704.speaker: Young
a10a-1762704.text: Rog.

a10a-1765408.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1765408.text: Apollo 10, this is Houston. Over.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1765408.text: Houston, go ahead.

a10a-1765408.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1765408.text: Roger. Using your vector and our machinery, we came up with burn of 2.2 feet per second [0.67 m/s] in X, 0 in Y, and minus 0.1 [fps, 0.03 m/s] in Z, compared with the observed calculations you had onboard of plus 2.50 [fps, 0.76 m/s] and minus 0.1 [fps, 0.03 m/s]. Over.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1765408.text: Roger.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Young
a10a-1765408.text: Ours plus, 2.5 and minus 0.1.

a10a-1765408.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1765408.text: Roger. That's what we saw on the DSKY. We got 2.2.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Young
a10a-1765408.text: What's the matter with your machinery down there?

a10a-1765408.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1765408.text: Yes. We've got one problem down here right now. There's a rumor going around that by stepping outside the Mission Control building, we can see you all with the naked eye. So a lot of us are out there looking.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Young
a10a-1765408.text: Did the machine go out there, too?

a10a-1765408.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1765408.text: We can see that the terminator is just passing over Houston right now.

a10a-1765408.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1765408.text: Roger. I believe that, but I haven't been outside in a couple of hours.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1765408.text: Did somebody really see us out there?

a10a-1765408.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1765408.text: That's the report. Charlie is out there looking right now, and we expect to have an eyewitness account in a minute or so.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1765408.text: I don't know what direction, but I would expect you would look to the southwest.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1765408.text: Yes. From our angle, Bruce, where we are looking at you, I would say to the southwest. We're up at an angle of at least 45 or 50 degrees. Over.

a10a-1765408.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1765408.text: Roger.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Young
a10a-1765408.text: Anybody can see something 30 feet long [9 meters] at 90,000 miles [167,000 km] has really got the eyeballs.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1765408.text: Hello, Houston. Apollo 10. Over.

a10a-1765408.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1765408.text: Go ahead, 10.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1765408.text: Roger. I'm sure you saw the TV pictures the other day when we left the Moon straight away? Over.

a10a-1765408.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1765408.text: Right.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1765408.text: OK. Well, right now it looks like we are just doing a reverse process, only we are heading straight for the center of the Earth above, but we all know that we're going to be entering west to east at a gamma of 6.5, don't we?

a10a-1765408.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1765408.text: Roger. We're working on that one, Tom.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1765408.text: [Laughing.] OK.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1765408.text: Sure hope that is a problem you've solve.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1765408.text: Bruce, from this position, it looks like we're going to hit oh, just down below Baja California, going straight in. Just watching the way it is slowly growing here. Over.

a10a-1765408.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1765408.text: Roger. Let me get you a current Entry Interface angle here.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1765408.text: Oh, no. No problem. We're just kidding about that. It's really funny to watch. It's just a reverse process of after we started to climb out from the Moon the other day. Over.

a10a-1765408.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1765408.text: Roger.

a10a-1765408.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1765408.text: Right now, 10, we're showing an Entry Interface angle of approximately minus 6.8 degrees. Over.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1765408.text: Roger. That sounds real decent. Thank you.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1765408.text: Houston, Apollo 10. Are the FIDO's pretty well squared away with our c.g., and where we are stowing things? Over.

a10a-1765408.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1765408.text: Roger, 10. We're in good shape down here on the stowage and c.g.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1765408.text: OK. Real fine. Thank you.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1765408.text: We haven't yet told you where we are going to stow the canister, because we're not sure. We are probably going to wrap it up at the base of one of the suits. We'll have to let you know that.

a10a-1765408.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1765408.text: OK. The last word I had on the canister was wrap it up in sleeping bag number 3 when you got through using it, and - let's see, you said that food compartment L3 still had food in it, I guess?

a10a-1765408.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1765408.text: Roger. You can tell the FIDO's that food compartment L2 and L3 all have - the ones here on the left - L2 and L3 are completely - no, I guess just L3 is just about completely filled with food, and our waste and one helmet is in B1 now.

a10a-1765408.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1765408.text: Say again what you got in B1 besides helmets, please.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1765408.text: Just waste wrappings from the food packs. There was one helmet in there and just the waste wrappings from food. Couldn't be over a couple of pounds.

a10a-1765408.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1765408.text: Roger. So, when you all find a stowage location for the lithium hydroxide canister, if you'll pass it down to us, we'll crank it in.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1765408.text: OK.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1765408.text: Houston, Apollo 10. Do the rates look good to start the PTC? Over.

a10a-1765408.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1765408.text: Roger, 10. They're looking good.

a10a-1765408.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1765408.text: 10, this is Houston. I'm afraid that report we got on visual observations of you earlier was erroneous. I think it was a planet over there.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1765408.text: Roger.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Young
a10a-1765408.text: Roger. I was going to recommend about a 20-power telescope. Maybe 40.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1765408.text: This is Apollo Control at 177 hours, 6 minutes. Apollo 10's distance from the Earth is 84,986 nautical miles [157,394 km], velocity 7,071 feet per second [2,155 m/s].

a10a-1765408.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1765408.text: OK, Houston. Apollo 10. We're going to start through the presleep checklist. We're going to purge the fuel cells, make the canister changes. Over.

a10a-1765408.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1765408.text: Apollo 10, this is Houston. Would you hold off on the fuel cell purge? You can proceed with the other items at the present time.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1765408.text: OK.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1765408.text: OK. Can I take the battery charge off?

a10a-1765408.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1765408.text: That's affirmative. Discontinue battery charging.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1765408.text: Thank you. [Long pause.]

a10a-1765408.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1765408.text: Hello, Houston. Will you give me a hack on when you want to start that fuel cell purge, and also do you desire to stay High Gain tonight?

a10a-1765408.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1765408.text: Roger. We'll give you the word on the fuel cells here in a minute.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1765408.text: Houston, Apollo 10. Are you ready to copy the CM RCS thruster temps? Over.

a10a-1765408.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1765408.text: Roger. Send your message, 10.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1765408.text: Roger. 5C is 5.1, 5D is 5.1, 6 Alpha is 5.1, 6 Bravo 5.1, 6 Charlie is 4.0, 6 Dog is 4.6. Over.

a10a-1765408.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1765408.text: Roger. We copy; And the S-band operations this evening will be Omni. Request you select Omni Bravo and Omni on board, and we'll do the switching from down here.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1765408.text: Okey doke. Going Omni at this time.

a10a-1765408.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1765408.text: Apollo 10, this is Houston. You can proceed with the oxygen purge on fuel cells 2 and 3. Over.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1765408.text: Roger.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1765408.text: OK, Houston. Apollo 10. We're ready for some onboard readouts on the batteries and RCS. Over.

a10a-1765408.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1765408.text: Roger, 10. Press on.

a10a-1765408.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1765408.text: Apollo 10, this is Houston. Go ahead with your onboard readouts.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1765408.text: Roger, Bruce. Batt C is 36.8 [VDC], Pyro Batt A is 36.8 [VDC], Pyro Batt B is 36.8 [VDC]. RCS A 53 percent, RCS B 65 percent, C is 65 percent, and D is 60 percent. Over.

a10a-1765408.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1765408.text: Roger, 10. We copied.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1765408.text: Houston, Apollo 10. Over.

a10a-1765408.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1765408.text: Go ahead, Apollo 10.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1765408.text: All right.
