Looking forward to tomorrow morning, we don't want to miss the major events; and so, what we'd like to have you do is wake us up about an hour earlier since we're going to hit the sack a little earlier tonight. We would like to have you wake us up at a GET of 85 hours. Over.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1765408.text: That is, 185.

a10a-1765408.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1765408.text: Roger. We'll wake you up at GET of 185 hours.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1765408.text: Roger. You can put a call into the desk and just have them wake us up with some soft music, please.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1765408.text: And, Bruce, put in an order for sausage and eggs, too, would you please?

a10a-1765408.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1765408.text: I suggest you hold off on those until lunch time.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1765408.text: OK. We'll try to. [Long pause.]

a10a-1765408.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1765408.text: Apollo 10, this is Houston. Over.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1765408.text: Go ahead, Houston.

a10a-1765408.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1765408.text: Roger. I've got your Cryo tank configuration for the night.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1765408.text: OK. Stand by 1 second. We'll get it.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Slayton
a10a-1765408.text: Sounds like things are lively up there in the malt shop tonight.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1765408.text: Hello there, Deke. Yes, we're just taking things easy here and relaxing and going through the total program for tomorrow morning. In fact, we've gone through the checklist a couple of times and rebriefed it; so we're just taking it easy, watching the scene outside; which is beautiful, and listening to some music. Over.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Slayton
a10a-1765408.text: Roger. That's great.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1765408.text: Yes. Did you hear me tell Bruce what our impression was of coming back to the Earth, how it looks just about opposite of going away from the Moon? Over.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Slayton
a10a-1765408.text: Roger.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Young
a10a-1765408.text: Boy, this is really something, Deke.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Slayton
a10a-1765408.text: That last couple of hours is going to be the bear.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Young
a10a-1765408.text: Yes.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1765408.text: Now, from this angle it looks like we're going to just approach the Earth here at a gamma of about 90 degrees. [Laughing.]

a10a-1765408.speaker: Slayton
a10a-1765408.text: Yes. We indicate about 78.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1765408.text: [Laughing.] Oh, that's great.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1765408.text: That food's getting to you.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1765408.text: OK, Houston. I'm ready for the Cryo fan. If you want to go right down the panel, I'll configure it.

a10a-1765408.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1765408.text: . OK. I'll just run down the row of switches here. H 2 heaters: 1 Off, 2 Off. O 2 heaters: 1 Off, 2 Auto. H 2 fans: 1 ON, 2 Off. O 2 fans: Off, Off. Over.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1765408.text: OK. I got heaters: H 2 1 is Off, 2 is Off; O 2 1 is Off, and 2 is Auto. On the fans: H 2 , I've got 1 ON, 2 Off; O 2 fans, 1 Off and 2 Off.

a10a-1765408.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1765408.text: Roger. Readback correct. I think you're properly configured for the evening.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1765408.text: Thank you.

a10a-1765408.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1765408.text: 177:22:04 This is Apollo Control estimating the change of shift news conference for 9:30 pm central daylight time.

a10a-1772716.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1772716.text: 10, this is Houston. What are your plans, as far as turning in now?

a10a-1772716.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1772716.text: OK, Houston. We're going to...

a10a-1772716.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1772716.text: Roger, Houston. This is 10. We're going to go ahead and sack out at this time. Over.

a10a-1772716.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1772716.text: Roger. Can you give us a crew status report prior to turning in?

a10a-1772716.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1772716.text: Oh, we'd be glad to do that, Houston.

a10a-1772716.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1772716.text: Roger. They're interested in getting a hack on the - the radiation now, and then after you get back down through the Van Allen Belt.

a10a-1772716.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1772716.text: Roger.

a10a-1772716.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1772716.text: Hello, Houston. This is 10.

a10a-1772716.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1772716.text: Roger. Go ahead, 10.

a10a-1772716.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1772716.text: OK. The CDR is 26048, the CMP is 05048, and the LMP is 15049.

a10a-1772716.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1772716.text: Roger. We copy the PRDs.

a10a-1772716.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1772716.text: And, we've never seen, on any of the checks we've ever taken, either in here or in the LM, anything more than about 0.001 off of the meter.

a10a-1772716.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1772716.text: Roger. Copy. Nothing more than 0.001 on the meter.

a10a-1772716.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1772716.text: Well, maybe that scale is 0.01, Bruce, but it's on the 0.1 scale and it's barely readable. Barely above zero. I guess it's 0.01.

a10a-1772716.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1772716.text: Roger. Barely readable on the1 tenth scale.

a10a-1772716.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1772716.text: I take it back. It is 0.001 is the highest we've ever seen anywhere.

a10a-1772716.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1772716.text: Roger. Copy 1, one thousandth.

a10a-1772716.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1772716.text: OK, Apollo 10. This is Houston. The Black Team is signing off here. On behalf of everybody in the MOCR, we want to wish you a good night and a safe re-entry and happy landings, and we'll all see you on the ground when you get back.

a10a-1772716.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1772716.text: Roger, Houston. We just want to say thanks a lot to the whole team down there. There's been some fantastic support that we've had. We're going to come around and thank all of you personally, after we get back there to Houston. Over.

a10a-1772716.speaker: McCandless
a10a-1772716.text: Roger. And the Maroon Team is taking over now.

a10a-1772716.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1772716.text: Roger.

a10a-1772716.speaker: Young
a10a-1772716.text: Well done there, Black Team.

a10a-1772716.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1772716.text: And, thanks a lot, guys.

a10a-1772716.speaker: Engle
a10a-1772716.text: OK, 10. This is Houston. That big maroon got the eyeballs on you, so you guys hurry up every chance you get and get on home.

a10a-1772716.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1772716.text: We're on our way, Joe baby. You just keep alert tonight, keep us in the corridor, and we'll see you soon.

a10a-1772716.speaker: Engle
a10a-1772716.text: Roger that. Go get some huggy pillow. We'll keep our eyeballs on you.

a10a-1772716.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1772716.text: Some what?

a10a-1772716.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1772716.text: You ever spend the night in the command module?

a10a-1772716.speaker: Engle
a10a-1772716.text: Roger that.

a10a-1772716.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1772716.text: That's right, you did, and you know.

a10a-1772716.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1772716.text: This is Apollo Control at 177 hours, 45 minutes, and we've completed the shift change here in control. The Maroon Team of flight controllers headed by Flight Director Milton Windler, has replaced the Black Team headed by Glynn Lunney, and our capsule communicator on this shift will be astronaut Joe Engle. You heard the crew advise that they would be turning in now, beginning their sleep period about 45 minutes early. They were able to do that because midcourse correction 6 which had been scheduled at 176 hours, 50 minutes has been deleted, and we intend to make that midcourse correction at the

a10a-1772716.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1772716.text: This is Apollo Control at 178 hours, 19 minutes. During the change of shift briefing, we had one brief conversation with Gene Cernan. We now presume that the crew is attempting to get to sleep. We'll play back that short conversation for you now.

a10a-1772716.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1772716.text: Hello, Houston. Houston, this is Apollo 10. Over.

a10a-1772716.speaker: Engle
a10a-1772716.text: Roger, 10. Go ahead.

a10a-1772716.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1772716.text: OK, Joe. I just - We're just getting all configured. I got the duty. I just want to make sure that I can hear you in case I have to, and I guess I can.

a10a-1772716.speaker: Engle
a10a-1772716.text: OK. Mighty fine. Well, get a good night's sleep, and I'll see you in about 7 hours and 10 minutes or so.

a10a-1772716.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1772716.text: OK, babe. Listen, any - any news from the home front, Mike? At home or anything. Everything shipshape?

a10a-1772716.speaker: Engle
a10a-1772716.text: Just came from there. Yes, everything's ship shape. We just made a run on your table there on your patio, and I think I'm going to need a little more practice on that.

a10a-1772716.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1772716.text: Oh, man. There's - there's a few things you got to know about that one.

a10a-1772716.speaker: Engle
a10a-1772716.text: Well, I got the lesson from the expert.

a10a-1772716.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1772716.text: Oh, I believe it. I believe it. Listen, we'll try it when I get back. We'll see you, and I'll - If there's any question about calling, call, will you? And I'll see you tomorrow.

a10a-1772716.speaker: Engle
a10a-1772716.text: Righto, Buddy. OK. Good night.

a10a-1772716.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1772716.text: Good night.

a10a-1772716.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1772716.text: At the present time Apollo 10 is 79,880 miles [147,938 km] from Earth and traveling at the speed of 7,295 feet per second [2,224 m/s]. At 178 hours, 20 minutes; this is Mission Control, Houston.

a10a-1772716.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1772716.text: This is Apollo Control at 179 hours, 29 minutes. The Flight Surgeon reports that Gene Cernan, the one crewman on whom we have biomedical data tonight, appears to be sleeping at this time. The crew advised that at 177 hours, 40 minutes that the they were going to begin their rest period a little early, with the plan of getting up a early for tomorrow's re-entry activities. About 20 minutes after announcing that they planned to begin the sleep period, Cernan appeared to be sleeping. At the present time, Apollo 10 is 74,921 nautical miles [138,754 km] from Earth and the spacecraft is traveling at

a10a-1843405.speaker: Houston Comm Tech
a10a-1843405.text: Honeysuckle, this is Houston Comm Tech, 1 2 3 4, 4 3 2 1, give me a short count.

a10a-1843405.speaker: Honeysuckle Comm Tech
a10a-1843405.text: This is Honeysuckle on GOSS, 1 2 3 4 5. 5 4 3 2 1.

a10a-1843405.speaker: MCC
a10a-1843405.text: (Bugle call)

a10a-1843405.speaker: Engle
a10a-1843405.text: Hello Apollo 10. Reveille. All hands heave out and face up! Sweepers, man your brooms! Clean sweep down fore and aft! Take all trash and garbage to the fan tails! Standing by, this is Houston.

a10a-1843405.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1843405.text: Oh, I love you. Where did you learn that kind of noise.

a10a-1843405.speaker: Engle
a10a-1843405.text: It's Navy noise.

a10a-1843405.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1843405.text: That's what I mean. Hey, you get a DS, that's 30 minutes early.

a10a-1843405.speaker: Engle
a10a-1843405.text: Negative on that.

a10a-1843405.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1843405.text: Huh?

a10a-1843405.speaker: Engle
a10a-1843405.text: I want to get you up because it's your last day to enjoy out there and I don't want you to miss anything. How you guys feeling today?

a10a-1843405.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1843405.text: Hey babe, I've been looking out that window all night long, so you ain't - you know I was waiting for that noise anyway. How are you?

a10a-1843405.speaker: Engle
a10a-1843405.text: Hey, real good. Looks like you have been up for a little while.

a10a-1843405.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1843405.text: Yes, off and on. Off and on. It gets pretty anxious up here with that world getting so big. It's beautiful, babe, it really is.

a10a-1843405.speaker: Engle
a10a-1843405.text: You look like you're just a hair over 50,000 [nautical miles, 92,600 km] out now, Gene-o.

a10a-1843405.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1843405.text: 50 grand huh, now? Beautiful!

a10a-1843405.speaker: Engle
a10a-1843405.text: Hey, why don't you guys come on home today?

a10a-1843405.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1843405.text: You know, I think we will.

a10a-1843405.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1843405.text: What have you been doing? Taking lessons from Jack or something? I didn't know you knew that kind of music.

a10a-1843405.speaker: Engle
a10a-1843405.text: Jack doesn't know what it means.

a10a-1843405.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1843405.text: Oh, here you come, Joe. Oh, my God, you're about - you're about ¾ the size of my side window, you're less than a full Earth. You're curved over at the poles which means we're going behind you which is good, and, oh my golly, are you getting big and beautiful, babe. I never thought I'd say that of you, but you sure do look good.

a10a-1843405.speaker: Engle
a10a-1843405.text: You been gone too long.

a10a-1843405.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1843405.text: Let me take a look in the monocular and find out where we are. [Long pause.]

a10a-1843405.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1843405.text: Joe, I'm looking at the Pacific and Indian Ocean, here. I've got the whole continent of India and Asia and coming over the horizon, it appears to be Africa. Beautiful.

a10a-1843405.speaker: Engle
a10a-1843405.text: OK. You got a pretty good looking weather forecast for your recovery area. It looks like about 18,000 [feet, 5,500 meters] scattered, 10,000 [feet, 3,048 meters] broken, high broken, 10 miles [18.5 km] and the wind's out of the east-southeast at about 12 knots [6.17 m/s]. The waves are 4 feet [1.2 meters], 5 seconds [interval]. 81 degrees [F, 27°C], and it says widely scattered showers, but you can probably get a better handle on that from up there.

a10a-1843405.speaker: Young
a10a-1843405.text: OK, Joe. What's the present weather?

a10a-1843405.speaker: Engle
a10a-1843405.text: We're getting it now, Gene-o.

a10a-1843405.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1843405.text: Joe, tell Captain Cruse to put it into the wind. We'll be down there in about 6 hours.

a10a-1843405.speaker: Engle
a10a-1843405.text: Say again, Gene-o.

a10a-1843405.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1843405.text: Tell Captain Cruse to put it into the wind and we'll be onboard in about 6 hours.

a10a-1843405.speaker: Engle
a10a-1843405.text: OK. We'll tell him.

a10a-1843405.speaker: Engle
a10a-1843405.text: Apollo 10, this is Houston. The weather - current weather, is just about the same as the forecast. It looks like it may be getting a little bit better. It looks like they're going about 2,000 [feet, 600 meters] scattered high-broken now.

a10a-1843405.speaker: Young
a10a-1843405.text: And the sea state?

a10a-1843405.speaker: Engle
a10a-1843405.text: Sea state's 4 feet [1.2 metres] and 5-second intervals.

a10a-1843405.speaker: Young
a10a-1843405.text: Sounds good, Joe.

a10a-1843405.speaker: Engle
a10a-1843405.text: OK. I'm going to sneak out of here and let the Marines take over. I'll see you guys a little later.

a10a-1843405.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1843405.text: Joe, thanks for everything, babe. We'll see you back at home.

a10a-1843405.speaker: Engle
a10a-1843405.text: Roger that.

a10a-1843405.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1843405.text: Good morning, Apollo 10. Just got off the gate. I wanted Joe to give you that reveille because I figured that if I gave it to you, you'd consider it a harassment.

a10a-1843405.speaker: Young
a10a-1843405.text: Oh, Jack, you're just too much.

a10a-1843405.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1843405.text: Jack, after 8 days, I got to make a public announcement. You're really a great guy, it's just your choice of services.

a10a-1843405.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1843405.text: I think you're talking about the oldest fighting service in the country and the best in the world, aren't you?

a10a-1843405.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1843405.text: And watch out for those lightning bolts.

a10a-1843405.speaker: Young
a10a-1843405.text: You're talking about that gate-guard branch of the U.S. Navy.

a10a-1843405.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1843405.text: I guess you're right, Jack. I don't know what the Navy would do if it wasn't for the Marines existence.

a10a-1843405.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1843405.text: Don't forget your astrocast from yesterday. It's the same today.

a10a-1843405.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1843405.text: Yes, and I'm not going to say anything about anybody today. This has got to be a good day.

a10a-1843405.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1843405.text: Roger.

a10a-1843405.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1843405.text: 185:19:15 This is Apollo Control, still monitoring air-ground with the spacecraft, now some 46,867 nautical miles [86,798 km] out from Earth, approaching velocity of 10,000 feet per second [3,000 m/s]. Actually 9,470 [fps, 2,886 m/s]. The reveille bugle call was played up from mission control for the last day of the mission. Gene Cernan had been awake for some time observing the Earth grow bigger in his window. There was a certain amount of banter back and forth between the ground, or the spacecraft communicator, Joe Engle and later Jack Lousma, here in Mission Control and Cernan. Weather in t

a10a-1852400.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1852400.text: Hello, Houston. This is 10.

a10a-1852400.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1852400.text: Roger, 10.

a10a-1852400.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1852400.text: Jack, the LM CO 2 canister is in the sleeping bag with the suit on the right-hand side, and it's at the foot of the sleeping bag, right next to A6.

a10a-1852400.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1852400.text: Roger. Copy. Thank you, Gene.

a10a-1852400.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1852400.text: Apollo 10, Houston. If you're eating breakfast and got time to listen, I've got some newspaper reports; otherwise, I've got some PADs, and so forth. Over.

a10a-1852400.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1852400.text: OK. Go ahead, Jack; we'll listen.

a10a-1852400.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1852400.text: OK. One technical item first, the hydrogen tank fans: we'd like number 1, Off, and number 2, On. Over.

a10a-1852400.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1852400.text: Number 1s coming off and number 2's on.

a10a-1852400.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1852400.text: OK. The Orange Bugle. Pasadena, California: Scientists have found minute forms of life on a volcano-racked Antarctic island. They believe it much like the polar regions on Mars. Dr. Roy E. Cameron, Jet Propulsion Laboratory microbiologist, said in a report released Monday that algae, fungi, and bacteria had started to grow in lava rubble a year after Deception Island was rocked by volcanic blasts in December 1967.

a10a-1852400.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1852400.text: Kansas City: The weather bureau Sunday night said that it had received many calls from people in Missouri and Kansas inquiring about a bright object seen to the left of the Moon. Many thought it possibly might be the Apollo 10 on its return trip to Earth. At first a recording from the weather bureau informed callers the bright object was the planet Mars but amateur astronomers in Kansas City said it was the planet Jupiter. In St. Louis, the weather bureau said it had been advised by the president of the Astronomical Society of St. Louis that the bright object near the Moon is definitely Jupite

a10a-1852400.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1852400.text: Aboard the USS Princeton: About $750,000 is being spent on live color television of Apollo 10's Monday splashdown in the Pacific. But the networks are uncertain about the quality of the pictures. The pictures will be beamed by communications satellites to Brusterflat, Washington. From there they will be transmitted by microwave circuit to New York. The trouble is nobody has ever tried to send a picture that far says Carl Hoffenberg, a National Broadcasting Company producer assigned to the TV pool aboard this prime recovery ship.

a10a-1852400.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1852400.text: Washington: President Nixon celebrated the sixth anniversary of the signing of The Organization of African Unity Charter in a colorful diplomatic reception Sunday evening and promised to work for the future progress and prosperity of that continent.

a10a-1852400.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1852400.text: London: Two Soviet Scientists Sunday congratulated the Apollo 10 astronauts for contributing to man's knowledge of space. Soviet astronomer Nikolai Kartochev said on the Moscow radio's English service, "I should like to believe that the American Moon flight and the Soviet Venus probes will promote further progress in space exploration. I wish the crew of Apollo 10 successful completion of their space mission." Professor Ela Messovitch, a Soviet space researcher, said on the same broadcast, "Soviet and American space probes are advancing world science."

a10a-1852400.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1852400.text: In the sports news, in baseball: Atlanta 4, Phillies 1; the Astros licked the Mets 6 to 3, having won 17 of the last 21 games; I don't think you want to hear about the Cubs; San Diego took a double-header from the Cubs - correction - San Diego 10, Cubs 2 - first game, Cubs 1, San Diego nothing in the second game. And in the golf world, Atlanta: Bert Yancey, America's lone hope on a day dominated by foreigners, sank his third consecutive birdie putt on the second hole, in a sudden death playoff Sunday, to edge Australian Bruce Devlin for the Atlantic Gold Classic's championship. Yancey and Devl

a10a-1852400.speaker: Young
a10a-1852400.text: OK, Houston. This is 10. We just picked up three more guys. We've got the suits stowed flat. The CMP suit is under the left couch with the helmet on it up in the - excuse me - up in the right couch with the helmet on it, as per directed yesterday, in the sleep bag. The LMP suit and the CDR suit are under the center couch, stowed as per directed by the North American document that shows one suit with its head stowed footward, the other head stowed toward the head of the couch with the hat on the top of it. Over.

a10a-1852400.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1852400.text: Roger. Copy. Thank you.

a10a-1852400.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1852400.text: And, Apollo 10, Houston. We have another bit of information here. Spacecraft 106 had a harness which would not release after latching, and the recommendation in your case is to, if you have time and can't get one released, to take it apart at the harness adjusters, or if you have to get out of it in a hurry keep a pair of scissors handy nearby to cut the straps, and both of these methods have been attempted and verified to work. Over.

a10a-1852400.speaker: Young
a10a-1852400.text: Do you mean which wouldn't let go at the buckle? Over.

a10a-1852400.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1852400.text: That's right.

a10a-1852400.speaker: Young
a10a-1852400.text: I'll be darn! How about that. Do you know which harness it was?

a10a-1852400.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1852400.text: No. I don't, but I can attempt to find out here.

a10a-1852400.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1852400.text: Apollo 10, Houston. We will make midcourse 7. It will be approximately 1½ feet per second [0.46 m/s] in order to bring the g-level down. Over.

a10a-1852400.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1852400.text: OK, Jack.

a10a-1852400.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1852400.text: 185:43:45 This is Apollo Control. The decision has been made to do midcourse correction burn number 7. RCS burn of about 1½ foot per second [0.46 m/s]. It will reduce the flight path angle to - from 6.65 degrees, -6.65 degrees to -6.5 degrees; about 15 hundredths of a degree change, which will thereby reduce the entry deceleration from a little over 7 gs to about 6.7 gs. Continuing to monitor air ground for resumption of conversation. A few moments ago the Entry Interface time was incorrectly identified as splash time. The clock identified as ET is time to Entry Interface or 400,000 fee

a10a-1852400.speaker: Young
a10a-1852400.text: Houston, this is Apollo 10. Over.

a10a-1852400.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1852400.text: Go ahead.

a10a-1852400.speaker: Young
a10a-1852400.text: Roger. When you give us this new REFSMMAT and we go to realign to it, can you give us that attitude which we will be able to avoid the prospect of gimbal lock Program Alarm to maneuver to, to do the realign? Over.

a10a-1852400.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1852400.text: Roger. I understand you want some angles to avoid the Program Alarm.

a10a-1852400.speaker: Young
a10a-1852400.text: Yes, sir.

a10a-1852400.speaker: Young
a10a-1852400.text: And some good angles to see the stars.

a10a-1852400.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1852400.text: Roger. Stand by. We'll get...

a10a-1852400.speaker: Young
a10a-1852400.text: If possible about 180 from the Sun.

a10a-1852400.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1852400.text: OK. Thank you.

a10a-1852400.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1852400.text: And, 10. That lap belt business. We don't know which seat that occurred in, but it was in spacecraft 108. Over.

a10a-1852400.speaker: Young
a10a-1852400.text: OK. Well that's no problem then. That's spacecraft 108's problem.

a10a-1852400.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1852400.text: Roger. I wasn't sure that I gave you the right number. But we just wanted to alert you to this potential problem that arose.

a10a-1852400.speaker: Young
a10a-1852400.text: Houston, according to my star chart, that thing out beside the Moon is Jupiter.

a10a-1852400.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1852400.text: Roger. Then the expert from St. Louis is correct, right?

a10a-1852400.speaker: Young
a10a-1852400.text: Also, according to the optics that little rascal has about three or four Moons running around it right now that you can see through the optics.

a10a-1852400.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1852400.text: Roger.

a10a-1852400.speaker: Young
a10a-1852400.text: Or maybe it's a fleet of - maybe it's one great big spacecraft with a fleet of a bunch of little ones. I guess we'd better not put that word out.

a10a-1852400.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1852400.text: Yes. Like somebody said before, you guys have been up there too long.

a10a-1852400.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1852400.text: Hello, Houston. Apollo 10.

a10a-1852400.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1852400.text: Morning, Tom.

a10a-1852400.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1852400.text: Roger. Say, how did the Soviet Venus probe go? Did it land OK? Over.

a10a-1852400.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1852400.text: Say again, please.

a10a-1852400.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1852400.text: Roger. What about the Soviet Venus probe? Did it land all right? Over.

a10a-1852400.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1852400.text: Let us research that and get some word.

a10a-1852400.speaker: Young
a10a-1852400.text: See if you can find out anything about the temperature measurements.

a10a-1852400.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1852400.text: Stand by on the Venus probe: we've got a - some super sleuths working on that.

a10a-1852400.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1852400.text: This is Apollo Control; 186 hours, 5 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. Apollo 10 now 42,616 nautical miles [78,924 km] from Earth; 9,909 feet per second [2.7 m/s] velocity. The prime recovery ship, Princeton, USB Princeton in the southwest Pacific, is now on station at 15.04 south latitude, 15.04 degrees south latitude; 164.41 west longitude. The Princeton reports the sea is as still as a mill pond. We're anticipating the maneuver PAD being passed to the crew before too long for midcourse correction number 7, the only one to be made during the return leg from the Moon; slightly over 1 foot per seco

a10a-1860354.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1860354.text: Hello, Houston. This is 10.

a10a-1860354.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1860354.text: Go ahead.

a10a-1860354.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1860354.text: Jack, you still want us to cycle the H 2 and O 2 fans, or just leave them in this configuration.

a10a-1860354.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1860354.text: Apollo 10, Houston. Leave the H 2 tank - or the tank fan configuration about the same as it is except that we'd like you to stir up the O 2 tanks for a minute or so. Over.

a10a-1860354.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1860354.text: OK. Thank you.

a10a-1860354.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1860354.text: Hello, Houston. This is 10.

a10a-1860354.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1860354.text: Roger I knew it was you calling.

a10a-1860354.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1860354.text: Oh, yes. In addition to those other angles that John was talking to you about earlier, can you gin us up some TV angles, please?

a10a-1860354.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1860354.text: Roger. I've got the TV angles right here. We'll get John's angles - oh, about the time we have the TV pass - but you ready to copy?

a10a-1860354.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1860354.text: Yes. Go ahead.

a10a-1860354.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1860354.text: OK. TV at 186:50, left-hand side window, looking at the Earth. Roll is all balls, pitch is 090, yaw is all balls. And your High Gain angles will be plus 18 degrees in pitch, and 268 degrees in yaw.

a10a-1860354.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1860354.text: Jack, what will our distance from the Earth and relative velocity be placed, at that time?

a10a-1860354.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1860354.text: Stand by one. We'll extrapolate that.

a10a-1860354.speaker: Young
a10a-1860354.text: OK, Houston. This is 10 again. The lithium hydroxide canister, for purposes of determining the c.g., is butt up against A6, between A6 and A11. It's wedged in there and the half a bag of water is stored in A5. Only it's 25 percent of that half bag of water is probably going to be bubbles. I don't know how you weigh that.

a10a-1860354.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1860354.text: Roger. We got some experts here that can figure out how much the bubbles weigh.

a10a-1860354.speaker: Young
a10a-1860354.text: OK. And it's half - half filled with water.

a10a-1860354.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1860354.text: Roger.

a10a-1860354.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1860354.text: They don't hardly weigh more than the water at zero g. [Long pause.]

a10a-1860354.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1860354.text: Gene, this is Houston. At 186:50, about TV time, you're going to be at 38,435 miles [71,182 km]. And your velocity will be 10,402 feet per second [3,171 m/s].

a10a-1860354.speaker: Young
a10a-1860354.text: Finally starting to pick up a little.

a10a-1860354.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1860354.text: Yes, you're getting there. You just crossed the 10,000 foot per second [3,000 m/s] mark right now and you're really starting to move out now.

a10a-1860354.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1860354.text: We were going so slow there for a while, Jack, I thought we were about to stall out. Over.

a10a-1860354.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1860354.text: Yes. I was kind of wondering about all of that mathematics and automechanics, you know. I thought maybe you were going to fall through this time, but it looks like it's going to hang in there.

a10a-1860354.speaker: Young
a10a-1860354.text: OK, Houston. On the upper hatch, there is considerable water up there, and I guess if I was going to design a water separator, this would be a good place to put it.

a10a-1860354.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1860354.text: Roger. We copy.

a10a-1860354.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1860354.text: Apollo 10, Houston. On the Venus probe, Venus 5 landed on 16 May. Venus 6 landed on 17 May. Both were launched in January, 6 days apart, as you recall, and Soviet Scientists say that they are fully satisfied with results. Each probe has returned much new information which indicates and I quote: "Man will never go there" unquote. Their probes made a soft landing, lasted about 30 minutes after landing, measured a temperature of 537 degrees Fahrenheit [280°C]. Over.

a10a-1860354.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1860354.text: Roger. We'll look into the manned aspect later, but the crew of Apollo 10 wish you would give them our congratulations on their total engineering and scientific success. Over.

a10a-1860354.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1860354.text: Roger. Copy. Congratulations to the Soviets on their engineering success with the Venus probes.

a10a-1862805.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1862805.text: Apollo 10, Houston. I have a Flight Plan update.

a10a-1862805.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1862805.text: Go ahead, Jack.

a10a-1862805.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1862805.text: OK. At 189 plus 10 hours, we'd like you to read out the Command Module RCS temperatures off the system test meter. Because if preheat is required, we'll want to bring fuel cell 1 back on the line. And at 189 plus 20, we'll reservice the primary evaporator, using 3 minutes of water - 3-minute service. And I have a change to your entry checklist, as a result of the fuel cell situation. And the change is on page E-Echo 2-2, step 6, line 12, change fuel cell 2 main A and B Off to read instead, fuel cell 1 main A and B Off. And in addition we're standing by for your crew status reports and we'd lik

a10a-1862805.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1862805.text: OK. On that - On that checklist now, I just want to make sure, the preceding line says fuel cell pumps, parentheses 3, Off. Corrected line now says fuel cell 1 Main A and B, Off, and then it says verified loads balanced. Right?

a10a-1862805.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1862805.text: That is affirmative. You've got that right.

a10a-1862805.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1862805.text: OK. We'll we have fuel cell 1, Main A, Main B, Off right now.

a10a-1862805.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1862805.text: Roger, 10. If we bring fuel cell 1 on, then this note will apply. Over.

a10a-1862805.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1862805.text: OK, Jack. I'm with you and at 1 - At 189 20, we're going to reservice the Evap for 3 minutes, and at 189 10, we'll read off the CM RCS temps and at that time well decide on fuel cell 1, and stand by for those RAD readings.

a10a-1862805.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1862805.text: Roger.

a10a-1862805.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1862805.text: OK. Crew status check. The CDR took 1 'Lomo' last night and he's going to take a decongestant just precautionary prior to re-entry. The crew slept well last night, from anywhere to 4 to 8 hours sleep apiece. The RadD readings are 26048, 05049, and 15050, and we've completed breakfast. The spacecraft is about 90 percent - 95 percent stowed, and we'll be in the couches here, and probably remain pretty much so there from now on in.

a10a-1862805.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1862805.text: Roger. We copy, Gene. Thank you.

a10a-1862805.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1862805.text: Houston, this is 10.

a10a-1862805.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1862805.text: Go ahead, 10.

a10a-1862805.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1862805.text: I'm going to High Gain Antenna at this time.

a10a-1862805.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1862805.text: Copy. [Long pause.]

a10a-1862805.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1862805.text: Hello, Houston. When do you want to conduct a Simplex checks?

a10a-1862805.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1862805.text: Apollo 10, Houston. We're monitoring the VHF and we'll notify when we need VHF check. Over.

a10a-1862805.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1862805.text: OK. Fine. We'll be standing by for it.

a10a-1862805.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1862805.text: Houston, Apollo 10. We're all squared away in the attitude for the final TV pass. Over.

a10a-1862805.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1862805.text: Roger. Copy, Tom.

a10a-1862805.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1862805.text: And, Houston, are you going to be receiving this live at MCC? Over.

a10a-1862805.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1862805.text: Stand by one.

a10a-1862805.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1862805.text: 10, Houston. TV will be live here.

a10a-1862805.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1862805.text: OK.

a10a-1862805.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1862805.text: 186:49:16 This is Apollo Control. As mentioned in the conversation between Jack Lousma and the crew, coming up on a television pass in less than a minute, according to the Flight Plan. It'll be routed through the Honeysuckle Creek, Australia tracking station over S-band relayed by satellite back to Mission Control, where it will be converted into color and distributed from there. Standing by for this morning's television pass, the final one of the mission, to begin.

a10a-1862805.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1862805.text: Houston, Apollo 10. We're ready to go with the TV, if you are.

a10a-1862805.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1862805.text: Stand by one.

a10a-1862805.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1862805.text: OK, Apollo 10. Houston. We're going to TV at this time. Over.

a10a-1862805.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1862805.text: OK, Houston. You ought to be starting to pick up a view of the Earth at this time. We're coming to you on our final TV pass. Let us know when you're getting it, Jack.

a10a-1862805.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1862805.text: Roger, Gene. We'll tell you when we're getting it here.

a10a-1862805.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1862805.text: Houston, Apollo 10. How does the screen look? Over.

a10a-1862805.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1862805.text: Roger, 10. We're not getting it yet. Apparently everything isn't quite warmed up yet. Oh, here she comes.

a10a-1862805.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1862805.text: Roger.

a10a-1862805.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1862805.text: She's coming in now.

a10a-1862805.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1862805.text: OK. We're getting TV of the Earth. We see the terminator, and you're getting it centered up pretty good right now.

a10a-1862805.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1862805.text: Good morning from Apollo 10. We're now approximately 38,000 miles [70,376 km] from the Earth and we're starting to accelerate rapidly as the Earth's influence becomes felt more and more the closer we get. We're doing now approximately 7,500 miles an hour [3,353 m/s], and we're 5 hours out from final entry into the Earth's atmosphere. This morning as we look out there we can see part of China, India is the most predominant feature. But also we can see Saudi Arabia, the Gulf of Oman, and the Indian Ocean at this time. And I'll try to give you a little zoom here in on Saudi Arabia and India.

a10a-1862805.speaker: Young
a10a-1862805.text: Tom's going to zoom the TV into the Gulf of Oman, now. See what you can see, there. OK. That's full zoom into the Gulf of Oman.

a10a-1862805.speaker: Young
a10a-1862805.text: The Gulf of Oman is in the center left part of your picture. How does it look down there?

a10a-1862805.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1862805.text: OK, 10. The globe is about centering the screen at this time, and we can see the darker landmasses and the Gulf of Oman is not apparent to a novice I guess you might say. But it's a beautiful picture and it's coming through well.

a10a-1862805.speaker: Young
a10a-1862805.text: Sure is a beautiful picture.

a10a-1862805.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1862805.text: I guess you might say that the artist that painted that one is a master.

a10a-1862805.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1862805.text: I know that looks real good to you guys, and the closer you get the better it looks.

a10a-1862805.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1862805.text: Jack, one reflection that we felt very strong about is when we show you our last telecast here of the Earth, is that we felt very strong about sharing with you some of the adventure, the excitement, the challenges, and the rewards of these 8 days, and through this endeavor, we have hoped that we made you and millions of people of the world, more of a part of the history that's being made in our day and age.

a10a-1862805.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1862805.text: I know everybody around the world has appreciated the TV pictures and all the effort you went to make them good. They've all been excellent and I know it's given everyone a better feeling for what we're actually doing and a better appreciation of the program in general.

a10a-1862805.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1862805.text: OK. Some final just color thoughts as we look in there. India appears to us to be a purplish tan over - I see that the - the Sun - the solar subpoint is right in the Gulf of Oman, now. It is nearly a yellowish bronze. Beyond that we have Saudi Arabia. And Saudi Arabia to us looks a sandy orange. Up to the right, up to the very top of your screen is covered mostly with clouds and this has been the cloud cover that has existed over the northern part of the world ever since we left Cape Kennedy nearly 8 days ago. Down below to the left, the long straight cloud is part of the ITC you can see it, o

a10a-1862805.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1862805.text: Roger, Tom. And I think the people around the world are kind of sad to see this to be the last TV shots from space for a while, and I know that they've been very interested and enthusiastic about the pictures and the total flight.

a10a-1862805.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1862805.text: Roger. It's kind of a feeling of the same way for us not to see these beautiful views. Of course, we're certainly looking forward to being back on the good Earth in about 5 hours. And it's really been a fantastic overall flight for us, and some of the experiences that we've had all the way, from liftoff on the Saturn V to seeing the Earth and Moon, the lunar orbit work, and the climb out from the Moon and all the way back. And why don't we take you inside the cockpit for one quick minute?

a10a-1862805.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1862805.text: OK. We have it inside the cabin now, Tom, and weve got a pretty good look at a clean shaven Command Module pilot there.

a10a-1862805.speaker: Young
a10a-1862805.text: This is your old retired philosopher speaking to you from outer space, and telling you that TV is on its way back.

a10a-1862805.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1862805.text: Roger. Thank you for those words from the old retired philosopher.

a10a-1862805.speaker: Young
a10a-1862805.text: We have a little more work to do and then we'll be back with you and it will sure be great to be back. It's been utterly unbelievable, the mission has. We've really enjoyed every bit of it, so until we see you again, we'll say so long.

a10a-1862805.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1862805.text: OK. We'll pan over on the right side of the cockpit where Commander Gene Cernan...

a10a-1862805.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1862805.text: Hello, Gene. How about saying a few words into the microphone?

a10a-1862805.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1862805.text: OK, Jack. I can't tell you what a rewarding and satisfying experience this has been. It's had its moments, as I said. I'm just thankful that through the medium of television we've been able to share it with so many people in real time. I'm convinced, after this mission, none of them are going to be easy, but nothing is impossible, and I think that the future of manned space flight for now and for many generations to come is going to uncover many, many other new challenges and experiences that we're yet really incapable of even conceiving at this time. It's been a great 8 days, and of course, w

a10a-1862805.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1862805.text: Hello there, Skipper.

a10a-1862805.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1862805.text: Good morning. On the final closeout telecast of Apollo 10, we just want to say that it has just been fantastic - the total views that we've seen on this total mission. Again, like Gene pointed out, no mission's easy, and it's been a lot of work. But we've enjoyed the whole thing greatly. And, also, the main thing is, we've been able to - in real time, on some of the major parts of the mission - to share this with you. Like we pointed out, that fantastic view when we left the Moon, Man has certainly progressed a long ways in such a short few years. And how much we're going to progress in the fu

a10a-1862805.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1862805.text: But, as you know, we had the Lunar Module with us, which we nicknamed "Snoopy." And Snoopy the ascent part of Snoopy - is on its way around the Sun now. The descent part is still in an orbit around the Moon, and right now we're in our code nickname of "Charlie Brown." And here's again our little mascot, Charlie Brown, code name for the Command Module, and Charlie Brown has been a real good boy. He's been with us all the way. The spacecraft has been fantastic with respect to its systems and its reliability. It's done a beautiful job for the whole program.

a10a-1862805.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1862805.text: And how does the color look for Charlie Brown down there, Houston?

a10a-1862805.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1862805.text: The color is perfect, Tom; Good morning, Charlie.

a10a-1862805.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1862805.text: And Charlie just wants to say "Good morning" to all you people and it's great to be on the mission. And here is our other friend that went along with us. And for a code name, and as we said, part of him is on the way around the Sun and the other part around the Moon, so he's got quite a split personality. Over.

a10a-1862805.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1862805.text: And here's the code name of our Lunar Module, "Snoopy." And Snoopy was a fairly good dog for us. In fact, he's a fantastic vehicle to fly. But again one thing we want to point out about Snoopy, this is a symbol of a manned flight awareness program and represents the good work and efforts of the hundreds of thousands of people who have made the manned space flight program so successful. And from the crew of Apollo 10, we'd just like to give all those people a salute and acknowledgment, and this is one way of doing it, just by naming a spacecraft after their symbol. And so from the five of us, G

a10a-1862805.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1862805.text: Roger. Thank you, Tom. Preparations are well underway for your return and recovery, and we're looking forward to seeing you real soon.

a10a-1870322.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1870322.text: Roger. Tell all the people around the world, Jack, and also in Houston, MCC, what a great job they've done, and we'll see them back there shortly. Over.

a10a-1870322.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1870322.text: Roger, Tom. Thank you and their congratulations to you and your crew. Over.

a10a-1870322.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1870322.text: Roger. We'll wait until we get onboard the carrier for that.

a10a-1871108-a2g.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1871108-a2g.text: Houston, Apollo 10. I'll stay in this attitude until you give us the update, and then we'll go down to zero, zero, zero. Over.

a10a-1871108-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1871108-a2g.text: Roger. We copy, 10.

a10a-1871108-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1871108-a2g.text: Apollo 10, Houston. We're ready with your update. We've got a state vector and entry REFSMMAT and a midcourse 7 target load, and if you will go to Accept. In addition, we're not reading anything on the VHF yet, and we'd like you to ensure that the VHF is cranked up. Over.

a10a-1871108-a2g.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1871108-a2g.text: OK, Houston. Apollo 10. We are in P00 and Accept. I've got the VHF warming up and we'll give you a call in just a minute. Over.

a10a-1871108-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1871108-a2g.text: Roger, 10.

a10a-1871108-a2g.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1871108-a2g.text: Hello, Houston. This is Apollo 10 on VHF A Simplex. How do you read? Over.

a10a-1871108-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1871108-a2g.text: Roger. I hear you loud and clear, 10, on VHF A.

a10a-1871108-a2g.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1871108-a2g.text: Roger, Houston. This is 10 reading you loud and clear. Over.

a10a-1871108-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1871108-a2g.text: Belay my last, 10. I think I'm getting you on S-band. We'll check with the VHF people. [Long pause.]

a10a-1871108-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1871108-a2g.text: Apollo 10, Houston. Carnarvon reads you loud and clear on VHF.

a10a-1871108-a2g.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1871108-a2g.text: Roger, Houston. Apollo 10. I'm reading you about three-by-three on VHF. How me?

a10a-1871108-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1871108-a2g.text: Apollo 10, Houston. I'm reading you here on S-band, and we'll have to check with the sites to see how the VHF is coming in.

a10a-1871108-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1871108-a2g.text: Apollo 10, Houston. We're on VHF only. How do you read? Over.

a10a-1871108-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1871108-a2g.text: Apollo 10, Houston. How do you read on VHF? Over.

a10a-1871108-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1871108-a2g.text: Apollo 10, Houston. Back on the S-hand. Apparently you weren't reading us on VHF. We'll give you another VHF check in about a half an hour.

a10a-1871108-a2g.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1871108-a2g.text: OK, Jack. [Long pause.]

a10a-1871108-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1871108-a2g.text: Apollo 10, Houston. The uplink is complete. You can go to Block.

a10a-1871108-a2g.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1871108-a2g.text: OK.

a10a-1871108-a2g.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1871108-a2g.text: Houston, Apollo 10. I'll go ahead and pitch down to 000 when you have everything the [garble] as far as the uplink is complete and verified. I guess it is verified now. Over.

a10a-1871108-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1871108-a2g.text: Roger. The uplink is complete, Tom, and you're clear to the new attitude.

a10a-1871108-a2g.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1871108-a2g.text: Roger, 10. And, Houston, 10. This attitude of 000 will be a good one to torque to the new REFSMMAT? Over.

a10a-1871108-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1871108-a2g.text: That's affirmative, 10.

a10a-1872813-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1872813-a2g.text: Apollo 10, Houston. We'd like you to go to wide beamwidth and High Gain Antenna and I have a maneuver PAD and an entry PAD for you.

a10a-1872813-a2g.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1872813-a2g.text: OK. We'll be with you in one second; I'm going to wide beamwidth right now.

a10a-1872813-a2g.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1872813-a2g.text: You're in wide, Houston, and we'll give you a call when we're ready to copy. We're still doing a few little chores here. Over.

a10a-1872813-a2g.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1872813-a2g.text: Hello, Houston, Houston. This is Apollo 10. We're ready to copy your P30 and your entry update.

a10a-1872813-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1872813-a2g.text: Roger, 10. Here's the maneuver PAD. MCC 7, RCS/G&N: 25232, Noun 48 is NA. Noun 33 is 188:49:56.75; plus three balls 16, minus all balls, minus four balls 1; three balls, 129, three balls; apogee is NA, perigee is plus 0021.2; three balls 16, two balls 7, three balls 16; 40, 295.9, 38.3; 033, Uniform 159, Lima 12. The rest is NA; your set stars are Deneb, 43; Vega, 36; 067, 174, 343. Your ullage is a two-quad burn, use Bravo and Delta. Read back maneuver PAD; let me know when you're ready with the entry PAD. Over.

a10a-1872813-a2g.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1872813-a2g.text: OK. MCC 7, RCS G&N: 25232; 48's NA; 188:49:56.2 - .75, plus three balls 16, minus all balls, minus four balls 1. Roll is 000, 129, 000. Apogee is NA; perigee is plus 0021.2, three balls 16, two balls 7, three balls 16; 40, 295.9, 38.3; 033, Uniform 159, Lima 12; Deneb, 43 and Vega, 36; 067, 174, 343. Using two quads, Bravo and Delta. And I'd like to read Noun 33 back to you again. That's 188:49:56.75.

a10a-1872813-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1872813-a2g.text: That's affirmative, 10. Entry PAD when you're ready.

a10a-1872813-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1872813-a2g.text: OK. The entry PAD is a Mid-Pac: three balls, 153, 001; 191:31:54; 268; minus 15.07, minus 164.67; 06.8, 36315, 6.52, 1204.1; 36395; 191:48:54; 00:28; Noun 69 is NA; D0 is 4.00; 028 - correction, 02:08; 00:18, 03:29, 08:17; 40, 262.1, 34.7; 033, Dog 089, Lima 22. Lift vector is Up. Comment: Use a nonexit pattern. Your horizon is dark at Entry Interface. Over.

a10a-1872813-a2g.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1872813-a2g.text: OK. Jack. Entry PAD. Area is Mid-Pac: 000, 153, 001; 191:31:54; 268; minus 15.07, minus 164.67; 068, 36315 6.52, minus 1204.1; 36395; 191:48:54; 00:28; Noun 69 is NA. Are you still with me?

a10a-1872813-a2g.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1872813-a2g.text: DO is 4.00; 02:08; 00:18, 03:29, 08:17; 40, 262.1, 34.7; 033, Delta 089 and Lima 22. The lift vector is Up; using a nonexit pattern and the horizon is dark at Entry Interface.

a10a-1872813-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1872813-a2g.text: Roger, 10. I have a late correction at the bottom. SPA is Dog 080, now. Over.

a10a-1872813-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1872813-a2g.text: And, 10. We'd like you to read the range to go back, please.

a10a-1872813-a2g.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1872813-a2g.text: OK. The range to go is 1204.1.

a10a-1872813-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1872813-a2g.text: Roger. We copy. And that's affirmative.

a10a-1872813-a2g.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1872813-a2g.text: 187:51:XX This is Apollo Control. To translate some of the exchange of numbers between the spacecraft and the ground; they were passed up a maneuver PAD for midcourse correction burn number 7; will be with the RCS thrusters. At 188 hours, 49 minutes, 56.75 seconds, 1.6 foot per second [0.49 m/s] velocity change, burn time of 7 seconds. The additional - the other PAD for the entry numbers to the Mid Pacific prime recovery line, nominally along 165 west longitude, showing target point of 15.07 south latitude, 164.67 west longitude. Maximum gs expected, 6.8; velocity at 400,000 feet [121,920 metr

a10a-1875821-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1875821-a2g.text: Apollo 10, Houston. We know the set - the DAP is now set up for four jets, and we think we ought to have two jets. That'd be B and D. Over.

a10a-1875821-a2g.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1875821-a2g.text: OK. Roger. You want - Since it's only a couple of feet per second here and everything, we've got plenty of fuel, but well go ahead and use two jets. Our checklist calls for four. Over

a10a-1875821-a2g.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1875821-a2g.text: Houston, this is 10. What's your feeling about putting fuel cell 1 on for the burn?

a10a-1875821-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1875821-a2g.text: Apollo 10, Houston. We don't need fuel cell 1 for the burn and don't intend to use it for the burn. Over.

a10a-1881834-a2g.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1881834-a2g.text: Houston, Apollo 10. We're starting through our P30 series now. Over.

a10a-1881834-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1881834-a2g.text: Apollo 10, Houston. We suspect that your suit circuit heat exchanger may be in the Bypass position and - well, for comfort, it ought to be on now, and go to Bypass at EI minus 50. Over.

a10a-1883033-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1883033-a2g.text: Apollo 10, Houston. When it's convenient, we'd like to get a GET time hack with you.

a10a-1883033-a2g.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1883033-a2g.text: It's convenient. Over.

a10a-1883033-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1883033-a2g.text: Roger. Go ahead and give us a time and we'll set our clocks.

a10a-1883033-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1883033-a2g.text: OK. Thank you very much. We're right on.

a10a-1883033-a2g.speaker: Young
a10a-1883033-a2g.text: That's computer time and GET time, and our mission time is right on.

a10a-1883033-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1883033-a2g.text: Roger. We're following right along with you.

a10a-1883033-a2g.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1883033-a2g.text: Houston, Apollo 10.

a10a-1883033-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1883033-a2g.text: Go ahead, 10.

a10a-1883033-a2g.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1883033-a2g.text: OK. We're going to go ahead and call up P41.

a10a-1883033-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1883033-a2g.text: OK. We'll be watching you.

a10a-1883033-a2g.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1883033-a2g.text: This is Apollo Control, 188 hours, 39 minutes Ground Elapsed Time, coming up on 10 mark to the burn, Mark, 10 minutes to ignition of midcourse correction burn number 7, air-to-ground still live.

a10a-1883033-a2g.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1883033-a2g.text: Houston, Apollo 10. Would you give us a hack at 5 minutes prior to the maneuver just so we can recheck our event timer? Over.

a10a-1883033-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1883033-a2g.text: Roger. Understand you want a time hack just prior to the burn. Is that affirmative?

a10a-1883033-a2g.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1883033-a2g.text: Give us one at 5 minutes. This event timer occasionally has been jumping numbers. Over.

a10a-1883033-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1883033-a2g.text: Roger. We'll give you a hack at 5 minutes. That'll be about a minute and a half yet.

a10a-1883033-a2g.speaker: Young
a10a-1883033-a2g.text: OK, Houston. We're showing 7 minutes.

a10a-1883033-a2g.speaker: Young
a10a-1883033-a2g.text: Mark.

a10a-1883033-a2g.speaker: Young
a10a-1883033-a2g.text: How's that sound?

a10a-1883033-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1883033-a2g.text: Yes. We're showing the same. That's confirmed, 7 minutes.

a10a-1883033-a2g.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1883033-a2g.text: OK.

a10a-1884437-a2g.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1884437-a2g.text: OK. We're proceeding here for the final trim.

a10a-1884437-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1884437-a2g.text: Roger, 10.

a10a-1884437-a2g.speaker: Young
a10a-1884437-a2g.text: Man, I mean to tell you.

a10a-1884437-a2g.speaker: Young
a10a-1884437-a2g.text: Boy, this is absolutely fantastic. Come all the way back to the Moon and do this kind of midcourse.

a10a-1884437-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1884437-a2g.text: Yes. That's pretty good shooting, isn't it?

a10a-1884437-a2g.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1884437-a2g.text: Tell Christopher C. and company looks like they have a pretty good rifle scope there to shoot us back in this target. Over.

a10a-1884437-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1884437-a2g.text: Roger. I guess all that mathematics really works after all.

a10a-1884437-a2g.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1884437-a2g.text: Roger.

a10a-1884437-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1884437-a2g.text: Apollo 10, Houston. We have a few configuration items we'd like to point out. Right...

a10a-1884437-a2g.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1884437-a2g.text: OK. We'll wait.

a10a-1884437-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1884437-a2g.text: Rotational hand controller power, Direct; BMAGS, Att 1, Rate 2. Over.

a10a-1884437-a2g.speaker: Young
a10a-1884437-a2g.text: Roger.

a10a-1884437-a2g.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1884437-a2g.text: 188:49:24 This is Apollo Control. Mark, 30 seconds to ignition.

a10a-1884437-a2g.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1884437-a2g.text: We're burning.

a10a-1884437-a2g.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1884437-a2g.text: OK. How we are on our residuals? You can read them? 0, minus 1, minus 1, and a Proceed.

a10a-1884437-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1884437-a2g.text: Roger. We copy.

a10a-1884437-a2g.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1884437-a2g.text: 188:51:21 This is Apollo Control. Midcourse correction burn number 7 scheduled for 7 seconds duration, was actually burned out at 6.6 seconds.

a10a-1884437-a2g.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1884437-a2g.text: Houston, Apollo 10. It's starting to get real cool in here. We'd like to go Bypass on the suit circuit heat exchanger. Over.

a10a-1884437-a2g.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1884437-a2g.text: And we can turn it on if it gets warm again. Over.

a10a-1884437-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1884437-a2g.text: Roger, 10. Go ahead.

a10a-1884437-a2g.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1884437-a2g.text: Bypass.

a10a-1884437-a2g.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1884437-a2g.text: Hello, Houston. This is 10. Could you give me a short count, and I'll cut off my S-band and see whether I can pick you up on VHF?

a10a-1884437-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1884437-a2g.text: Stand by one, please.

a10a-1884437-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1884437-a2g.text: Apollo 10, Houston. We'll try a VHF voice check as soon as we get the sites configured and you can go to left antenna. Over.

a10a-1884437-a2g.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1884437-a2g.text: OK. Thank you, Jack.

a10a-1884437-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1884437-a2g.text: Apollo 10, Houston. Set up your VHF and S-band turned down. We're going to try the VHF check in a minute.

a10a-1884437-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1884437-a2g.text: Hello, Apollo 10. Houston on VHF through Guam. How do you copy? Over.

a10a-1884437-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1884437-a2g.text: Apollo 10, Houston. How do you read? Over.

a10a-1884437-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1884437-a2g.text: Apollo 10, we're back up on S-band. We weren't able to read you on VHF. Over.

a10a-1884437-a2g.speaker: Young
a10a-1884437-a2g.text: Roger. We heard some kind of transmissions there in the background, but we never gave you a call on VHF. Over.

a10a-1884437-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1884437-a2g.text: Roger. I asked for a radio check on VHF. Apparently we're not quite in range yet.

a10a-1884437-a2g.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1884437-a2g.text: 188:59:24 This is Apollo Control. Apollo 10 now 24,469 nautical miles [45,317 km] out from Earth; velocity now 12,794 feet per second [3.900 m/s]. Still monitoring air to ground, live.

a10a-1884437-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1884437-a2g.text: Apollo 10, Houston. All sites are monitoring VHF downlink. When you're ready, make a transmission and they'll see if we can pick you up.

a10a-1884437-a2g.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1884437-a2g.text: Roger, Houston. This is Apollo 10 transmitting on VHF on the short count. 5, 4, 3, 2, 1. How do you read? Over.

a10a-1890044-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1890044-a2g.text: Apollo 10, Houston. Sites apparently aren't reading you yet on VHF. We recommend that you transmit simultaneous S-band and VHF; and, when the sites can read VHF, why, they'll let us know, and we'll conduct the radio check. Over.

a10a-1890044-a2g.speaker: Young
a10a-1890044-a2g.text: Roger. That's what we're doing. Over.

a10a-1890044-a2g.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1890044-a2g.text: OK, Houston, Apollo 10. We're all squared away and way ahead on the checklist. The next thing we're waiting for is just to read out the Command Module RCS temps and service the primary Evap and the logic check coming up. Over.

a10a-1890044-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1890044-a2g.text: Roger. And there's no significant change in the weather in the landing area. The altimeter is 29.88, or plus 38 feet, and we have a splashdown computed time of 192:03, and sunrise will be 25 minutes later. Over.

a10a-1890044-a2g.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1890044-a2g.text: Roger 192:03, sunrise 25 minutes later. Thank you.

a10a-1890044-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1890044-a2g.text: Roger. And you copy altimeter 29.88.

a10a-1890044-a2g.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1890044-a2g.text: Roger.

a10a-1890044-a2g.speaker: Young
a10a-1890044-a2g.text: Hey, Jack, we don't have any place to set the altimeter. But thanks for the plus 38 feet.

a10a-1890044-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1890044-a2g.text: Roger. Plus 38.

a10a-1890044-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1890044-a2g.text: And, 10, we're ready for your RCS temps when you're ready to read them down.

a10a-1890044-a2g.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1890044-a2g.text: Houston, here's our readings: 5-Charlie is 5.0; 5-Delta is 4.8; 6-Alpha is 5.1; 6-Bravo is 5.1; 6-Charlie is 4.2; 6-Delta is 4.9.

a10a-1890044-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1890044-a2g.text: Roger, 10. We copied the temperatures. Thank you.

a10a-1890044-a2g.speaker: Young
a10a-1890044-a2g.text: Houston, at 45 minutes to EI - to RRT time Could you give us a time hack? Over.

a10a-1890044-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1890044-a2g.text: Roger. You want a time hack at 45 minutes to EI.

a10a-1890044-a2g.speaker: Young
a10a-1890044-a2g.text: That's affirmative.

a10a-1890044-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1890044-a2g.text: And your computer landing time precisely is now 192:03:57.

a10a-1890044-a2g.speaker: Young
a10a-1890044-a2g.text: Houston, we're going back On with the suit circuit heat exchangers. It doesn't take very long.

a10a-1890044-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1890044-a2g.text: Roger to On.

a10a-1890044-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1890044-a2g.text: Apollo 10, Houston. Late correction on your landing time is 192:02:57.

a10a-1890044-a2g.speaker: Young
a10a-1890044-a2g.text: [Laughter.] Roger. 192:02:57.

a10a-1890044-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1890044-a2g.text: Buddy, you're going to get there. It doesn't really matter does it?

a10a-1890044-a2g.speaker: Young
a10a-1890044-a2g.text: Yes. We'll get back.

a10a-1890044-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1890044-a2g.text: Yes. We could put you in a holding pattern for a minute there, maybe.

a10a-1890044-a2g.speaker: Young
a10a-1890044-a2g.text: As long as our RET times are OK, we're in good shape.

a10a-1890044-a2g.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1890044-a2g.text: Houston, Apollo 10. Over.

a10a-1890044-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1890044-a2g.text: Go ahead.

a10a-1890044-a2g.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1890044-a2g.text: Roger. Wish you would relay on to Captain Cruse, the skipper of the Princeton, that at the time there, at 192:03, we expect to be right on top of the aim point and hope this big ship is close by. Over.

a10a-1890044-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1890044-a2g.text: Roger. We'll pass the word on, and you just holler "Meat Ball" when you see it.

a10a-1890044-a2g.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1890044-a2g.text: Will do.

a10a-1890044-a2g.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1890044-a2g.text: 189:10:38 This is Apollo Control. To recap that last exchange, predicted touchdown time, in Ground Elapsed Time 192 hours, 2 minutes, 57 seconds. Back to air to ground.

a10a-1890044-a2g.speaker: Young
a10a-1890044-a2g.text: OK, Houston. Our data up here shows no preheat.

a10a-1890044-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1890044-a2g.text: Roger. We confirm that, 10.

a10a-1890044-a2g.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1890044-a2g.text: 189:18:53 This is Apollo Control. Mark; 2 hours, 30 minutes to Entry Interface, or sensible atmosphere at 400,000 feet (121,920 metres] above the surface. Apollo 10 now 22,150 nautical miles [41,022 km] out from Earth. Velocity beginning to increase - air to ground here.

a10a-1891848-a2g.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1891848-a2g.text: Houston, this is 10. The glycol Evap water-flow valve will come on in two zero minutes.

a10a-1891848-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1891848-a2g.text: Roger. Two zero minutes.

a10a-1891848-a2g.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1891848-a2g.text: I'll leave it On for 3; then to Auto. Is that correct?

a10a-1891848-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1891848-a2g.text: That's affirmative, 10.

a10a-1891848-a2g.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1891848-a2g.text: OK. Thank you.

a10a-1891848-a2g.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1891848-a2g.text: 189:19:42 Velocity now 13,399 feet per second [4,084 m/s], beginning to build up as they get back closer into Earth - air to ground still live.

a10a-1891848-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1891848-a2g.text: Apollo 10, Houston. We would like to have all heaters and fans Off in the Cryo tanks. Over.

a10a-1891848-a2g.speaker: Young
a10a-1891848-a2g.text: Roger. Heaters and fans going off in the Cryo tanks.

a10a-1891848-a2g.speaker: Young
a10a-1891848-a2g.text: They're all Off.

a10a-1891848-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1891848-a2g.text: Roger.

a10a-1891848-a2g.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1891848-a2g.text: Houston, the Evap servicing is complete, and for the record, of course, we had been there before, but I had gone to Manual Increase again on the valve.

a10a-1891848-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1891848-a2g.text: Roger. We copy, and Manual Increase.

a10a-1891848-a2g.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1891848-a2g.text: And I know I've got the water flow in Auto.

a10a-1891848-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1891848-a2g.text: Roger, Gene.

a10a-1891848-a2g.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1891848-a2g.text: Houston, this is 10.

a10a-1891848-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1891848-a2g.text: Go ahead, 10.

a10a-1891848-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1891848-a2g.text: Apollo 10. Houston. Go ahead.

a10a-1891848-a2g.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1891848-a2g.text: Roger. We're requesting an in-route descent commencing 1200 Out, and we'd also like expeditious handling, CCA down near the Princeton. We'll be making a vertical descent from about 24,000 (ft, 7,300 metres]. And request No Go-around this pass.

a10a-1891848-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1891848-a2g.text: Roger. Report crossing 25 miles (40 km) at 6,000 [ft, 1,800 metres]. Over.

a10a-1891848-a2g.speaker: Young
a10a-1891848-a2g.text: How about that? Houston approach hasn't changed a bit.

a10a-1891848-a2g.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1891848-a2g.text: We hope on this one, Houston approach at 6,000 [ft, 1,800 metres] will be within about a half to a quarter of a mile [0.8 to 0.4 km]. Over.

a10a-1891848-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1891848-a2g.text: Roger. You can write your deviation up when you're on the ground.

a10a-1891848-a2g.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1891848-a2g.text: Roger.

a10a-1891848-a2g.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1891848-a2g.text: Hello, Houston. 10. What's our range to Mother Earth?

a10a-1891848-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1891848-a2g.text: OK, 10. We're reading 19,660 [nautical miles, 36,410 km] at this time.

a10a-1891848-a2g.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1891848-a2g.text: OK. And how fast we going?

a10a-1891848-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1891848-a2g.text: You're coming in about 14,100 feet per second [4,300 m/s] right now. You're really picking it up.

a10a-1891848-a2g.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1891848-a2g.text: Thank you, sir.

a10a-1891848-a2g.speaker: Young
a10a-1891848-a2g.text: It's that last 10,000 miles (18,520 km) that's more interesting anyway.

a10a-1891848-a2g.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1891848-a2g.text: Hello, Houston. Apollo 10. Over.

a10a-1891848-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1891848-a2g.text: Go ahead, 10.

a10a-1891848-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1891848-a2g.text: Apollo 10, Houston. Go ahead.

a10a-1891848-a2g.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1891848-a2g.text: Roger, Houston. We still have lots of propellant in our primary propellant tanks, but we wanted to know, for the Service Module jettison, if you want us to open the secondary propellants. Over.

a10a-1891848-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1891848-a2g.text: Stand by one, please.

a10a-1891848-a2g.speaker: Young
a10a-1891848-a2g.text: Roger.

a10a-1891848-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1891848-a2g.text: Apollo 10, Houston. Proceed as per the checklist. Over.

a10a-1891848-a2g.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1891848-a2g.text: Roger. As per checklist.

a10a-1894203-a2g.speaker: Young
a10a-1894203-a2g.text: OK, Houston. We're ready for the logic sequence check now.

a10a-1894203-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1894203-a2g.text: OK, Apollo 10. We're ready to go with the check. Over.

a10a-1894203-a2g.speaker: Young
a10a-1894203-a2g.text: OK. The ELS logic is coming on. ELS going to Auto. SECS logic is coming on. OK. We're all set up.

a10a-1894203-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1894203-a2g.text: OK. Apollo 10, Houston. We'll give you a Go for Pyro Arm.

a10a-1894203-a2g.speaker: Young
a10a-1894203-a2g.text: Roger. SECS logic coming back off.

a10a-1894203-a2g.speaker: Young
a10a-1894203-a2g.text: Houston, this is 10. We completed the sextant star check and Altair was within about 6 minutes of being right in the middle of the optics.

a10a-1894203-a2g.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1894203-a2g.text: Do you want to remain High Gain here until just before Sep?

a10a-1894203-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1894203-a2g.text: Apollo 10, Houston. Let's stay in High Gain until Sep and then go to Sep C. Over.

a10a-1894203-a2g.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1894203-a2g.text: OK. That's Sep Charlie; is that right, Jack?

a10a-1894203-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1894203-a2g.text: Sep Charlie at Sep. Let's stay in High Gain until that time. Over.

a10a-1900518-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1900518-a2g.text: I think you're lucky there in a Noun 05.

a10a-1900518-a2g.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1900518-a2g.text: Wait until you see the next one.

a10a-1900518-a2g.speaker: Lind
a10a-1900518-a2g.text: That's not bad for a young fellow.

a10a-1900518-a2g.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1900518-a2g.text: I told you. Wait until the next one.

a10a-1900518-a2g.speaker: Lind
a10a-1900518-a2g.text: You're just a show off; that's all.

a10a-1900518-a2g.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1900518-a2g.text: José can work with those optics.

a10a-1900518-a2g.speaker: Lind
a10a-1900518-a2g.text: Who's doing that, you or José?

a10a-1900518-a2g.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1900518-a2g.text: No. That's José; I'm just narrating here.

a10a-1900518-a2g.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1900518-a2g.text: Apollo 10, Houston. Our tracking data now shows you right in the middle of the fairway with a 6.53-degree entry angle. Over.

a10a-1900518-a2g.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1900518-a2g.text: Roger. Right in the middle of the corridor with 6.53. Roger.

a10a-1902123.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1902123.text: Houston, we checked Noun 61 and it looks loaded correctly now.

a10a-1902123.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1902123.text: Roger, 10. We're checking it.

a10a-1902123.speaker: Young
a10a-1902123.text: Roger. Our sextant - our alignment check sextant star on Nunki - the Auto optics put the star within the center of the reticle.

a10a-1902123.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1902123.text: Roger. Copy, John.

a10a-1902123.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1902123.text: Hello, 10. Noun 61 looks good to us.

a10a-1902123.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1902123.text: Alrighty.

a10a-1902123.speaker: Young
a10a-1902123.text: Roger.

a10a-1902123.speaker: Young
a10a-1902123.text: OK, Houston. EMS tests passed successfully.

a10a-1902123.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1902123.text: Roger. EMS. Thank you.

a10a-1902123.speaker: Young
a10a-1902123.text: OK. Houston, as I was driving the scroll down to - down to the pattern, the thing stopped scribing.

a10a-1902123.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1902123.text: Roger. She stopped scribing.

a10a-1902123.speaker: Lind
a10a-1902123.text: Say again, John.

a10a-1902123.speaker: Young
a10a-1902123.text: I say, the EMS stopped scribing as I was driving it down to the test pattern to set it up on the exit range.

a10a-1902123.speaker: Lind
a10a-1902123.text: Oh, you mean driving it down to 37 K?

a10a-1902123.speaker: Young
a10a-1902123.text: Yes. I can't get this one. I say it stopped scribing.

a10a-1902123.speaker: Lind
a10a-1902123.text: You say the needle's not scraping, or it's not driving in this tape?

a10a-1902123.speaker: Young
a10a-1902123.text: It's not - the tape is driving, but the needle is not leaving any mark.

a10a-1902123.speaker: Lind
a10a-1902123.text: Understand.

a10a-1902123.speaker: Young
a10a-1902123.text: I believe I'll go ahead and run it on down here anyway.

a10a-1902123.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1902123.text: Roger.

a10a-1902123.speaker: Lind
a10a-1902123.text: You might as well.

a10a-1902123.speaker: Young
a10a-1902123.text: Get some gs on it; it might work OK.

a10a-1902123.speaker: Lind
a10a-1902123.text: It's worth a try.

a10a-1902123.speaker: Young
a10a-1902123.text: OK. We're set up at 37 K.

a10a-1902123.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1902123.text: Roger. Maybe it'll come back in.

a10a-1902123.speaker: Young
a10a-1902123.text: On a non-exit pattern. [Long pause.]

a10a-1902123.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1902123.text: Houston, this is 10. Have I got a Go to activate the primary Evaps?

a10a-1902123.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1902123.text: Standby one.

a10a-1902123.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1902123.text: 10, Houston. Activate the primary Evaps.

a10a-1902123.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1902123.text: OK. Here goes.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Young
a10a-1903727.text: OK. Houston, we are going to maneuver to the Sep attitude now.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1903727.text: Roger. Maneuvering to Sep attitude.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1903727.text: Apollo 10, Houston. John, if you haven't already tried it, you might, on that EMS scroll, try running the tape back a half inch backwards and back and forth between the 37K line, and if that doesn't work, why, you can try the next pattern, and maybe this will break up that emulsion a little bit.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Young
a10a-1903727.text: Roger. Understand. Run the scroll back and forth between where and where? Over.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1903727.text: Make sure you run it backwards first, backwards no more than half an inch, and then forwards no more than the 37K line. Over.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Young
a10a-1903727.text: Roger.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Young
a10a-1903727.text: By golly, that fixed it. Good thought there. What I did was I had it on range set, I went back to test 5. Does that mean that I have to go all the way through the EMS counterclockwise anymore, or if I go to range set, will it still be initialized at 37K. Over.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1903727.text: Roger, John. Say again how far back you went please.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Young
a10a-1903727.text: About three-eighths of an inch.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1903727.text: Stand by one. [Long Pause.]

a10a-1903727.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1903727.text: Hello. Houston. This is 10.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1903727.text: Go ahead.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1903727.text: Roger. We're getting a lot of noise on the High Gain in this Sep attitude. How about me going to Sep at this time?

a10a-1903727.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1903727.text: Stand by.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1903727.text: Apollo 10, Houston. Let's go to Sep Charlie by the checklist. Over.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1903727.text: OK. We'll hold off on it, then; but it's awful noisy up here.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1903727.text: OK. Houston, we're going back to the initial Entry Interface attitude. This noise is about to drive us wild up here on that High Gain.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1903727.text: Roger, 10. It's OK to go Sep Charlie, now, if you'd rather.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1903727.text: OK. We can go there now, huh? OK. Because we're a little bit ahead of the checklist in going into this attitude. That's why I asked. OK. We'll go to Sep Charlie at this time.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1903727.text: Roger.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1903727.text: Apollo 10, Houston. It's not clear to us exactly what you did with the EMS. Will you describe it one more time so we can give you an answer? Over.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Young
a10a-1903727.text: Roger. I was on Range Set when you said wiggle it back and forth, so I went back to test 5 and brought it back approximately three-eighths of an inch toward 38K, and it started scribing. So I quit and went back to 37, and I'm now on test 5.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1903727.text: Roger.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Young
a10a-1903727.text: My question is...

a10a-1903727.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1903727.text: Go ahead with your question.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Young
a10a-1903727.text: Do I have to go through another scroll pattern or go clean through the EMS test to get it reset at 37K?

a10a-1903727.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1903727.text: Roger. We'll get an answer for you in just a minute.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Young
a10a-1903727.text: I think the answer is no.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1903727.text: Apollo 10, while we're coming up with that answer, we're ready to uplink a state vector. Can we have the computer? Over.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1903727.text: We're in CMC and Accept.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1903727.text: Roger. Thank you.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1903727.text: Apollo 10, Houston. We're a little delayed on our uplink. It'll be up momentarily. It's coming now.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1903727.text: 190:48:50 This is Apollo Control. Mark 1 minute to Entry Interface at which point the Apollo 10 will come back into the, effectively, the Earth's atmosphere at 400,000 feet [121,920 metres].

a10a-1903727.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1903727.text: Apollo 10, Houston. I have an update to your entry PAD. There are only five numbers that are different than the last PAD. Over.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1903727.text: OK, Jack. Take them one at a time, will you? And let me confirm them would you?

a10a-1903727.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1903727.text: OK. Our gamma at 400K is now 6.54. Over.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1903727.text: 6.54 gamma at 400K.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1903727.text: That's affirmative, and our RET at 0.05g is 00:27.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1903727.text: OK. That's affirmative. And the next three numbers are in the blackout block. Begin blackout at 00:17, end at 03:28, and drogues at 08:16, Over.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1903727.text: OK. I got begin blackout at 00:17, and blackout at 3:28, and drogues at 8:16.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1903727.text: That's affirmative.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1903727.text: Thank you.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1903727.text: 190:50:51 This is Apollo Control. To correct statement earlier in reading the clock it's now 57 minutes to Entry Interface, instead of 1 minute.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1903727.text: Houston, Apollo 10. Are you finished with the uplink? Over.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Lousma
