a10a-1903727.text: Apollo 10, we're finished with the uplink.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1903727.text: Roger. Back to Block.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1903727.text: Shows we got a 22.2-mile vacuum perigee. It looks good.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1903727.text: Roger, 10. And on your EMS, you can go directly to Range Set and it'll work. Over.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Young
a10a-1903727.text: Roger. Thank you. I thought it would.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1903727.text: And, Houston, we're ready to activate the secondary Evaps.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1903727.text: Apollo 10, Houston. Let's hold off until EI minus 50, about 6½ more minutes, for the secondary Evap. Over.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1903727.text: OK. We'll hold off.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1903727.text: 190:52:29 This is Apollo Control. Distance is now down to 9,136 nautical miles [16,920 km], velocity building up now at 19,128 feet per second [5,830 m/s].

a10a-1903727.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1903727.text: Apollo 10, Houston. We'd like to proceed with the VHF check now, and we're configured at the sites. If you'll transmit, well listen. Over.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1903727.text: Roger. We're reading you right now VHF and short count follows: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1903727.text: Roger. You came in way down in the mud. You faded out, then came back in.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1903727.text: Roger. You're about three by and down in the mud.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1903727.text: Roger. And I've got one more number to change on your entry PAD.

a10a-1903727.speaker: Young
a10a-1903727.text: It's OK to get on the S-band, huh, Jack?

a10a-1903727.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1903727.text: Roger.

a10a-1905431.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1905431.text: Hello, Houston. This is 10. How do you read?

a10a-1905431.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1905431.text: Read you loud and clear now, 10.

a10a-1905431.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1905431.text: OK. You're still down in the mud. Go ahead with that update.

a10a-1905431.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1905431.text: OK. The next change is on EMS range to go, should read 12061. Over.

a10a-1905431.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1905431.text: Roger. 12061.

a10a-1905431.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1905431.text: That's affirmative.

a10a-1905431.speaker: Young
a10a-1905431.text: OK. It sounds like you're transmitting on VHF and S-band, too, Jack. Could you go back to S-band only? Over.

a10a-1905431.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1905431.text: Roger. S-band only.

a10a-1905431.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1905431.text: Apollo 10, Houston. We have a change to your altimeter. Your Delta-H will be a plus 57. The recovery ship's on station, the aircraft are en route . Over.

a10a-1905431.speaker: Young
a10a-1905431.text: Roger. Plus 57.

a10a-1905431.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1905431.text: OK, Houston. I'm going to activate the secondary Evap.

a10a-1905431.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1905431.text: Roger, 10. Go ahead.

a10a-1905431.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1905431.text: [Garble] fire?

a10a-1905431.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1905431.text: Apollo 10, Houston. There's no change in the weather in the landing area; 2,500 [feet, 760 metres], scattered, and 10. Winds are 120 at 10 knots, a 3-foot [0.9 metres] swell, and we're coming up on our 45-minute check momentarily.

a10a-1905431.speaker: Young
a10a-1905431.text: Roger.

a10a-1905431.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1905431.text: OK, John. Stand by for a 45-minute check; 4, 3, 2, 1.

a10a-1905431.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1905431.text: Mark.

a10a-1905431.speaker: Young
a10a-1905431.text: OK. Thank you.

a10a-1905431.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1905431.text: Roger.

a10a-1905431.speaker: Young
a10a-1905431.text: We need a Go for Pyro Arm to check the RCS.

a10a-1905431.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1905431.text: OK, John. We're Go for Pyro Arm.

a10a-1905431.speaker: Young
a10a-1905431.text: Roger.

a10a-1905431.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1905431.text: Stand by to fire the Pyros; 3, 2, 1.

a10a-1905431.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1905431.text: Mark.

a10a-1905431.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1905431.text: Apollo 10, Houston. Both rings look good here.

a10a-1905431.speaker: Young
a10a-1905431.text: Roger. They look good to us, too.

a10a-1905431.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1905431.text: 191:05:52 This is Apollo Control. Some 43 minutes now from Entry Interface. Present distance 6,916 nautical miles [12,808 km] out. It's reported that Rescue Aircraft Numbers 1, 2, and 3, staging out of Samoa are now on station. Ground Elapsed Time now 191 hours, 6 minutes. Continuing to monitor air-ground as the crew approaches the separation time at the Entry Interface minus 15 minutes. Now 42 minutes from Entry Interface.

a10a-1905431.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1905431.text: 191:06:54 This is Apollo Control. Both rings of the Command Module Reaction Control System have been pressurized. Pyrotechnics are armed, both rings are showing normal pressure at this time.

a10a-1905431.speaker: Young
a10a-1905431.text: Houston, how'd it look?

a10a-1905431.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1905431.text: Youre looking real good there, John.

a10a-1905431.speaker: Young
a10a-1905431.text: Boy, it feels real good. It's a real crisp firing.

a10a-1905431.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1905431.text: 191:08:23 This is Apollo Control. The three rescue aircraft are C130 herkybird turboprop aircraft. Rescue 1 aircraft commander is Captain Jerald D. Parker of Barberton, Ohio. He is with the 76th Air Rescue squadron out of Hickam Air Force Base, Hawaii. Rescue 2, Captain John D. Ott, Milwaukee, Wisconsin, 79th Air Rescue squadron, Andersen Air Force Base, Guam. Rescue 3 aircraft commander is Captain Anthony A. Vanagas, of Carnei, New Jersey, 76th Air Rescue squadron, Hickam Air Force Base. 39 minutes to entry. Standing by on air ground live.

a10a-1911336.speaker: Young
a10a-1911336.text: OK, Houston. The bus ties are on the line okay. Tape recorder is going to rewind. And the Sun is setting just like you said.

a10a-1911336.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1911336.text: And here comes the Earth.

a10a-1911336.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1911336.text: Roger, 10. And the Batts look good.

a10a-1911336.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1911336.text: Roger. It's amazing to see an airglow on the horizon again. Over.

a10a-1911336.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1911336.text: Yes. You guys are a little out of your environment now aren't you?

a10a-1911336.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1911336.text: Yes. Didn't see that up there around the Moon.

a10a-1911336.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1911336.text: It's a good round one; I'll tell you that.

a10a-1911336.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1911336.text: 191:20:55 This is Apollo Control; present altitude, 4,296 nautical miles [7,956 km]; 27 minutes away from Entry Interface. About 12 minutes away from separating the Service Module from the Command Module; this takes place at 15 minutes prior to 400,000 feet (121,920 metres], or what is called Entry Interface. Still live on air-to-ground.

a10a-1911336.speaker: Young
a10a-1911336.text: OK, Houston. Were halfway through the Sep checklist, and were maneuvering to the separation attitude

a10a-1911336.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1911336.text: Roger. We're watching you.

a10a-1911336.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1911336.text: Houston, 10. Looks like we might have a primary Evap.

a10a-1911336.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1911336.text: That's affirmative, 10. Primary Evap is working.

a10a-1911336.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1911336.text: 191:27:06 This is Apollo Control, 21 minutes from Entry Interface...

a10a-1911336.speaker: Young
a10a-1911336.text: OK, Houston. We're in Sep attitude now. We've completed the Sep checklist.

a10a-1911336.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1911336.text: Roger, 10.

a10a-1911336.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1911336.text: OK, Houston. We're calling up Program 61.

a10a-1911336.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1911336.text: Roger, 10. Program 61.

a10a-1911336.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1911336.text: Apollo 10, Houston. We'd like to verify that the S-band power amp switch is in Low. Over.

a10a-1911336.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1911336.text: That's affirmative. It's been in Low.

a10a-1911336.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1911336.text: Thank you.

a10a-1911336.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1911336.text: Apollo 10, Houston. We'd like to update your landing cue card. You pass 90,000 feet [27,432 metres] at 06:26. Over.

a10a-1911336.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1911336.text: Roger.

a10a-1911336.speaker: Young
a10a-1911336.text: Roger. Thank you.

a10a-1911336.speaker: Young
a10a-1911336.text: I guess we have a Go for Pyro Arm here separate here, MSFN.

a10a-1911336.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1911336.text: That's affirmative, 10. You are Go for Pyro Arm.

a10a-1911336.speaker: Young
a10a-1911336.text: Roger.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: OK. We're showing Sep time.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1913240.text: Roger, 10. Go ahead.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1913240.text: OK. We'll go on and separate it about 30 seconds early. At 44:30.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1913240.text: Sep.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1913240.text: RCS transfer to Command Module.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: I think separation was nominal.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1913240.text: Roger, 10. We copy.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1913240.text: 191:33:59 This is Apollo Control. Good separation has been confirmed. Apollo 10 just crossing the West Australian Coast and a long track toward the splashdown point, 350 nautical miles [650 km] east of Pago Pago, American Samoa. Leaving air-ground live for any transmissions that do take place prior to entry and beginning of black out.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: OK, Houston. That was a good Sep.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1913240.text: Roger, 10. We confirm a good Sep.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: What happened there was it had started out EMS, and I wonder how to reinitialize that. Do we run all the way through the test pattern?

a10a-1913240.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1913240.text: Stand by. We'll get an answer for you.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1913240.text: 191:37:29 This is Apollo Control. Present altitude, 1,385 nautical miles [2,565 km].

a10a-1913240.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1913240.text: Apollo 10, Houston. On the EMS situation, best thing to do is to go counterclockwise on your switch back around to test 5, then advance to the next non-exit skip pattern.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: Roger.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1913240.text: Reset your range and your V 0 , and you're ready to go again. Over.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: Roger. That's what I figured.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1913240.text: 191:38:31 This is Apollo Control...

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: And it's scribing right now.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1913240.text: Roger, 10. We copy.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1913240.text: 191:38:53 This is Apollo Control, the discussion has to do with the Entry Monitor System in which a visual display is given to the crew for describing the entry range to go from Entry Interface. Apparently, the thing has sorted itself out, certain amount of levity here in the control room as the recovery plot television display shows the Red Baron on station.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1913240.text: 36,395 - 36.4, John, is what you're looking for. There's the Moon.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: I don't understand it. The son of a bitch is already [garble].

a10a-1913240.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1913240.text: Boy, we sure are moving with respect to the Moon.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1913240.text: [Garble] we still pitching to the entry attitude.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1913240.text: Ok.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: That water boiler's yawing us. That's what it is.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: Got to go clean through this one.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1913240.text: Yes.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1913240.text: [Garble] The check satisfy you, John - or can you see anything?

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: I can't see the horizon out there. Might be able to when it's dark-adapted.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1913240.text: OK, you got 10 minutes to go - about 9 minutes. There's the Moon and there's Mars - Jupiter.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1913240.text: Just as we left him, huh?

a10a-1913240.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1913240.text: OK, Gene-o, you've got it set at f:11, 250th. Are you [garble] the power on?

a10a-1913240.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1913240.text: Yes.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: T.P., you got a lot of guts to sit here and watch this.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1913240.text: Huh?

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: You got a lot of guts...

a10a-1913240.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1913240.text: No.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: ...to sit here and watch. I can't stand it. It's driving me out of my mind.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1913240.text: What do you mean?

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: OK, here we go. We're back...

a10a-1913240.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1913240.text: OK, John, the numbers; V I0 is 364.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1913240.text: 191:40:42 This is Apollo Control. The Red Baron has been replaced now by the Apollo Range Instrumented Aircraft ARIA number 5. However, the small sketch of an airplane looks right out on the recovery plot strangely looks like a Sopwith Camel.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: I don't want that. I want the other one.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1913240.text: You want the range?

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: Yes.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: Also, can you set that time?

a10a-1913240.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1913240.text: I'll get it.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: Let me get right at the attitude to see if I can see anything on the horizon here.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: OK, Houston. We're approaching the entry attitude.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1913240.text: Roger, 10.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: How many minutes to - to Entry Interface here?

a10a-1913240.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1913240.text: 1206.1. There you go - 8 - 7 minutes and something. 1206.1. Oh shit.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1913240.text: There you go. John.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: OK.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1913240.text: Ready - go - go to D 0 .

a10a-1913240.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1913240.text: So you get 36...

a10a-1913240.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1913240.text: 395. if you can read that close.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: Entry.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1913240.text: Entry. And Normal.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1913240.text: And Normal.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: Yes. Normal.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1913240.text: There you go.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1913240.text: Look at that rascally thing yaw us off.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1913240.text: Yes.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1913240.text: They're really boiling water, both of them.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: What we're doing up here in entry attitude is just compensating for a little water boiling off.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1913240.text: You want to turn the light down real quick, John?

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: Yes, turn it down just a hair.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1913240.text: I got that fixed on there, too.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: Fixed?

a10a-1913240.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1913240.text: Turn those on.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: I can't see a freaking thing. It doesn't make a difference [garble]. I ain't going to check that bunch. That's...

a10a-1913240.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1913240.text: Yes.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: ...asinine. There's nothing we can do about it anyway.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1913240.text: Yes.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: Turn the goddam light back on.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1913240.text: Hell, I feel like I'm really pulling gs.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1913240.text: Yes, I do, too.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: [Garble] not pulling any gs...

a10a-1913240.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1913240.text: OK. We're showing 0.0664.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: Houston, could we have a Mark at 5 minutes to RRT? Over.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1913240.text: Roger. Mark. 5 minutes at RRT.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: OK, Entry and Normal

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: And we're all set up in EMS configuration, ready to go, and I believe it's going to work.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1913240.text: Roger. We copy.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1913240.text: And we're in P63. I'm sure you can read it on your DSKY, and R-to-go is decreasing, and V I is increasing. Everything looks good. Over.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1913240.text: Roger, 10.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: Want me to check out all that - directions?

a10a-1913240.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1913240.text: Yes.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: [Garble].

a10a-1913240.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1913240.text: OK.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: [Garble].

a10a-1913240.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1913240.text: About the only thing you got left when it gets there is Rate Command and the CMC in Auto.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: Si, si.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1913240.text: The rest is up to you, babe.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: The rest is up to you, machine.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1913240.text: Apollo 10, we missed your Mark at 5 minutes. 4 minutes and 50 seconds coming up.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1913240.text: Mark.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: OK.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1913240.text: 191:44:19 This is Apollo Control. Four minutes, 34 seconds to entry; 18 minutes, 34 seconds to splash.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1913240.text: Is R circular? Yes, 208.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: 208. OK, now, we're at - Pyro's are not armed right now, and at 50K, we're going to arm those...

a10a-1913240.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1913240.text: [Garble].

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: ...and we'll go to Boost Entry on this here R thing right here. That's what we do next.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1913240.text: OK: And I'll be looking for it, John.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: Gene, pull your shoulder harness in if you didn't already because it's certainly going to be a good ride.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1913240.text: When do you go to Boost Entry on that thing, John?

a10a-1913240.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1913240.text: Huh?

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: Did he miss our mark at...

a10a-1913240.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1913240.text: It doesn't say here.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1913240.text: 50K [ft, 15,000 metres].

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: Yes, does...

a10a-1913240.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1913240.text: It sounds like you switched antennas there, Jack, and we missed your mark. He gave us a mark at 04:50, didn't he?

a10a-1913240.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1913240.text: 191:45:08 This is Apollo Control. We're estimating S-Band communications blackout at 18 seconds after Entry Interface which is about 3 minutes, 37 seconds from this time.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1913240.text: Yes, yes, I did quite a while ago.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: I'll get this yaw over there where it belongs. Get my head where it belongs, too. How's that pressure holding on Reg 1? Good? How's it on Reg 2?

a10a-1913240.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1913240.text: 191:45:54 This is Apollo Control. Velocity now up to 35,317 feet per second [10,764 m/s] climbing about 10 feet [3 metres] each second or so as the display turns over. Range to go 23,000 no - as you were. Move the decimal point over, 2,292 nautical [miles, 4,245 km].

a10a-1913240.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1913240.text: Beautiful. No difference - about 3300. The temperature's good; the pressure's good; and the manifolds are both good.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: OK, and we're Go here.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1913240.text: [Garble}...

a10a-1913240.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1913240.text: Apollo 10, Houston. Spacecraft and guidance looking real good from here. We'll be attempting to contact you again after blackout at 328. Over.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: Roger. You working through an ARIA now?

a10a-1913240.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1913240.text: Negative. Not yet. We will be then, however.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: Roger. OK. The guidance is coming in. Looks good.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1913240.text: Roger, 10.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1913240.text: We're going to pull some gs, baby.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1913240.text: 191:47:32 Apollo Control here. 35,927 feet per second [10,950 m/s], increasing rapidly. 1,845 nautical [miles, 3,417 km], range to touchdown.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1913240.text: We're another minute.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1913240.text: Yes.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1913240.text: 191:47:56 Mark. 1 minute to Entry Interface.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1913240.text: One minute, 10. You're looking good.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: Roger.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1913240.text: Starting to trim much?

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: No. We're still coming down like a stone.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1913240.text: You feel the gs?

a10a-1913240.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1913240.text: No. Here's our range to go. We're going to be there sizzling in about - at this distance - in about 30 seconds. All we got left to go is your Rate Command, three of them, and CMC in Auto.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: Yes.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1913240.text: And watch the sky turn blue out there.

a10a-1913240.speaker: Young
a10a-1913240.text: I ain't looking out. I'm keeping my head right where it belongs. Entry and Normal. OK.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1914853.text: 191:49:03 Mark, Entry Interface. Velocity 36,331 [fps, 11,074 m/s] still increasing; downrange to splash point, 1,315 nautical miles [2,435 km].

a10a-1914853.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1914853.text: OK. Stand by for re-ent - Oh, look at that.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1914853.text: Look at that. God damn. God damn. [Garble]...

a10a-1914853.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1914853.text: Look at that. Just looks like daytime. 0.2, 0.3, 0.4 - We're trimming in good.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1914853.text: We had S-Band blackout on predicted time; about 17 or 18 seconds after Entry Interface. Estimate coming out of the blackout at 3 minutes, 29 seconds after Entry Interface at 400,000 feet [121,920 metres]. Maximum g loading of the spacecraft and crew will be in the neighborhood of 6.7 gs. Drogue parachute deployment now predicted for 8 minutes, 17 seconds Retro Elapsed Time or Entry Elapsed Time in this case, since there has been no retrofire from a lunar return mission. All aircraft in the primary recovery area are on station. Splashdown will be approximately 25 minutes prior to local daylight

a10a-1914853.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1914853.text: Oh, you'd better believe here comes some gs. Here comes the water, too. Just sit back anyway.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Young
a10a-1914853.text: Here comes the water, too. Just sit back anyway.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1914853.text: You got to be kidding, José. That...

a10a-1914853.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1914853.text: OK baby; you keep flying it.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1914853.text: [Garble] my hand controller. John, it's looking good...

a10a-1914853.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1914853.text: Is this a long [garble] - Oh, we're starting [garble].

a10a-1914853.speaker: Young
a10a-1914853.text: Start to roll. Go, machine. It's rolling good.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Young
a10a-1914853.text: It's fine; it's good. It knows just what it's doing.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1914853.text: It knows just what it's doing.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Young
a10a-1914853.text: Go on. Keep that lift vector down.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1914853.text: Oh, man. That - the first one was a bitch...

a10a-1914853.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1914853.text: Coming up on 26 - Heck, we're only 2.5 gs.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Young
a10a-1914853.text: [Garble]. We're in good shape. Good shape. Good shape. OK...

a10a-1914853.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1914853.text: Two minutes past Entry Interface. About a minute and 29 seconds left in blackout. Velocity now 36,363 feet per second [11,083 m/s]. Apparently that was the last velocity in tracking prior to blackout.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Young
a10a-1914853.text: OK, now we'll pick it back up. There it goes.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1914853.text: Look at that fireball when you do that. God dang!

a10a-1914853.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1914853.text: Program 67 - it's looking good. Still says keep the lift vector up, baby. And we got 60 miles (111 km) to go, and we're 4.2 north. 4.4, 28 miles (52 km). 16 [garble] command to roll attitude.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1914853.text: Going a little north. You got a 5 undershoot. Now we're back like - just like the simulator.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1914853.text: OK, I'll give you a hack when we're out of blackout, John. We got 20 more seconds. We're just about out.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1914853.text: OK, it's looking good. 12 north - 13 north, 5 to go.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Young
a10a-1914853.text: EMS is working good. It's just right on the money.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1914853.text: God, what a fireball. Boy, look at that mother.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1914853.text: 191:52:32 Should be out of blackout at this time. We have a first report that Samoa rescue 1 aircraft, staging out of Hickam Air Force Base, has a visual contact. We have a report of visual contact from Air Boss 3 on station near the Princeton.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1914853.text: Coming back up, it says let's roll left. baby, to about half left. It says 60 degrees left. She's doing good. Just coming right on the old pike. OK. It says plus 20; and we got to go south and start...

a10a-1914853.speaker: Young
a10a-1914853.text: Golly, looking out of the window; it's beautiful.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1914853.text: Isn't that a beautiful purple? Golly, that's pretty!

a10a-1914853.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1914853.text: It's going to increase the bank; you got a little overshoot; and we're coming from north to south at 77 degrees.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Young
a10a-1914853.text: Yes, we're only pulling one g now. 1.5 gs.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1914853.text: OK, you're out of blackout, John.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Young
a10a-1914853.text: Houston, this is Apollo 10 out of blackout. How do you read? Over.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1914853.text: You're through ARIA, so - Look at that. That's beautiful.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Young
a10a-1914853.text: Houston, Apollo 10, through blackout transmitting in the blind. EMS is working properly. The CMC is working properly. The g meter; we're working properly, and I guess we are, too.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1914853.text: 81 degrees [garble] angle. We're 10 north decreasing we're 9 north. 19 downrange - we're 4 off the downrange end. 8.9 to the north. 18 overshoot. We're coming in just beautifully.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1914853.text: 191:53:45 It's reported from the Princeton that they on board the prime recovery vessel have visual contact of Apollo 10. Apparently that is radar contact rather than visual. No confirmation of visual at the present time.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1914853.text: This is our second peak, Gene-o.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Young
a10a-1914853.text: OK, we're going down on peak g again.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1914853.text: We have another peak to come in.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Young
a10a-1914853.text: OK, it's - this [garble] - it's only - it's only up to 2 gs now - 3 gs. 2.5.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1914853.text: Here comes the water again on my feet [laughter).

a10a-1914853.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1914853.text: Man, it's got the cross range right out.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1914853.text: [Garble]. It's going to pulse the lift vector up.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Young
a10a-1914853.text: 4 gs. Going to go lift vector up.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1914853.text: We'll let her shoot, lift vector up.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1914853.text: It says you better roll right, then left.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Young
a10a-1914853.text: OK, Houston, we're showing 6 miles [11 km] short right now, and we're coming on in. Pulling about 4 gs. This machine is flying like crazy. Boy, it's really great.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1914853.text: Roger, 10. We copy, and we've got you on TV.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Young
a10a-1914853.text: [Laughter.] Well I tell you, this thing is beautiful.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1914853.text: It shows a 2 miles [3.7 km] overshoot, 1.7 [nautical miles, 3.1 km], 1.2 [nm, 2.2 km] cross range.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Young
a10a-1914853.text: And we're pulling about 3½ gs now. We're rolling right 60 degrees, and we're practically on top of the target. EMS is reading 21 miles [39 km] to go. Come down - looks like it's - We're about 150K [feet,45,720 metres] right now.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1914853.text: Steam pressure. Get the steam pressure...

a10a-1914853.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1914853.text: OK, we ought to be hitting 90 K [feet, 27,432 metres] any minute.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Young
a10a-1914853.text: You get the steam pressure yet?

a10a-1914853.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1914853.text: I'm watching it. No. But there's their 90K [feet, 27,432 metres] time right now.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1914853.text: No. I didn't get the steam pressure, but that's their 90K [feet, 27,432 metres]. We're past it.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1914853.text: Apollo 10. If the Princeton's there, we're going to be there shortly.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1914853.text: OK, there goes the steam pressure.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Young
a10a-1914853.text: OK, we show 90K [feet, 27,432 metres] right now.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1914853.text: Man, is that thing ever flying!

a10a-1914853.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1914853.text: OK, see what's 50K [feet, 15,240 metres] time. OK.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1914853.text: OK, I'd estimate 50K [feet, 15,240 metres] here pretty quick, John. You ought to be off the - off the - thing here pretty...

a10a-1914853.speaker: Young
a10a-1914853.text: They're coming off the peg; we're at 60K [feet, 18,288 metres] right now.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1914853.text: OK, latitude is minus 15.09; longitude, 164.68. Over. 50K [feet, 15,240 metres] Pyros Armed.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Lousma
a10a-1914853.text: Apollo 10, Houston. You're coming in broken, but we still have you visual. Over.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1914853.text: OK. we ought to get drogues here at...

a10a-1914853.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1914853.text: OK. there's 8 minutes. We ought to get drogue on ground time in 17 seconds.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1914853.text: You can see the altitude. John?

a10a-1914853.speaker: Young
a10a-1914853.text: We're only pulling a g, you guys.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1914853.text: How about your ELS Auto Logic. On. Huh?

a10a-1914853.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1914853.text: Drogues ought to be coming out on their time.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1914853.text: God damn! There's the drogues! There they are. babe.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Young
a10a-1914853.text: God damn. we're on the drogues.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Young
a10a-1914853.text: Rock, rock, old baby; rock, rock. This son of a gun...

a10a-1914853.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1914853.text: You want me to kill the Rate Command. There's sunrise out there.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1914853.text: Houston, Apollo 10. We've got good drogues.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Young
a10a-1914853.text: OK, we're going through 18,000 [feet, 5,500 metres] right now.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1914853.text: OK, Boost/Entry on those valves, babe.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1914853.text: 191:57:45 It's reported from the prime recovery vessel Princeton that they heard a sonic boom from Apollo 10. Samoa Rescue 2 aircraft has S-band contact. A lot of speculation as to whether the item in the television picture from the ship is actually the spacecraft or the Service Module.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1914853.text: Can you get them? OK. Sun's just coming up.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Young
a10a-1914853.text: OK, go through that VHF checklist.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1914853.text: OK, VHF Antenna is Recovery. VHF A is coming to Simplex. VHF A is Simplex. VHF Beacon is On. Get your light on, Tom. Postlanding Beacon, low. Put it on. They'll find us faster.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1914853.text: 191:59:13 Recovery aircraft 3 has a visual with the spacecraft on parachutes. A lookout on board the Princeton reports sighting the spacecraft on the main parachutes. We're still about 25 minutes away from sunrise at the Princeton.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Recovery 2
a10a-1914853.text: This is Recovery 2 with the recovery beacon showing 2252 also have a visual on the light.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1914853.text: OK, did you get the purge done?

a10a-1914853.speaker: Photo 1
a10a-1914853.text: This is Photo 1. All three chutes are deployed normal.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1914853.text: We're [garble]. We got fire out. We got fire out. [Garble].

a10a-1914853.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1914853.text: 192:00:27 It's reported from photographic aircraft in the area that all three chutes are deployed, which is quite obvious from the television coming from the prime recovery vessel. It's early twilight, early morning dawn at the ship. Still enough daylight to see the spacecraft.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Young
a10a-1914853.text: OK, we show ourselves coming through 5,000 feet [1,500 metres].

a10a-1914853.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1914853.text: ...Tom, I got fire out the right window.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1914853.text: Houston, we have [garble] when we hit the water, goes out.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Young
a10a-1914853.text: [Garble] transmitting in the blind. We show ourselves at 15.07, minus 164.65.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1914853.text: Want to close this? Do you want...

a10a-1914853.speaker: Air Boss
a10a-1914853.text: Apollo 10, this is Air Boss. Over.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Young
a10a-1914853.text: Roger, Air Boss. Read you loud and clear.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Air Boss
a10a-1914853.text: Roger. Reading you loud and clear. Say again your position. Over.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1914853.text: Roger. We're 15.07 west, 164.67. We should be right on top of your carrier.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Air Boss
a10a-1914853.text: Roger. Understand. Right on top. We have good beacon on you, and we have good chutes on you. Over.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Air Boss
a10a-1914853.text: Apollo 10, Air Boss. Give us a call when passing through 5 [thousand feet, 1,500 metres] and 3,000 [feet, 900 metres]. Over.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Air Boss
a10a-1914853.text: Air Boss 3 control [garble] first pilot position.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Air Boss
a10a-1914853.text: 3,000 [feet, 900 metres]; Roger. Marking it, and I did not get your latitude initially. Over.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1914853.text: I never got to copy it, babe.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1914853.text: 1507 at 16467 [15.07° south, 164.67° west]. We should be right on top of you if you're down there.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Air Boss
a10a-1914853.text: That's affirmative. You are - Repeating - 15.07 and 164.67.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1914853.text: OK, John; stay in Dump until 800 feet (240 metres]...

a10a-1914853.speaker: Photo 1
a10a-1914853.text: This is Photo 1. I'm about level with you, Apollo 10. I'm following you down.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1914853.text: Roger, this is Apollo 10. [Garble]. We are in great shape. Over.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Air Boss
a10a-1914853.text: This is Air Boss, and we have two helos in your immediate vicinity. We're closing all other forces. Over.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Stafford
a10a-1914853.text: Roger. We're 1,500 feet [450 metres] and everything is Go.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Air Boss
a10a-1914853.text: Airborne aircraft, this is Air Boss. Position from Princeton...

a10a-1914853.speaker: Cernan
a10a-1914853.text: Tell them we're going off the air. Bus Ties [Garble].

a10a-1914853.speaker: Recovery 3
a10a-1914853.text: This is Recovery 3. Splashdown was Stable 1. Repeat, Stable 1.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1914853.text: And we had splashdown at 192 hours, 3 minutes, 25 seconds approximately. The spacecraft is in stable 1, that is apex up, about 4 miles [7 km] estimated from the Princeton.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1914853.text: Latest estimate now 3 miles [5 km] from the Princeton.

a10a-1914853.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1914853.text: This is Apollo Control. Recovery Helicopter Number 3 is now presently on approach to drop swimmers. The swim team, first one to go out in the jumping order will be Boatswain Mate First Class J. L. Boisvert of Imperial Beach, California who was also, involved in Apollo 6 recovery. Second man out will be Seaman Michael G. Mallory, of Alderwood Manor, Washington. Number 3 man out will be Lieutenant Junior Grade Wesley T. Chesser of Arlington, Virginia. We'll rejoin what readable conversation there is between Air Boss and the crew of Apollo 10 through the carrier.

a10a-1921133.speaker: Young
a10a-1921133.text: OK, rescue, this is Apollo 10. Take your time and take it easy. We've got a good sea state and we want you all to be careful.

a10a-1921133.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1921133.text: Recovery 3 moving into position for dropping the first swimmer; Recovery 3 is piloted by Commander Charles B. Smiley, of Chula Vista, California. Co-Pilot is Lt. Jay Scott Walker of Long Beach, California, who was also involved in the Apollo 8 recovery operation.

a10a-1921133.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1921133.text: First swimmer has jumped into the water.

a10a-1921133.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1921133.text: This is Apollo Control; we had confirmation that all three swimmers are in the water.

a10a-1921133.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1921133.text: This is Apollo Control; the 3 swimmers in the water presently are attaching the flotation collar underneath the Command Module.

a10a-1921133.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1921133.text: Flotation of the collar now approximately half way around the spacecraft.

a10a-1921133.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1921133.text: Princeton reported now 2,000 yards (1,830 metres] away from the spacecraft and making its approach. Flotation collar now being inflated.

a10a-1921133.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1921133.text: Inflation of the flotation collar complete.

a10a-1921133.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1921133.text: Three swimmers are now sitting on the collar, that flotation collar that's supporting the Command Module. The landing platform helicopter Princeton, carrier Princeton, affectionately known by its crew as "Sweet Pea" is skippered by Captain Carl M. Cruse of Woodville, Texas, who coincidentally is a distant cousin of Orange Team Flight Director Pete Frank. To go back and review splash time; 192 hours, 3 minutes, 25 seconds.

a10a-1921133.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1921133.text: We've had confirmation from the recovery vessel Princeton that the Command Module hatch has been opened and the Apollo 10 crew egress is likely to take place as they climb out onto the raft and await pickup by the recovery helicopter.

a10a-1921133.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1921133.text: 192:29:24 Recovery vessel Princeton now estimates 1,100 yards (1,000 metres] from the ship to where the Command Module is floating.

a10a-1921133.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1921133.text: One crewman of Apollo 10 is out on the raft as reported from the ship, unknown at this time which one it is.

a10a-1921133.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1921133.text: It's reported that all three crewmen are now in the raft awaiting pickup by the recovery helicopter.

a10a-1921133.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1921133.text: Helicopters now moving into position to lower the net for picking up the crew.

a10a-1921133.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1921133.text: The device lowered from the helicopter is known as a Billy Pugh net.

a10a-1921133.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1921133.text: Here in Mission Control the room is getting rather crowded as people from the back rooms and off-duty flight controllers move in to watch the recovery operations on the 10 by 10 television projector which is showing the commercial TV from the prime recovery vessel on the front screen of Mission Control Center. There goes the first astronaut up into the helicopter in the Billy Pugh net.

a10a-1921133.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1921133.text: One crewman aboard, second one will be picked up momentarily as the helicopter lowers the net for the second pickup.

a10a-1921133.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1921133.text: Second crewman being hauled up now in the Billy Pugh net toward the Recovery 3 helicopter.

a10a-1921133.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1921133.text: Third and last crewman is now being hoisted up into the helicopter.

a10a-1921133.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1921133.text: This is Apollo Control. A few moments ago Manned Spacecraft Center Flight Operations Director Chris Kraft shouted across the control room to Rear Admiral Fred E. Bakutis, who is commander of Manned Spacecraft Recovery Force, Pacific, Carrier Task Force 130 his congratulations for a job well done in the Princeton recovery area. Recovery Aircraft number 3 now approaching the Princeton.

a10a-1921133.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1921133.text: Flight Controllers here in Mission Control gathering ever more tightly here, crowding around looking at the large 10 by 10 television projector at the front of the Mission Control Center as the helicopter lands on the deck of the Princeton awaiting the crew stepping out of the chopper onto the carrier. On deck at 41 minutes past - 31 minutes past the hour. I think the boxes of cigars are being broken out here in Mission Control as the helicopter touches down on deck.

a10a-1921133.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1921133.text: NASA Administrator Thomas. O. Paine here in the Control Center, as is Manned Spacecraft Center Director Dr. Robert Gilruth. Almost elbow to elbow in here. Cigars are beginning to light up all around the room. [Applause onboard the recovery ship.]

a10a-1921133.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1921133.text: Great deal of applause here in Mission Control as the crew steps out of the helicopter; control room is elbow to elbow, from door to door. Cigars have been passed around, I have no estimate on boxes of cigars. On the center screen, 10 by 20 scribing projector, we have a large American flag, 20 feet wide - next to that is the Apollo 10 crew patch on a 10 by 10 projector. Here in Mission Control, they just hung the Apollo 10 patch along with the rest of the manned Apollo mission patches, up next to the ceiling, along one sidewall; there's a large number of American flags on all the consoles, lot

a10a-1921133.speaker: Mission Control
a10a-1921133.text: This is Apollo Control. This Control Center I doubt could hold more than about 3 more people, pandemonium personified; cigars, cameras, flags, people, lot of exhilaration, exuberance here, hand shaking, congratulations going in all directions, various people among the Department of Defense, and the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, after a very successful lunar mission, a predecessor to lunar landing in Apollo 11. At 192 hours, 49 minutes Ground Elapsed Time; this is Apollo Control, signing off.
